summary: Stage 3: feed live CoCo audio via cross-core SPSC ring (IRQ consumer)
description:
Fourth stage of PIZERO-35. Switch the IRQ-side encoder (PIZERO-38) from the synth sine to the live coco_machine_audio_read() ring. This moves the ring DRAIN from core 0 to the core-1 DMA IRQ -> core 0 producer, core 1 consumer. Verify coco_machine's ring is a clean single-producer/single-consumer ring callable from IRQ context; if not, add a minimal SPSC read entry point (head/tail indices with __dmb() on the producer side) in lib/coco_machine. Correctness item: no torn reads, no lost/duplicated samples, hold-last-sample on underrun as today. [2026-06-08 DONE (commits 008486c + 9f495d4). Made the ring true SPSC: writer (audio_emit) owns g_audio_w only + __dmb publish; reader (coco_machine_audio_read) owns g_audio_r, does reader-side overflow catch-up, __dmb, and is RAM-resident (.time_critical) for the IRQ. summary: Sound matches desktop XRoar in pitch and tone
description:
OPEN. A/B on hardware (SOUND 159,255): desktop xroar plays a clean, correctly-pitched square wave; the PiZero plays it ~1 SEMITONE SHARP and BUZZIER/more-distorted. Discovered after PIZERO-38/39 fixed the HDMI delivery warble + overflow fast-forward.

PROVEN **NOT** an HDMI-delivery / clock issue:
* HDMI_STD_TIMING (standard 25.2MHz pixel / 252MHz sysclk) changed NEITHER the pitch NOR the buzz -> not the off-spec 24MHz pixel clock.
* This sink IGNORES HDMI ACR entirely: CTS 25176 -> 26674 -> 50000 (would be ~1 octave if honored) had ZERO audible effect on pitch. So PIZERO-32's ACR lever is inert on this monitor.
* AUDIO_OUTPUT_LPF (re-enable the 2-pole TV-bandwidth filter) did NOT change the buzz.
* Streaming ring telemetry is healthy under the residual (fill~RING/2, skips=0), so it is not a ring over/underrun artifact.
Therefore BOTH the pitch and the buzz are SOURCE-side (emulation / resampler), not delivery -- which is good news (software-fixable).

INVESTIGATE (in order):
1. CONFIRM CONFIG FIRST (cheapest, likely cause of the semitone): what machine/ROMs is the user's DESKTOP xroar running? PiZero = NTSC Tandy CoCo, bas12.rom + extbas11.rom, 6809 @ 0.895MHz (EVENT_TICK_HZ 14318180/16). A Dragon, a different CoCo model, or PAL on desktop would by itself shift SOUND's pitch ~6% (SOUND is a CPU-timing-loop tone). If configs differ, that IS the semitone -> fix is config, not code.
2. MEASURE THE SOURCE NUMERICALLY via the pizero_wavmeas env (no HDMI; only the WAV-dump drains the ring; boots clean BASIC; autotypes SOUND159,255; streams base64 WAV over USB-CDC). Decode + analyse on host for EXACT fundamental freq + spectrum. CAVEAT: the dump arms only when Serial/DTR is asserted -> capture with a DTR-asserting reader (pyserial), and UPLOAD BEFORE attaching any reader (a reader holding the CDC port blocks the 1200bps BOOTSEL reset; also pass --upload-port /dev/cu.usbmodem2101 so pio doesn't grab the wrong cu.* port).
3. If the source is genuinely sharp: compare the resampler rate constants (COCO_AUDIO_RATE=48000, EVENT_TICK_HZ=14318180, COCO_AUDIO_CPUCLK_X4) and the 6809 cycle timing vs desktop xroar; for the buzz, inspect the integrate-and-dump square rendering (lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp audio_emit/audio_integrate) vs xroar's filtered output.
V1.0 audio-quality item. Discovered during PIZERO-38/39. [2026-06-16 PARTIAL on HW via PIZERO-45's in-spec 60Hz/252MHz clock: user reports audio 'sounding better in general' but NOT clearly as clean as desktop xroar -> the in-spec sink clock helped some but did NOT fully close the residual. Confirms the gap is largely SOURCE-side (resampler/square rendering) as suspected; pursue the pizero_wavmeas numerical measurement + resampler/cycle-timing comparison next.]

[2026-09-17 Summary rewritten in the PIZERO-107 triage, move 4, to say what this delivers rather than how. Previous summary: "Audio fidelity vs desktop xroar: live CoCo SOUND ~1 semitone sharp + buzzier (SOURCE-side, not HDMI)"]

[2026-09-17 RE-TEST FIRST, do not re-investigate. Two things changed since this was written: PIZERO-45 moved the machine to in-spec 60 Hz timing, and PIZERO-119 removed a sustained 0.9% audio delivery shortfall that had the stream repeating a sample 250-650 times a second. Either could account for the buzz. Also carry the PIZERO-118 leftover: confirm tone>0 appears in the telemetry while something audible plays, which has never been observed.]

[2026-10-16 FIRST MEASUREMENT OF THE REAL HDMI OUTPUT. A $9 HDMI-to-USB capture stick ("Guermok USB3 Video", shows up in macOS as an AVFoundation device) records the board's HDMI audio bit for bit: L and R identical sample for sample, silence is exact digital zero, 48000 Hz s16. Capture: ffmpeg -f avfoundation -i "none:Guermok USB3 Video" -t 15 -c:a pcm_s16le cap.wav (the video side can't be opened while another app is viewing it, but the audio side can). 13.3 s of DAC music (board 50D37286DD1820A6, product firmware, [aud] tone=8460/s, under=0, skips=0): clean, band-limited square waves; no clipping; no isolated sample glitches (the 4 candidates were short, smooth musical pulses); edge timing is sub-sample (fractional edge phase spread across the sample, not snapped to it); edges and sample differences are evenly spread across the 800-sample video frame, so no 60 Hz frame-locked artifact. Level is low: peak 6921 (-13.5 dBFS), RMS about -28 dBFS. The user says it sounds great through the stick. So the source is clean as delivered. Still to do: capture SOUND 159,255 and measure its pitch against desktop XRoar to settle the semitone claim; then compare against what the development monitor does with the same stream (its sink, which ignores ACR, may be where the earlier buzz lived).]

[2026-10-16 PITCH SETTLED, SOURCE CLEAN. SOUND 159,255 captured off the HDMI stream. Reference from the Color BASIC 1.2 ROM ($A964-$A98F): each period is four DAC writes ($7E, $FE, $7E, $02), each step 7+2+5+4+5*(256-159)+5 = 508 cycles, plus 8 for LDX/BNE: 2040 cycles = 438.7 Hz at 894886 Hz before the 60 Hz IRQ. Board: steps measured at 508/509 and 514/515 cycles (cycle exact), mean 437.5 Hz; every 16.7 ms one step runs about 129 cycles long (BASIC's IRQ handler, authentic). So the old 'one semitone sharp' is gone (a semitone would be 6%; we are 0.3% low, which the IRQ explains). CAPTURE STICK CAVEAT: the stick (MacroSilicon, 'Guermok USB3 Video') delivers only about 42,600 samples per second while labelling them 48 kHz, and drops whole 512-sample blocks (about 11 a second) to get there. The same 42,592/s was measured with an Apple TV as the source, so it is the stick, not our stream (we send CTS=25200 N=6144 at 25.2 MHz, encoding checked in lib/libdvi/dvi_data_island.c dvi_di_set_acr). Anyone analysing captures from it must expect a 14,000-count jump at each dropped block and must not read those as firmware glitches; segments between drops are bit exact. Remaining observations, not defects: level is low (music peaked at -13.5 dBFS; SOUND peaks about -11 dBFS), and (corrected later the same day) ACR goes out on every vblank line, about 2,700 a second, not once per frame as first written here; see PIZERO-32.]

[2026-10-16 DONE, user confirmed. Pitch is cycle exact against the ROM, the waveform is clean, and the user says it sounds great through the capture stick. The low output level was filed as PIZERO-230; the ACR send rate was noted (and corrected) on PIZERO-32.]

summary: Investigate full 60Hz HDMI output (monitor compat + correct game speed)
description:
OPEN / discussion. Current refresh = 24MHz pixel / (880x525) = ~51.95Hz -- off-spec; some monitors may reject a non-60Hz signal (consumer-QA exposure). KEY CLARIFICATION: this is NOT a render-speed limit -- core 0 has ~4ms/frame slack (cpu ~13.5ms of 19.25ms) and rendering a whole line at a time is cheap; the refresh is set by the TMDS timing (pixel clock x total pixels), independent of how fast we render the framebuffer. The 24MHz pixel = sysclk/10 and sysclk=240MHz is forced by PIO-USB (needs 120/240MHz).\n\nPaths to 60Hz:\n(a) PIO-USB at ~252MHz: sysclk 251.75MHz -> 25.175MHz pixel -> STANDARD 640x480p60 (800x525) AND keep USB. BEST outcome if PIO-USB tolerates ~252MHz (its bit-banging timing is calibrated for 120/240 -- UNCERTAIN; needs a HW experiment). FIRST EXPERIMENT: build 252MHz + true 800x525 60Hz timing + USB enabled; check DVI stable @60Hz and whether the USB keyboard enumerates.\n(b) Reduced-blanking 60Hz at 24MHz: 800x500 = exactly 60.0Hz, keeps USB, but vblank=20 lines is non-standard (CVT-RB-ish) -> may HURT monitor compat (opposite of the goal) and squeezes the audio-island back porch. Lower confidence.\n(c) USB-less standard timing: 252MHz + true 800x525 60Hz, universal monitor compat, but DISABLES USB keyboard/gamepad (PIO-USB) -> not shippable for a console. Diagnostic/fallback only.\n\n60Hz BONUSES beyond monitor compat: game speed becomes correct (CoCo NTSC = 59.92Hz; at 52Hz we run ~13% slow) and audio cadence simplifies (48000/60 = 800 samp/frame). NB: the off-spec 24MHz is also the root of PIZERO-41's source-side... no -- 41 is source-side, independent. Decide after the (a) PIO-USB-at-252MHz experiment, which is the highest-value test.

[2026-06-16 IN-PROGRESS -- Path (a) experiment built (env pizero_60hz, flag HDMI_60HZ_TEST): 252MHz sysclk (vreg 1.25) + true 800x525 timing @ 25.2MHz pixel = 60.0Hz + USB host ENABLED, on the no-audio base (the audio build's wide h_bp=130 can't fit in 800-total, so this test drops audio). ENCOURAGING FINDING: Pico-PIO-USB computes its dividers from clock_get_hz(clk_sys) (no hard 120/240 assert), and 252MHz divides EXACTLY (252/48=5.25, /6=42, /12=21, /96=2.625 -- all representable in the PIO 16.8 divider), so 252 should give a CLEAN 48MHz USB bit clock, not jittery. Builds (RAM 96.8% -- double-buffered base, tight but fits). HW test BLOCKED: the upload failed mid-flash (recurring USB-drop flakiness during the 1200bps reset) and left the board USB-dead (no CDC, no BOOTSEL) -- needs manual BOOTSEL (hold BOOT + plug) to flash via picotool. PENDING: flash pizero_60hz via BOOTSEL; check (1) monitor locks 60Hz, (2) usb= after a COLD boot with keyboard attached (warm-reboot usb=0 would be ambiguous vs the known warm-reenum flakiness). If both pass -> 60Hz+USB achievable; then re-fit audio (likely needs ~277MHz to keep the wide audio back porch at 60Hz, or a different island placement).

[2026-06-16 *** PATH (a) CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE *** pizero_60hz flashed: sys=252000kHz, fps=60, and usb=1 -- PIO-USB ENUMERATES at 252MHz (comes up usb=0 for ~1s then locks usb=1). USER CONFIRMED: monitor locks 60Hz and looks right, keyboard works. So 60Hz + USB host + correct game speed ALL coexist at 252MHz -- the central blocker is SOLVED. (No sound in this test build, as designed.)

NEXT (audio re-fit at 60Hz) -- and a better plan than 277/288MHz: stay at 252MHz/800-total but reshape blanking to fit ONE streaming island (PIZERO-38 uses 1 packet/active line, not the old 3). At h_total=800: h_fp=8, h_sync=96, h_bp=56, h_active=640 -> h_bp=56 = 28 words, and one island needs ~27 words (preamble4+guard1+island16+guard1 + video-preamble4+guard1). FITS. So: 252MHz + 60Hz + streaming audio is geometrically possible without a higher overclock. Also set AUDIO_SAMPLES_PER_FRAME=800 (48000/60) and single-buffer fb. BONUS to check: at STANDARD 60Hz timing the sink clock is now in-spec, which may also change PIZERO-41's pitch/buzz. Plan: make a pizero_stream variant at 252MHz/60Hz/h_bp=56; if clean, promote 60Hz to the default and retire the 24MHz/52Hz timing.

Findings written up in docs/hdmi-audio-notes.md. The implementation (promote 60Hz to default WITH streaming audio re-fit at h_bp=56) is split into PIZERO-45.]

summary: Promote 60Hz to default: re-fit streaming audio at 252MHz/60Hz (h_bp=56)
description:
OPEN / implementation (follows PIZERO-44, which CONFIRMED 60Hz+USB work at 252MHz). Goal: a single 60Hz product build with streaming HDMI audio, then make it the default and retire the off-spec 24MHz/52Hz timing. Strict upgrade: standard 640x480p60 (monitor-friendly) + correct game speed + keeps USB + audio.

PLAN (all at 252MHz, vreg 1.25 -- proven by pizero_60hz):
1. TIMING: 800x525 @ 25.2MHz = 60.0Hz, but split blanking to fit ONE streaming island in the back porch: h_fp=8, h_sync=96, h_bp=56 (=28 words), h_active=640. (PIZERO-44 confirmed one island needs ~27 words; the no-audio test used h_bp=48 which is too narrow for an island.)
2. AUDIO: enable HDMI_DATA_ISLAND + HDMI_STREAM_AUDIO; set AUDIO_SAMPLES_PER_FRAME = 800 (48000/60, was 924 at 52Hz); single-buffer fb (audio build already does). The streaming pool/meter/IRQ-encode path is unchanged -- only the cadence constant + timing.
3. PACING: CYCLES_PER_FRAME/FRAME_PERIOD_US for exactly 60fps (16667us; ~14915 cyc @ 0.894886MHz).
4. Likely a new flag (e.g. HDMI_60HZ that implies the timing) composed with the streaming build; or fold 60Hz into the default pizero_stream and drop HDMI_60HZ_TEST/the 52Hz path once validated.
5. VERIFY ON HW: monitor locks 60Hz, keyboard enumerates (usb=1, check after a COLD boot), audio plays, fps=60, no warble, watchdog/freeze-log intact. BONUS to listen for: standard in-spec sink clock may reduce PIZERO-41's residual pitch/buzz.
6. On success: make 60Hz the default build, retire the 24MHz/52Hz timing + the now-redundant diagnostic envs (coordinate with PIZERO-42 cleanup), and update docs/BUILD.md + docs/hdmi-audio-notes.md + README/product-plan.
RISK: h_bp=56 is tight for the island (28 words vs ~27 needed) and h_fp=8 is a short front porch -- if a monitor balks, fall back to ~277/288MHz to keep the wider h_bp (288/48=6.0 exact, also clean for PIO-USB) at the cost of a higher overclock. Refs: docs/hdmi-audio-notes.md (60Hz section), PIZERO-44. [2026-06-16 IMPLEMENTED, build-verified (RAM 70.4%), awaiting HW listen/look-test. summary: Document emulation pacing & CoCo high-speed (SAM double-speed) behavior
description:
Write up how guest CPU speed-up holds up end-to-end, since the pacing model is non-obvious and the headroom limit is real. Key findings (verified in code): (1) No host fast-forward toggle; the only double-speed is the CoCo's own SAM high-speed POKE (POKE 65495/65497, address-dependent vs full), implemented in vendored XRoar mc6883.c (8 ticks/fast cycle vs 16). (2) coco_machine_run_cycles paces by FIXED EMULATED TIME per frame, not fixed instruction count: run_cpu_with_audio sets cycles_remaining = cycles*16 TICKS (coco_machine.cpp:793) and each mem access subtracts ncycles ticks (:486). So a frame always advances CYCLES_PER_FRAME*16 = 238640 ticks ~= 16.667ms emulated time regardless of SAM speed. (3) Therefore audio pitch and video are correct BY DESIGN (samples are tick-keyed -> still 800/frame in fast mode; no resampler distortion; the hdmi-audio-notes 'fast-forward distortion' was a separate startup ring-overflow bug). (4) The real limiter is core-0 host headroom: fast mode executes ~2x as many 6809 cycles within the same per-frame budget, so emulation host cost ~doubles (README perf ~9.4ms -> ~18.8ms est) and exceeds the 16.67ms frame budget (only ~31% slack at 1x). Pacing then resyncs/drops the deficit -> guest runs slower than 2x AND the audio ring under-produces vs the real-time core-1 consumer -> underruns after ~1s. Threshold ~1.6-1.7x: address-dependent (~1.3-1.5x) likely squeaks by; full ~2x overruns. Video stays 60Hz (decoupled core 1) but shows the lag. (5) Not yet characterized on-device -- next step is to measure via the per-second [run] fps/cpu/blit serial telemetry (PIZERO-15) under a tight high-speed-POKE loop, and decide whether to cap/ignore the full-speed bit. New doc docs/cpu-speed.md; cross-link from docs/pipeline.md and README Performance.

[2026-09-29 CORRECTION from the PIZERO-172 documentation sweep] The findings above describe the SAM double-speed POKE as working but costly. It has no effect at all: coco_mem_cycle (lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp) charges a flat 16 ticks for every RAM, ROM and I/O access, so the guest always runs at 1×. That is PIZERO-132. docs/cpu-speed.md now says so and frames the headroom analysis as what honoring fast mode would cost.

summary: Map USB numeric-keypad HID usages (0x53-0x63) to CoCo keys
description:
src/main.cpp hid_table_init() only maps the main keyboard HID-usage block (0x04-0x52); keypad usages 0x53-0x63 all hit the 0xFF no-mapping sentinel and are silently dropped, so a numeric keypad produces nothing. Fix: extend g_hid_to_dscan -- KP1-9 (0x59-0x61)->K_1..K_9, KP0 (0x62)->K_0, KP Enter (0x58)->K_ENTER, KP . (0x63)->K_DOT, KP - (0x56)->K_MINUS, KP / (0x54)->K_SLASH; leave Num Lock (0x53) and the shifted KP * / + (0x55/0x57) unmapped initially. Works if the keypad enumerates and speaks boot protocol (default already HID_PROTOCOL_BOOT). To use keypad AND main keyboard together via a hub, also enable -DCFG_TUH_HUB=1 (keep CFG_TUH_HID=4). Conditional fallback only if hw test shows it sends no mappable 8-byte report: tuh_hid_parse_report_descriptor in mount_cb. Verify on hw: keypad digits echo in BASIC, KP Enter runs a line.

[2026-09-28] Built as part of PIZERO-163: kt_translate maps keypad usages 0x54-0x63 (/ * - + Enter 1-9 0 .) to their characters whatever Num Lock says. Close with 163's hardware check.

summary: Quick header joystick -> CoCo port 0 (ADC axes + new coco_machine joystick API)
description: No joystick path exists in the port (coco_machine exposes only press/release_key). Add a quick joystick wired to the free header pins, independent of USB. Recommended hw: analog thumbstick module -- X->GPIO26 (ADC0), Y->GPIO27 (ADC1) (only free ADC pins; ADC2/3 are USB D+/D-), fire->GPIO3 (digital, internal pull-up, active-low), mapped to port 0 (right CoCo game port). Alt: digital switch/D-pad (full-throw). Firmware: new coco_machine_set_joystick_axis(port,axis,0..65535)/set_joystick_fire(port,bool) in coco_machine.h; add js_axis[2][2] (default 0x8000) + js_fire[2] to g_m; extend coco_pia0_preread_a (coco_machine.cpp:131) to overlay the DAC comparator onto PIA0 PA7 using CB2/CA2 selectors per upstream coco3.c:joystick_update; fire button into PA0/PA1 row line (verify wiring vs ~/github/xroar). Sample adc_read GPIO26/27 (12->16bit <<4) + fire GPIO each frame in loop(); init adc/gpio in setup(). Gate behind -DJOYSTICK_HEADER so default product env is unaffected. Verify: PRINT JOYSTK(0) sweeps 0..63, fire registers. [2026-06-28 DEMOTED to low / FALLBACK: user prefers the USB-gamepad route (PIZERO-13) with a controller they already have. Keep this as the hardware-independent backup if PIO-USB won't enumerate the controller. Build this issue's coco_machine joystick-injection API FIRST regardless -- PIZERO-13 reuses it; only the GPIO/ADC read-path is specific to this fallback.] [2026-07-19 BUMPED back to high / PREFERRED player-1 route: user now favors wiring a REAL CoCo joystick (2x 500k pots + 1-2 buttons) directly to the RP2350 header as a 'hat'. Authentic feel, sidesteps the USB CPU budget entirely (no hub needed), and lands in the same DAC-comparator injection API. Note the pots wire as dividers to 3.3V; only ADC0/ADC1 (GPIO26/27) are free, so one stick (X+Y) is clean but a second analog stick needs an external mux (74HC4051 or I2C ADC on I2C0 6/7). Calibrate observed ADC span in firmware. Build the coco_machine injection API first as before.] [2026-07-19 REAL-JOYSTICK WIRING DETAIL: The stick is passive -- 2 pots + a switch, no active parts; all the cleverness (DAC ramp + comparator) is emulated in firmware, so the hw job is just read 2 pots + 1-2 buttons. Connector exposes 5 signals: X wiper, Y wiper, +V (pot top rail), GND (pot bottom + button common), Fire (switch->GND). DIN-5 pin NUMBERING VARIES across CoCo1/2/3, left vs right port, 1- vs 2-button -- BUZZ OUT the actual connector with a multimeter, do not trust a pinout table (find wipers by watching R-to-rail change as the stick moves; button by continuity when pressed). KEY RULE: power the pot top rail from the board 3V3, NOT 5V -- each pot is just a divider, so 3V3 makes the wiper sweep 0-3.3V (exactly ADC range) and keeps 5V off the not-5V-tolerant GPIO; DO NOT connect the stick's original +5V wire. Wiring (one stick -> right/port 0): pot top->3V3; pot bottom/GND->GND; X wiper->GPIO26/ADC0; Y wiper->GPIO27/ADC1; Fire->GPIO3 (input, internal pull-up, active-low = LOW when pressed); optional 2nd button->any free GPIO (same pull-up+to-GND pattern). GOTCHAS: (1) 500k is a HIGH source impedance for the SAR ADC (~125k at mid-throw, far over spec) -> slow-settling/noisy reads; fix cheapest-first: ~10nF cap from each ADC pin to GND (charge reservoir + noise filter), then lengthen ADC sample time, then (overkill) op-amp follower per axis. Only 6-bit needed (JOYSTK 0-63) so cap+slow-sample suffices. (2) never route the stick's +5V pin to an ADC pin; keep every signal <=3.3V (the 3V3-rail move handles this). (3) CALIBRATION: real pots don't sweep full-scale (~0.3-3.0V typical) -> firmware learns/observes per-axis min/max, applies center+deadzone, maps to 0-63. PLAYER 2: no ADC left after 1 stick (2 axes = both free channels); options: 74HC4051 8:1 analog mux (3 select GPIOs funnel all 4 axes through 1 ADC channel, sampled sequentially/frame) OR external I2C ADC e.g. ADS1115 4ch on I2C0 (SDA6/SCL7). Either fine at 60Hz; defer until player-1 proven.]

summary: Unplug and replug USB without rebooting the machine
description:
Implementation of the fix diagnosed in PIZERO-11b (child of it). On this rev3 board the disconnect is invisible to line_state/connected/ep_error/ints (the PIO SM pins the bus at J/FS); instead, an unplugged device makes PIO-USB flood ~180 byte-identical phantom HID reports/sec (HW-confirmed 2026-06-29). DESIGN: (1) DETECT -- in tuh_hid_report_received_cb (src/main.cpp), per (daddr,idx) track the previous report bytes + a consecutive-identical counter; when >=N identical reports arrive in a row (phantom flood; N~50-100, i.e. <~0.5s at 180/s), declare the device gone. A real boot keyboard sends reports only on key transitions, so it never trips; tune N against a real device held-key case (held key = repeated identical reports too -> may need 'identical AND rate>threshold', or exclude the held-key case by requiring the report to be the IDLE/all-zero report, since the phantom is the SM-held idle line). (2) RECOVER -- on detection, call pio_usb_host_stop() then pio_usb_host_restart() (both in pio_usb.h) to tear down + re-enumerate the root port so a freshly-attached or replugged device mounts cleanly; reset g_usb_devices / per-interface phantom counters. (3) SAFETY -- gate behind a flag (e.g. -DUSB_HOTPLUG_RECOVER); keep OFF the freeze-prone hot path (PIZERO-33); the stop/restart touches the shared PIO1 while libdvi runs on PIO0/core1 -- validate it does NOT wedge video/audio or trip the watchdog. PRE-WORK: add report-PAYLOAD logging to confirm phantom reports are byte-identical/idle (current diag build only COUNTS them). VERIFY ON HW: cold-boot keyboard works; unplug -> within ~1s a '[usb] re-enumerating' log + pio restart; replug (or attach a different device) -> [usb] device attached + usb=1 + rpts resumes on keypress; video stays 60fps, no freeze. ALTERNATIVES already RULED OUT by PIZERO-11b: E9-drain re-enable (line is driven, not leaking) and transfer-error detection (no errors fire). Parent PIZERO-11b. Roadmap: docs/ROADMAP.md. [2026-07-22 IMPLEMENTED (flag-gated, awaiting HW confirm). src/main.cpp: per-(daddr,idx) consecutive-byte-identical-report counter (hotplug_note_report); >=USB_PHANTOM_FLOOD_N (default 100, ~0.55s @180/s) identical reports on an interface sets g_usb_recover_pending. loop() handles recovery AFTER USBHost.task() returns (not nested in the tuh callback): logs the flood, usb_release_all_keys() to drop stuck keys, pio_usb_host_stop()+pio_usb_host_restart(), zeroes g_usb_devices + resets the tracking runs. All gated behind -DUSB_HOTPLUG_RECOVER; new env pizero_hotplug (extends pizero_stream_60). Detection lives outside hid_keyboard_apply so real keystrokes (report changes) reset the run and never trip it. Builds clean (pizero_hotplug RAM 70.6%); default pizero_stream_60 unchanged (all code #ifdef'd out). docs/BUILD.md env table + flag matrix updated. TODO on HW: cold-boot kbd works; unplug -> '[usb] phantom flood ... re-enumerating' within ~1s; replug/new device -> [usb] device attached + rpts resumes; video stays 60fps, watchdog doesn't trip. RISK to watch: whether the tuh layer above pio-usb needs extra reset after stop/restart, and the held-key false-positive (mitigate by requiring the idle/all-zero report or raising N if a real device ever floods identical). Payload logging still to add if the phantom turns out non-idle. Then curate diag per PIZERO-42.] [2026-07-22 HW TEST #1 -> ROOT-CAUSE REFINED. Boot+kbd OK; unplug stopped input (flood detected); replug re-lit the keyboard LEDs but NO keystrokes. Diagnosis: pio_usb_host_stop()/restart() only cancel/resume the PIO SOF timer -- they never touch the TinyUSB tuh layer, so the stale device stayed mounted and our receive_report stayed armed on a dead address; the replug re-enumerated only electrically. CONFIRMED in the vendored libs: TinyUSB's pio-usb HCD (hcd_pio_usb.c pio_usb_host_irq_handler, a strong override of the lib's weak symbol, called from the SOF service pio_usb_host.c:349) only umounts on PIO_USB_INTS_DISCONNECT, and pio-usb only raises that from connection_check() when the line reads SE0 -- which never happens here (SM pins J/FS). FIX v2 (flashed): drop stop/restart; add usbdiag_force_disconnect() in src/usb_hotplug_diag.c that replicates connection_check()'s disconnect branch (connected=false, suspended=true, raise DISCONNECT int, retire in-flight transfers). Effect: next SOF service -> HCD umount frees the address; and because clearing connected RELEASES the SM, the connect-check (pio_usb_host.c:335) then reads the line's TRUE state -- SE0 while empty (no phantom re-attach), FS/LS idle once a real device is replugged -> clean CONNECT + fresh enumeration -> tuh_hid_mount_cb re-arms reports. This is grounded in the PIZERO-11b observation that a RELEASED SM reads SE0 on an empty bus (only pinned J/FS while polling). Also added phantom-payload logging to the recovery line (pre-work) and let tuh_umount_cb/mount_cb own g_usb_devices. Builds clean (RAM 70.6%), flashed to /dev/cu.usbmodem101. AWAITING HW TEST #2: unplug -> '[usb] phantom flood ... forcing disconnect' + '[usb] HID unmount'/'device removed'; replug -> '[usb] device attached'/'HID mount'/'receive_report armed' + rpts resumes on keypress; video stays 60fps, watchdog freezes= unchanged.] [2026-07-22 HW TEST #2 -> force-disconnect WEDGES the port; PIVOT to reboot-recovery. With fix v2 (usbdiag_force_disconnect), a 30s serial capture across unplug+replug was DEAD FLAT: usb=0 conn=1 ls=J/FS rpts=0 ints=0, ZERO [usb] events, no re-enum. Mechanism: force-disconnect clears connected, but the SAME SOF connect-check (pio_usb_host.c:335, needs !connected) immediately RE-LATCHES connected=true off the phantom J line (on this rev3 board the released SM still reads J/FS when EMPTY -- E9 leak -- NOT the SE0 I'd hoped, contradicting the transient-SE0-during-reset observation for the steady state); tuh then tries to enumerate a non-existent device, fails, and the port is WEDGED (connected=1, usb=0, no endpoint polling) -- unrecoverable, because connection_check needs SE0 to clear connected (never comes) and the flood detector needs polling to re-fire (gone). CONFIRMED IMPOSSIBLE: a clean full re-init -- the pio-usb TinyUSB HCD implements NO hcd_deinit and pio-usb exposes no host_deinit (pio_usb_host_init re-claims PIO SMs on a 2nd call). CONCLUSION: on this board the USB line is unusable as a presence signal (reads J whether present or absent), the only proven enumeration path is a COLD BOOT, and there is no in-place re-enumeration primitive. FIX v3 (flashed): RECOVERY = REBOOT. On phantom-flood detection, tag scratch[4]=USB_REPLUG_MAGIC and watchdog_reboot(0,0,30) -> cold-boot enumerates whatever is attached at reset (~2s, automatic). setup() recognizes the sentinel and reports '[usb] re-enumeration reboot' WITHOUT counting it as a PIZERO-33 freeze (carries the freeze tally across). Strictly better than status quo (today an unplug wedges USB and needs a MANUAL power-cycle). TRADEOFF: the running emulator state is lost on a device swap. Builds clean (RAM 70.6%), flashed. AWAITING USER DECISION on the reboot tradeoff + HW test: cold-boot kbd works; unplug -> '[usb] phantom flood ... rebooting'; board auto-reboots ~2s; whatever's plugged at reboot enumerates (usb=1, keys work); '[usb] re-enumeration reboot' banner; freezes tally NOT bumped. NOTE: header-joystick (PIZERO-50) sidesteps USB entirely for player-1 and avoids this whole class of problem.] [2026-07-22 RESULTS-TO-DATE SUMMARY + confidence review (do NOT treat this ticket as closed; fluid USB still being pursued). Reassessing after the user flagged that test attention/sequencing was loose -- separating mechanism-proven facts from possibly-artifactual observations.
SOLID (source- or schematic-confirmed, not just a single HW observation):
  * Phantom-flood DETECTION works and is the only reliable presence signal (a gone device floods ~180 identical idle HID reports/s; a real one reports on change). Keep this regardless of recovery method.
  * pio_usb_host_stop()/restart() cannot recover: they only cancel/resume the PIO SOF timer and never notify the TinyUSB tuh layer (verified in pio_usb_host.c + hcd_pio_usb.c). [was fix v1]
  * No clean in-place USB host re-init: the pio-usb TinyUSB HCD implements NO hcd_deinit and pio-usb exposes no host_deinit (a 2nd pio_usb_host_init re-claims the PIO SMs). tuh_deinit/tuh_init exist but the pio-usb backend doesn't support deinit. (source-confirmed)
  * NO software VBUS switch on the PIO-USB host port: board header has no USB-power pin, vendor demo never toggles one, and docs/RP2350-PiZero-schematic.pdf shows the PIO-USB connector VBUS hardwired (no load-switch/enable-GPIO). So the device cannot be power-cycled under firmware control. (schematic-confirmed)
SHAKY (single observations, possibly test-sequence/human-error artifacts -- NEED clean re-test):
  * 'force_disconnect (fix v2) WEDGES the port' (usb=0 conn=1 flat for 30s). The capture may have started already-wedged, or the physical unplug/replug may not have landed in the window; the flood->force-disconnect was never watched fire LIVE. Re-test needed before calling force-disconnect dead.
  * 'A warm/watchdog reboot does NOT re-enumerate' -- CONTRADICTED by HW test #1, where the very first warm picotool flash DID come up with the keyboard working. The later usb=0 warm-reboots all happened AFTER the port was (maybe) wedged, so warm-reboot-fails may be a symptom of the wedge, not a general rule. If a CLEAN watchdog reboot re-enumerates an attached device, fix v3 (reboot-recovery) is viable -- possibly with a good swap UX (reboot, then a deliberate few-second window to insert the new device before USB init).
CONFIRMED HW FACT: cold power-cycle WITH keyboard attached always enumerates + types (user, multiple times).
CODE STATE: all experiments are flag-gated behind -DUSB_HOTPLUG_RECOVER / env pizero_hotplug; default product build pizero_stream_60 is untouched and re-flashed to the board. main.cpp currently carries fix v3 (flood-detect -> watchdog_reboot with scratch[4]=USB_REPLUG_MAGIC sentinel so setup() reports a replug-reboot, not a freeze) plus the usbdiag_force_disconnect() shim (fix v2, now unused by loop()). NOT reverted -- kept for the re-test.
NEXT / RE-TEST PLAN:
  (T1 ISOLATION -- does a warm/watchdog reboot re-enumerate an ATTACHED device? zero unplug variables): flash pizero_wdtest, COLD-boot with keyboard (confirm usb=1 + keys), let the ~10s self-test hang -> watchdog warm-reboots with the keyboard STILL attached -> check usb= after. usb=1 => warm reboot enumerates => fix v3 path is alive. usb=0 => reboot-recovery is dead, focus shifts.
  (T2 confirm/deny the force-disconnect wedge, watched LIVE): flash pizero_hotplug@v2 (force_disconnect), cold-boot (usb=1), then unplug while monitoring serial in real time -- watch the flood line + force-disconnect fire, and whether a replug ~5s later mounts (rpts resumes) or wedges.
  (T3 if T1 passes): refine v3 with a deliberate post-reboot insertion window + retest the real swap flow.
Header-joystick (PIZERO-50) remains the USB-free player-1 path in parallel, but USB fluidity is NOT abandoned.] [2026-07-22 T1 RESULT (clean isolation test) -> reboot-recovery CONFIRMED DEAD; VBUS is the crux. Flashed pizero_wdtest, user COLD-booted with keyboard (keys work, so device fine + attached). Captured 3 consecutive watchdog WARM-reboots (freeze #3/#4/#5) with the keyboard NEVER unplugged. EVERY post-reboot boot came up usb=0 rpts=0 conn=1 -- the attached keyboard did NOT re-enumerate after a warm/watchdog reboot, 3x in a row. This is a controlled test (no unplug/replug timing variables), so it SETTLES the earlier shaky finding: a warm reboot does NOT re-enumerate. Fix v3 (watchdog_reboot on flood) is therefore non-viable. (Reconciles with HW test #1's 'warm flash worked' only if the board had been cold-booted at some point that session; the controlled test overrides it.) KEY MECHANISTIC OBSERVATION from the capture: each post-boot [usb-evt] shows the line transiently reading SE0 (line=J/FS -> SE0 -> J/FS) during the port-reset window EVEN WITH THE KEYBOARD ATTACHED -- proving the stack's SE0/disconnect detection is NOT broken; it simply never sees SE0 on a physical unplug because unplug leaves D+/D- FLOATING (E9 leak -> reads phantom J), not low. ROOT TRUTH (now solid): only a real VBUS power-cycle enumerates this device; every host-side software path (re-init, reset, warm reboot) fails because the DEVICE is never power-cycled, and there is no software VBUS switch (schematic-confirmed). FORWARD PATH for fluid USB (needs a small HW mod, matches user's willingness to solder): add a GPIO-controlled load-switch/P-FET on the HOST-PORT VBUS (keeping D+/D- wired). Mechanism hypothesis: cutting VBUS while data stays connected leaves the unpowered device's 1.5k pull-up inactive, so the host's D+/D- pulldowns win -> the line reads a GENUINE SE0 -> pio-usb connection_check fires DISCONNECT -> tuh umounts cleanly; restoring VBUS -> device cold-starts, asserts pull-up -> line J -> CONNECT -> fresh enumeration -> mount, WITH EMULATOR STATE PRESERVED (no reboot). Because VBUS control yields honest line states, a pulse-until-mounted retry loop is safe (no phantom wedge). Firmware: on flood-detect, pulse VBUS off ~200ms then on; retry until a device mounts or timeout. RISKS/UNKNOWNS to validate: (a) does the host port actually have 15k D+/D- pulldowns so VBUS-cut reads SE0 despite E9 (check schematic detail / measure)? (b) inrush on VBUS restore; (c) which spare GPIO + switch part. ALTERNATIVE zero-solder probe of the same idea: a powered hub with per-port power switching (PPPS) could cut a downstream port's VBUS in software -- but needs CFG_TUH_HUB (PIZERO-54) + hub PPPS support. CODE: fix v3 still in tree (flag-gated); to be reworked toward the VBUS-pulse design or reverted once HW path chosen. Board re-flashed to default pizero_stream_60 after the test.] [2026-08-16 HW TEST of fix v3 (pizero_hotplug) -> reconfirms reboot-recovery is dead; adds one NEW source-confirmed bug. Board cold-booted OK (usb=1, spacewarp running, 60fps). User did one unplug/replug. THREE results, all solid:\n  (1) NEW BUG -- the scratch[4] sentinel CANNOT work: scratch[4] is RESERVED by the pico-SDK. watchdog_reboot(pc=0,...) sets scratch[4]=0 in its else branch (hardware_watchdog/watchdog.c:108), wiping USB_REPLUG_MAGIC written immediately before it; watchdog_enable() also claims it (WATCHDOG_NON_REBOOT_MAGIC, watchdog.c:84). So every deliberate replug-reboot logged as '*** FREEZE RECOVERED ***' and INFLATED the PIZERO-33 freeze tally (reached 4 in one session). FIX if any reboot path is ever kept: move the sentinel to scratch[2] (unused; 0=WD_MAGIC, 1=phase, 3=freeze count). summary: Firmware config/launcher overlay UI ("BIOS" menu over HDMI, function-key toggle)
description:
No way to choose what to load without a rebuild/flash; media is fixed at build time (AUTORUN). Add a firmware-drawn overlay menu -- NOT emulated 6809 code -- that the port renders directly into the HDMI framebuffer, toggled by a function key (or a key held at boot). Scope: (1) input hook -- reserve a hotkey (e.g. F12 / Menu) in the HID path (src/main.cpp) that raises an overlay flag without reaching the guest; (2) render -- REUSE the real MC6847 alphanumeric renderer so the menu IS a native CoCo text screen (not a lookalike): render_alpha_frame() in coco_machine.cpp:924 already walks a 32x16 grid, pulls each glyph from the authentic font_6847t1[] char ROM into g_m.vdg_buffer, green-on-black, and flows through the existing coco_boot_blit_vdg_pizero() -> DVI path. Approach: REFACTOR render_alpha_frame(base) to accept a source pointer (const uint8_t *screen) instead of reading g_m.ram+base (~5-line change to the one chrow= line + expose it in the header) so the overlay owns a PRIVATE 512-byte screen-code buffer and never clobbers guest video RAM (the paused game's screen is preserved behind the menu). Alt (simpler, rejected): write into emulated text RAM 0x0400 and save/restore 512 bytes. SELECTION HIGHLIGHT is free: bit 6 of a screen code = inverse video (black-on-green, the iconic BASIC look) -- set it on the selected row's bytes, zero extra render code. Optional fancy border: bit 7 set -> SG4 2x2 semigraphics colour blocks. CONSTRAINTS (both authentic, lean in): uppercase-only 64-glyph set (ch&0x3F|0x40 -> @,A-Z,punct,0-9; no lowercase) needs a tiny ASCII->screen-code map; 32 cols x 16 rows grid (header + ~13-14 file entries + footer hint; long filenames truncate/scroll). Flow: fill menubuf (uppercase codes, bit6 on selected row) -> render_alpha_frame(menubuf) -> vdg_buffer -> existing pizero blit. COST is ~free: render ONCE per cursor change (not per frame) while emulation is paused, so the PIZERO-48 headroom concern does not apply -- a single alpha-frame render on each keypress. pause/freeze emulation while open; (3) SD browse -- list images on the microSD (SPI pins SCK30/MOSI31/MISO40/CS43, hw_config) filtered by type (cas/dsk/rom/cart); (4) actions -- load+mount selected image and (re)boot the machine; expose a few firmware-only settings the guest can't reach: SAM high-speed cap (see PIZERO-48), joystick source (USB gamepad vs header hat vs off, see PIZERO-50), audio env; (5) persist last selection/settings to SD or flash. Design the SD-listing + image-loader layer as a clean reusable module so a future in-emulator 'same-feel' CoCo-ROM launcher (v2, much larger lift) can reuse it. Gate the whole feature behind a build flag initially; validate it does not disturb 60Hz video / audio while open (emulation is paused, but the overlay composite runs on the same core-0 budget -- see PIZERO-48 headroom). Cross-link docs/ROADMAP.md. Depends on nothing hard; pairs naturally with SD work. [RE-SCOPED 2026-08-05: the disk-image SWITCHING half is now PIZERO-81 (F12 launcher, keyboard-driven, sub-sliced 81a-81d) and last-launched persistence is PIZERO-82. PIZERO-53 remains the SUPERSET -- the firmware-only settings menu (SAM-speed cap, joystick source, audio env) -- built on PIZERO-81's overlay renderer and state machine. ALSO: this ticket's planned 'small source-pointer refactor' of render_alpha_frame is UNNECESSARY -- coco_boot_blit_vdg_pizero_src(const uint8_t*, uint16_t*) already exists at coco_boot.h:76, and PIZERO-81b's card renderer draws font_6847t1 glyphs directly rather than reusing render_alpha_frame at all. Settings persistence still needs PIZERO-67.]

[2026-10-11 CLOSED at ~80% in the tracker clean-up. The overlay exists (F9 to F12 lists, F1 INFO, pad navigation: PIZERO-81, 153, 156, 169), and the firmware-only settings this ticket listed are in /coco/settings.txt with an on-screen editor (PIZERO-145, 146), which the user chose over a settings GUI. Last-launched persistence is PIZERO-82. Nothing concrete is left here that is not owned elsewhere, so no remainder is filed.]

summary: USB hub support: simultaneous keyboard + gamepad via external hub (CFG_TUH_HUB)
description:
Board has no internal USB hub and one root port (PIO-USB D+=28/D-=29). To use more than one USB device at once (e.g. keyboard AND a USB gamepad, or keyboard+keypad per PIZERO-49) an EXTERNAL hub is required. Enable TinyUSB hub support: -DCFG_TUH_HUB=1 and raise device/interface counts (keep CFG_TUH_HID>=4); ensure g_usb_devices tracking + the mount/unmount and report-received paths handle multiple daddr/idx pairs (they are already keyed per (daddr,idx)). RISK: PIO-USB is CPU-heavy and shares the fabric with libdvi; core-0 has only ~31% slack at 1x (PIZERO-48), and more endpoints = more polling cost. Must validate under load that video stays 60fps and audio does not underrun, and that it composes with hot-replug recovery (PIZERO-51 stop/restart must re-enumerate through the hub). Gate behind the existing USB build flags. NOTE: for player-1 joystick the header-hat route (PIZERO-50) sidesteps USB entirely and is preferred -- this hub work is mainly for keyboard+keypad and for USB gamepads (PIZERO-13). Verify on hw: hub enumerates, keyboard + a second device both report; 60fps held; unplug/replug through hub recovers.

[2026-09-28 FIRST HARDWARE ATTEMPT, user's multi-port USB-C hub, pad and Keychron K2 behind it.] Nothing enumerated, even with only the pad on the hub. New diagnostic env pizero_usbdebug (TinyUSB host log on the serial console; docs/BUILD.md) showed why, in two layers:
(1) FIXED: the USB-C hub is TWO hub chips chained: a Terminus FE1.1s (1A40:0101) with a Genesys Logic hub (05E3:0610) on its port 3. The build allowed one hub, so the second was refused ('All addresses are occupied, try to increase CFG_TUH_HUB'). The Adafruit TinyUSB RP2040 config (tusb_config_rp2040.h) hard-codes CFG_TUH_HUB 1, CFG_TUH_DEVICE_MAX and CFG_TUH_HID with no #ifndef, so -D flags could not change them; our -DCFG_TUH_HID=4 had in fact always been overridden to 12. New scripts/patch_tinyusb.py (a pre: extra_script in [pizero_base]) guards those three defines in the downloaded library, idempotently; platformio.ini now sets CFG_TUH_HUB=2 and CFG_TUH_HID=8. RAM +140 bytes. Both hubs now mount (addresses 8 and 9).
(2) OPEN: the pad (a full-speed USB 1.1 device behind the second hub) gets its address, then during the 2 ms post-SET_ADDRESS delay the FIRST hub reports a connection change on its port 4 (something built into the USB-C hub, likely a card reader), TinyUSB issues a hub GET_PORT_STATUS on the shared control pipe, and the pad's next request (Get Device Descriptor) fails 'enum_delay_async 1627: ASSERT FAILED' in host/usbh.c. The enumeration is abandoned and never retried, so the pad never mounts. A TinyUSB race between hub status handling and an in-progress enumeration; present in Adafruit TinyUSB 3.7.7, the latest release. Options: a simpler hub with no built-in devices (quick test), a retry in TinyUSB via the patch script, or upstream TinyUSB master if it has fixed it.

[2026-09-28 CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE (user): keyboard and gamepad at once through a simple 4-port hub.] Hub: Realtek 0BDA:5401. Pad (GameSir 3537:1094) and a Keychron (3434:0430) both mounted and worked together; 60 fps for all 150 s logged, audio clean (under=0, skips=0). The keyboard was plugged into the hub while the board ran and still mounted: the hub reports the new device, which the bare root port cannot (PIZERO-51), so a hub may be the practical hot-plug path; replug not yet tried, noted on PIZERO-51. A Keychron K2 on the same hub was never seen by the hub at all (no port connection change); a K3 on the same hub worked. Suspected power: the K2 charges its battery over the cable and the hub is bus-powered from the board. Not investigated further. Closed at ~80%; the multi-chip USB-C hub failure (TinyUSB enumeration race) is filed as PIZERO-159.

summary: GIME-style programmable palette for classic 6847 modes + BIOS editor + per-title .pal profiles
description:
Non-traditional extension: give the classic MC6847 modes a CoCo3/GIME-style PROGRAMMABLE palette (real CoCo1/2 VDG colors were fixed -- this is impossible on original hw). The architecture is already 90% there: every renderer (render_alpha_frame/render_rg6_frame/render_graphics_frame in coco_machine.cpp) emits a 4-bit SEMANTIC palette index (PAL_GREEN..PAL_BRIGHT_ORANGE) into vdg_buffer, and the pizero blit does exactly one index->RGB lookup per pixel via g_vdg_rgb565_native[16] (coco_boot.cpp:488). That 16-entry LUT between VDG-index and output RGB IS the GIME palette-register architecture; it is just const today. PART 1 -- WRITABLE LUT + API: drop const on g_vdg_rgb565_native (already RAM-resident), add coco_set_palette_entry(idx,rgb) / get; keep a separate const MASTER copy for factory reset. Blit reads the LUT every frame so edits PREVIEW LIVE with zero repaint plumbing. No locking: LUT written by BIOS, read in blit; a torn read of one 16-bit entry mid-frame is cosmetically invisible for one frame. Only g_vdg_rgb565_native matters on this board (the byte-swapped g_vdg_rgb565 twin is dead AMOLED-path code). Current 12 named entries: 0 GREEN,1 YELLOW,2 BLUE(also RG6 artifact blue),3 RED,4 WHITE,5 CYAN,6 MAGENTA,7 ORANGE(also RG6 artifact orange),8 BLACK,9 DARK_GREEN,10 DARK_ORANGE,11 BRIGHT_ORANGE; 12-15 unused. NOTE indices are SEMANTIC so editing entry 0 recolors VDG green EVERYWHERE it appears (text ink, CG green, semigraphics, border) -- natural GIME behavior, intended; per-mode-independent palettes would need separate index spaces per mode = OUT OF SCOPE. Bonus: entries 2/7 double as RG6 NTSC-artifact colors so the same editor tunes the artifact red/blue tint (ties to PIZERO-43 phase work). PART 2 -- BIOS EDITOR (depends on PIZERO-53 overlay): pick an entry, adjust color, live-preview on whatever is on screen. Color depth: DEFAULT to CoCo3-authentic RGB222 (6-bit, 64-color GIME gamut) picker with an 'advanced/full-RGB565' toggle for 65k-color freedom. Render swatches as VDG semigraphics cells, inverse-video the selected one (reuse render_alpha_frame machinery from PIZERO-53). Actions: edit / reset-to-factory (copy master back) / save. PART 3 -- PER-TITLE .pal PROFILES: bind a saved 16-entry palette to a specific DSK/BIN/CAS/ROM so each game remembers its colors. Storage = SIDECAR file next to the image (SPACEWAR.DSK -> SPACEWAR.PAL), ~34 bytes: magic + version + 1-byte depth-mode flag + 16 entries stored as RGB222 (6-bit, output-depth-independent, survives future packing changes). Chose sidecar over a central manifest: matches the launcher's by-filename model, travels with the image on copy, no central corruption/dangling-entry risk. LOAD flow (hooks PIZERO-53 action step 4 load+mount): resolve palette in FALLBACK ORDER per-title <name>.pal -> user-global custom palette -> factory default; so untuned games look normal and tuned ones always come up right. SAVE flow: 'Save for this title' writes the sidecar keyed to the CURRENTLY-LOADED image path (launcher already tracks it for mount). EDGE CASES: built-in AUTORUN media has no path -> falls back to user-global (or reserve AUTORUN.PAL); image loaded outside the launcher -> no path -> global only. Persist the user-global custom palette too (PIZERO-53 persistence). PART 4 -- GUEST-SIDE GIME PALETTE (subsumes PIZERO-26, closed as superseded): beyond the BIOS editor, optionally let a RUNNING PROGRAM recolor live by intercepting guest writes to the real GIME palette addresses $FFB0-$FFBF on the CoCo bus (6-bit R-G-B, 2 bits/channel = 16 colors from 64) and routing them into the same writable LUT. This mirrors real CoCo3 VDG-compatible behavior -- a $FFB0+ recolor POKE program behaves the same here as on real hardware -- and stays fully TRANSPARENT: default LUT = stock CoCo colors, so unmodified games look normal until they poke the registers. Mirror the GIME addresses so CoCo-3-aware code just works; also optionally expose an extended RGB565 palette at our own addresses for beyond-hw color. WRINKLE (from PIZERO-26): PIZERO-15 precomputes glyph->packed-word LUTs with colors baked in (e.g. g_alpha_lut), so a palette write must REBUILD those small LUTs -- cheap, since palette writes are rare (once per screen, not per frame). TODO before coding Part 4: verify the exact GIME VDG-compatible default slot->color mapping against GIME docs rather than guessing. BOUNDARY: VDG+palette only, NOT full GIME/CoCo3 (no hi-res GIME bitmap modes, extra RAM/MMU, hw scroll, or GIME interrupts -- those remain PIZERO-16). Product context: docs/product-plan.md ('open platform you can extend' story). Gate behind a build flag. Depends on PIZERO-53 (overlay + SD + persistence); cross-link docs/ROADMAP.md. Verify on hw: edit green live in a running game; save; reboot/reload -> colors restored; a second game keeps its own; reset-to-factory works.

[2026-08-17 TWO SOURCE-CONFIRMED CONSTRAINTS ON THIS TICKET (verified against ~/github/xroar and lib/libdvi, not from memory).

(1) DESKTOP-XROAR CROSS-TEST COMPATIBILITY -- $FFB0-$FFBF CONFLICTS WITH NOTHING, AND `xroar -m coco3` IS AN EQUIVALENT TEST TARGET.
On CoCo 1/2 -- and on this port today -- $FFB0-$FFBF is unmapped and writes are silently ignored (coco_machine.cpp:450, 'ROM and other I/O writes ignored'), so no existing software or test setup breaks. Better than merely harmless: the GIME applies its palette in VDG-COMPATIBLE mode as well as its own modes. tcc1014.c:1400-1421 sits inside `if (gime->COCO)` and indexes palette_reg[]. The CG (2bpp) path there reads
    c0 = c1 = gime->palette_reg[cg_colours + ((gdata >> 6) & 3)];    (tcc1014.c:1408)
which is the SAME arithmetic as our render_graphics_frame
    uint8_t c = cg_base + ((b >> 6) & 3);                            (coco_machine.cpp:1041)
with cg_colours = !CSS ? TCC1014_GREEN : TCC1014_WHITE (= 0 or 4, tcc1014.c:1317) matching our cg_base = css ? PAL_WHITE : PAL_GREEN. The two implementations converged independently, so a palette-poking test program can be developed on desktop xroar -m coco3 and run unchanged here.
  * INDEX MAP -- entries 0-7 MATCH EXACTLY: GREEN, YELLOW, BLUE, RED, WHITE, CYAN, MAGENTA, ORANGE (tcc1014.h:35-36 vs our PAL_* defines at coco_machine.cpp:882). Entries 8-15 DIVERGE: GIME uses 8-11 for the RG colour-set fg/bg pairs (RGCSS0_0, RGCSS0_1, RGCSS1_0, RGCSS1_1) and 12-15 for the alpha/semigraphics pairs (DARK_GREEN, BRIGHT_GREEN, DARK_ORANGE, BRIGHT_ORANGE); we use 8=BLACK, 9=DARK_GREEN and leave 10-15 at 0x0000. So $FFB0-$FFB7 pokes behave identically on both, $FFB8-$FFBF do not. ADOPTING GIME'S 8-15 ASSIGNMENT COSTS NOTHING TODAY because those slots are currently unused -- do it if cross-testing matters at all.
  * REGISTER FORMAT -- GIME palette registers are 6-BIT: palette_reg[A & 15] = *CPUD & 0x3f (tcc1014.c:792), i.e. RGB222, 64 colours. They are also READABLE, returning the stored 6 bits with the upper 2 from open bus (tcc1014.c:795). Many sources assume write-only; xroar implements them readable, so match that.
  * TRAP -- if the 'advanced full-RGB' path is implemented by WIDENING $FFB0-$FFBF to accept 16-bit values, desktop xroar stops being an equivalent test target. Keep $FFB0-$FFBF strictly 6-bit GIME-compatible and put any wider format at DIFFERENT addresses or behind an explicit mode bit.

(2) THE OUTPUT PRECISION CEILING IS RGB565, AND IT IS NOT SYMMETRIC ACROSS CHANNELS.
Full chain: 4-bit palette index (vdg_buffer, coco_machine.cpp:92) -> RGB565 via g_vdg_rgb565_native[16] (coco_boot.cpp:488) -> framebuffer -> dvi_static_framebuf_main_16bpp on core 1 (main.cpp:204) -> per-channel bit extract (configure_interp_for_addrgen, tmds_encode.cpp) -> 6-bit TMDS LUT -> 10-bit TMDS symbols -> wire. BOTH libdvi tables are 6 BITS PER CHANNEL: tmds_table.h's own header says it 'converts a 6 bit data input into a pair of TMDS data symbols with data content almost equal (1 LSB off) to input value left shifted by two', and tmds_table_fullres.h indexes on 'the sign bit of current running disparity, with 6 bits of colour channel data'. So the wire is nominally 8-bit/channel per the DVI standard, but only 64 levels per channel ever reach it. Against RGB565 (R5 G6 B5): GREEN is an exact 6/6 match; RED and BLUE are limited by the FRAMEBUFFER at 5 bits and each give up one bit the encoder could have carried.
  * CONSEQUENCE FOR GIME COMPATIBILITY: none. RGB222's 64 colours expand into RGB565 by bit-replication with enormous room to spare.
  * CONSEQUENCE FOR THE 'FULL RGB' AMBITION: it means 5/6/5, NOT 8/8/8. Do not promise 24-bit colour in the BIOS editor UI or in docs/. RGB666 would exactly match the encoder with no waste on any channel, but it is not a 16-bit pixel format, so it would cost a larger framebuffer and a different libdvi encode path -- out of scope unless the framebuffer format decision is deliberately re-opened.]

[2026-09-17 PRIORITISED by the user (medium -> high) as one of the two affordable CoCo 3 features, alongside the timer PIZERO-62. Split the work by what it depends on: PART 1, the writable LUT and its register interface, needs nothing new and should land first; the BIOS editor and per-title .pal profiles need the overlay (PIZERO-81/53) and follow it. Keep PIZERO-85 as the register-file shape so the two agree rather than inventing two palettes.]

[2026-09-17 REGISTER FILE BUILT ONCE, shared, as both tickets asked. It lives in lib/coco_machine/src/coco_palette.h (header-only, machine-free, host-testable) with the storage owned by coco_machine, which is what sees the bus writes; src/coco_boot.cpp's blit now reads it through coco_machine_palette(), hoisting the pointer once per frame instead of reloading a global per pixel.
FORMAT TAKEN FROM XROAR, NOT FROM MEMORY, because desktop `xroar -m coco3` is the cross-test target: the GIME byte is six bits interleaved bit5 R1, bit4 G1, bit3 B1, bit2 R0, bit1 G0, bit0 B0 (~/github/xroar src/coco3.c:611-613), and the four intensity levels are NON-LINEAR, 0.000/0.460/0.736/0.920 (coco3.c:69). A linear 0/85/170/255 ramp would look plausible and be wrong in every mid-tone; a test pins this.
TRANSPARENCY: the table powers on holding the stock VDG colours and reports whether a guest has touched it, so an unmodified game looks exactly as before. Guest writes to $FFB0-$FFBF land behind -DGIME_PALETTE (env pizero_gime, alongside the timer); reads return the register with the top two bits undriven, as the GIME does.
THE PIZERO-26 WRINKLE DOES NOT APPLY HERE: our render LUTs (alpha, SG4, RG6) store palette INDICES, not colours, so a palette write needs no LUT rebuild. Worth recording because the ticket warned about it.
COST: the default build grew 56 bytes (the table moved from .rodata to .data, plus the factory copy); the GIME build adds 548 over the default. Per-pixel cost is unchanged, and the blit may be marginally cheaper for hoisting the pointer, though that cannot be measured until the soak ends.
TESTED: 14 host tests, 58 in the suite. They cover the bit layout per channel, the non-linear ramp, all 64 GIME colours staying distinct through the RGB565 squeeze, per-entry isolation, six-bit masking, read-back, reset-to-factory, direct RGB565 access for the future editor, and that the decode claims no CoCo 2 address and does not overlap the PIZERO-62 timer block.
NOT DONE, and deliberately so: parts 2 and 3 of PIZERO-55, the BIOS editor and per-title .pal sidecars, both of which need the overlay. Hardware validation waits for the soak to finish.]

[2026-09-18 PART 1 IS CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE: a guest POKEing $FFB0-$FFBF recolours the machine live (see PIZERO-85, now closed). What remains here is purely the UI half: the BIOS editor and per-title .pal profiles, both waiting on the overlay. The register file they will drive is done and proven.]

summary: Higher-fidelity NTSC artifact rendering (beyond the 2-bits->4-colors LUT)
description:
FUTURE / fidelity enhancement. The current artifact path is a deliberate performance SHORTCUT, not composite decoding: render_rg6_frame (coco_machine.cpp:958) and its twin in vendored mc6847.c:52 map RG6/PMODE4 pixel PAIRS to one of four fixed palette entries (00->BLACK, 01->artifactA, 10->artifactB, 11->WHITE; A/B swapped by CSS + the compile-time phase flag). This nails the canonical 4-colour PMODE4 look that most artifact games rely on, but a real NTSC composite chain is an analog signal through finite chroma/luma bandwidth and produces things a context-free 2->4 LUT cannot: (1) MORE THAN 4 HUES -- specific multi-pixel patterns land at intermediate phase/amplitude and yield extra colours (greens/purples/half-luma shades demos + some games coax out); ours only ever emits black/A/B/white. (2) POSITION+NEIGHBOUR-DEPENDENT colour -- real hue depends on running phase and adjacent luma; ours decodes each pair in isolation, identically everywhere. (3) FRINGING / colour bleed / dot crawl at mono<->colour edges -- absent (hard-edged palette indices). (4) COVERAGE -- only RG6/GM7 artifacts; render_graphics_frame (other CG/RG modes) does straight fg/bg with NO artifacting, and the high-res 2-colour modes that also artifact on real hw are clean here. (5) fixed idealized PAL_BLUE/PAL_ORANGE swatches vs a real set's tint/temperature/power-on-phase drift (see PIZERO-43). WHY deferred: XRoar upstream HAS a phase-accurate composite renderer but this port dropped it; true composite sim is a per-pixel multi-tap filter -- expensive, and core-0 has only ~31% headroom at 1x (PIZERO-48). OPTIONS to close the gap, cheap->dear: (a) WIDER PATTERN LUT keyed on 3-4 pixels of context (precomputed) to fake the common extra hues without a real filter -- likely the best effort/quality tradeoff, still a table lookup in the hot blit; (b) extend artifacting to the other high-res mono modes; (c) a proper composite/NTSC decode pass (luma/chroma separation + bandpass) for full-gamut fidelity -- measure against the frame budget, likely needs core-1 headroom or a lower internal res. Pairs naturally with PIZERO-55 (both are 'what RGB does a given VDG pattern become'); a wider LUT could feed the same programmable-palette machinery. PRE-WORK: capture reference photos/captures of real-hardware artifacting for the target games to validate against. Not scheduled; log only. Cross-link docs/ROADMAP.md, PIZERO-43, PIZERO-55.

summary: Loadable/customizable VDG font from SD (.FNT + BIOS loader + per-title profiles)
description: Let the MC6847 alpha font be replaced from the SD card instead of being fixed at build time. Current font = const font_6847t1[1536] (128 glyphs x 12 rows, 8px wide, one byte/row MSB-first) in lib/xroar_core/src/mc6847/font-6847t1.c, placed in a .time_critical RAM section; the active renderer reads it at coco_machine.cpp:948. KEY: font loading is CLEANLY DECOUPLED from the PIZERO-55 palette work -- g_alpha_lut is indexed by the glyph ROW BYTE (0-255), not by character, so it bakes in COLORS not glyphs; a palette change rebuilds that LUT but a FONT change touches nothing but the font bytes. No LUT rebuild on font swap. PART 1 -- SWAPPABLE FONT + API: replace the direct font_6847t1[...] reference with an indirection g_font (default = the const ROM font); coco_load_font() fills a 1536-byte RAM buffer (keep it in .time_critical fast RAM so the hot render loop is unaffected -- 1.5KB is trivial on 520KB) and repoints g_font. ONLY render_alpha_frame (coco_machine.cpp:948) needs the change -- mc6847.c:427's per-scanline path is dead at runtime on this port. Keep the const font_6847t1 as the factory MASTER for reset-to-ROM (just repoint back). PART 2 -- FILE FORMAT: raw 8x12 bitmap, one byte/row MSB-first (same layout as the array); full 1536 bytes (128 glyphs) or just the 64-glyph alpha slot (768 bytes, the $40-$7F range). Small header (magic + version + width + height + glyph-count) so the loader VALIDATES: the renderer hard-assumes 8x12, so a font that isn't 8x12 must be REJECTED, not rendered garbled. Extension .FNT. PART 3 -- BIOS LOADER (depends on PIZERO-53 overlay): browse .FNT files on SD, load into the buffer, LIVE-PREVIEW (the menu itself redraws in the new font = instant feedback via the shared render_alpha_frame path), reset-to-ROM. PART 4 -- PER-TITLE SIDECAR: bind a font to a specific image, GAME.DSK -> GAME.FNT, mirroring PIZERO-55's .pal design exactly; FALLBACK ORDER per-title <name>.fnt -> user-global custom font -> factory ROM. So a game can carry BOTH its palette (.pal) and its font (.fnt). SAVE keyed to the currently-loaded image path (launcher tracks it). CONSTRAINT (state up front): alpha mode masks the screen code ch&0x3F|0x40, so it only ever indexes 64 GLYPHS ($40-$7F: @,A-Z,punct,0-9). A custom font REDEFINES those 64 (restyle/international-ish/game-matched look) but cannot ADD a 65th (no free lowercase) without changing the decode addressing -- note as a possible later extension, tie-in with the launcher lowercase discussion. EDGE CASES mirror PIZERO-55: AUTORUN/outside-launcher media has no path -> user-global font only. Persist the user-global font choice (PIZERO-53 persistence). Gate behind a build flag. Depends on PIZERO-53 (overlay + SD + persistence); sibling to PIZERO-55 (palette). Cross-link docs/ROADMAP.md. Verify on hw: load a .FNT, BASIC text redraws in the new glyphs; reset-to-ROM restores; a game's GAME.FNT auto-applies on load and a different game keeps its own.

summary: Bench: measure synth voice budget on real silicon (N dummy voices vs [run] telemetry)
description:
PRE-WORK for PIZERO-17 (custom wavetable/sampled synth): validate the back-of-envelope cycles/voice + voice-count estimate on real RP2350 hardware BEFORE committing an engine architecture. Estimate to confirm: ~1100 cyc/sample total synth budget at ~3.5 ms/frame (of the ~5.3 ms core-0 headroom), giving ~4-5 Blofeld-grade voices (250 cyc/sample) up to ~10 simple voices (100 cyc/sample). METHOD: a flag-gated bench build (-DSYNTH_BENCH) that runs N dummy synth voices each frame in the core-0 audio path (audio_emit), generating into the SPSC ring (or a discard sink), and watches the existing [run] fps/cpu/render/blit serial telemetry (PIZERO-15). Sweep N upward until core-0 frame time approaches 16.67 ms / fps drops below 60, to find the real ceiling. VARIABLES to characterize: (1) per-voice complexity tiers -- (a) wavetable + linear interp + ADSR, (b) + resonant SVF filter + 2D wave morph, (c) full Blofeld-grade (morph + multimode filter + 2 env + 2 LFO); report cyc/sample for each. (2) FLOAT (M33 FPU) vs Q15 fixed-point (DSP MACs) inner loop -- measure both, pick the winner. (3) wavetable source: XIP-from-FLASH per-sample read vs SRAM-cached active-frame -- QUANTIFY the XIP cache-miss jitter that motivates the SRAM active-frame mirror, and the PCM pitched-playback (non-unity-rate flash walk) worst case. (4) RAM cost headroom -- SRAM is already ~89-94% used (PIZERO-18 audio + double-buffer video); report how much a realistic voice/wavetable-cache footprint adds and whether it fits. OUTPUT: a short docs note (or PIZERO-17 comment) with measured cyc/sample per tier, the safe max voice count at the 3-4 ms/frame budget, the float-vs-Q15 decision, and the flash/SRAM wavetable-access verdict -- these set PIZERO-17's configurable voice cap and memory model. Gate behind the bench flag; no product-env impact. Verify on hw: telemetry logs N, cyc/sample, and frame time; identify the N where fps first drops.

summary: Internal MIDI bus/router + CoCo bit-banger serial MIDI transport (firmware becomes Lyra's external UART box)
description:
The CoCo-facing half of the MIDI subsystem. CORRECTED TRANSPORT (per user 2026-07-19): apps like Lyra do NOT use a cartridge ACIA -- they use the CoCo's built-in BIT-BANGER serial port (software-timed async serial toggled on a PIA1 line) feeding a CUSTOM EXTERNAL UART BOX (powered by +5V from the joystick port) that converts to MIDI DIN. EMULATION INSIGHT: the firmware simply BECOMES that external box -- tap the emulated bit-banger line, decode the async serial in firmware, forward as MIDI. No cartridge, no physical box, no joystick +5V needed (none of it is physical anymore) -> this is the zero-extra-hardware path. REUSES the cycle-accurate PIA-tap infrastructure from the audio work (PIZERO-18 already samples PIA1 PORT A at emulation-tick resolution; the DAC tap is the template). TRANSPORT: (1) OUT (CoCo->MIDI) -- tap the RS-232 serial-out bit (CoCo bit-banger, believed PIA1 PA1 / $FF20 bit 1, CONFIRM via PIZERO-61), watch its transitions over emulated cycles, software-UART-decode async frames at Lyra's baud into MIDI bytes, push to the router. (2) IN (MIDI->CoCo) -- synthesize the async serial waveform on the serial-in line (believed PIA1 PB0 / $FF22 bit 0, CONFIRM via PIZERO-61) with cycle-accurate bit timing so Lyra's software-UART-receive reads incoming MIDI. ROUTER: an internal software MIDI bus carrying parsed events (handle running status, SysEx, MIDI clock); ANY source -> ANY sink, configurable. SOURCES: the bit-banger transport (guest), external endpoints (PIZERO-60). SINKS: the synth (PIZERO-17), external endpoints (PIZERO-60), the bit-banger IN (back to guest). So Lyra can play the internal synth AND drive real gear simultaneously; a DAW/controller can drive the synth OR feed Lyra. COCO2 UNTOUCHED: the serial tap/inject only runs when MIDI is ENABLED (config toggle); no bus/tap cost otherwise; router runs only on traffic; buffers are a few hundred bytes. Build-flag gated, off in the product env. NOTE (real-hardware only): Lyra's box occupied the joystick port for +5V, so a purist using REAL Lyra hardware would conflict with the PIZERO-50 joystick hat -- irrelevant to the all-emulated path (joystick port stays free). DEPENDS ON: PIZERO-61 (Lyra serial params: PIA bits, baud, framing, whether Lyra bit-bangs 31250 directly or the box reclocks) to set the decoder; PIZERO-17 for the synth sink (but testable EARLY by routing to a PIZERO-60 USB-MIDI endpoint before the synth exists). Cross-link docs/ROADMAP.md, docs/hdmi-audio-notes.md (shared PIA-tap technique), PIZERO-60. Verify on hw: run Lyra, notes reach the internal synth / USB-MIDI out at correct pitch+timing; external MIDI in reaches Lyra; plain CoCo2 boot unaffected with MIDI off.

[2026-09-16 DEFERRED in the PIZERO-107 triage. Not rejected, parked: it is an idea, not scheduled work, and leaving it open misrepresented intent. REVISIT TRIGGER: Revisit as a set with PIZERO-60/61 if MIDI becomes a goal rather than an idea.]

summary: External MIDI I/O endpoints (USB-MIDI device + host; optional DIN-5)
description:
The outside-world half of the MIDI subsystem: physical/virtual endpoints that plug into the PIZERO-59 router. Three endpoints, only one needs added hardware. (1) USB-MIDI DEVICE via NATIVE USB -- NO EXTRA HARDWARE. This board's native RP2350 USB is already a DEVICE (it runs the CDC serial console + WAV dump). Add a MIDI interface to the existing TinyUSB/Adafruit_TinyUSB COMPOSITE descriptor (CDC + MIDI) so the board appears to a PC/DAW as a class-compliant MIDI port over the cable that's ALREADY plugged in. This is the marquee 'external integration without additional hardware' path: Lyra -> PIZERO-59 router -> USB-MIDI -> DAW/hardware synth, and back. Use Adafruit_USBD_MIDI; verify it composes with the existing CDC (do not break the serial console/telemetry). (2) USB-MIDI HOST via PIO-USB -- NO EXTRA HARDWARE beyond the class-compliant controller itself. Enumerate a USB-MIDI keyboard/controller on the PIO host port (GPIO28/29); pairs with the hub (PIZERO-54) so a keyboard + a MIDI controller coexist. Needs TinyUSB MIDI-host class support on the Pico-PIO-USB stack (verify availability; may need a report/class handler like the HID path). (3) DIN-5 SERIAL MIDI -- THE ONLY option needing hardware: a UART on a free GPIO + standard MIDI circuit (optocoupler 6N138 input / current-loop output, DIN jacks). Optional, for vintage gear. All three are build-flag gated and cost nothing when inactive (USB polling only when an endpoint is present) -> CoCo2 path untouched. DEPENDS ON: PIZERO-59 (router). Composes with PIZERO-54 (hub) for the host path. Cross-link docs/ROADMAP.md, docs/BUILD.md (new flags). Verify on hw: (1) board enumerates as a USB-MIDI device on a PC and passes notes both ways while CDC still works; (2) a USB-MIDI controller on the host port drives the synth; (3) [if built] DIN in/out with real gear.

summary: Pre-work: reverse-engineer Lyra's bit-banged serial MIDI driver (params for PIZERO-59)
description:
PRE-WORK / RESEARCH that GATES PIZERO-59's serial transport. User-confirmed mechanism (2026-07-19): Lyra drives the CoCo's built-in BIT-BANGER RS-232 serial port into a CUSTOM EXTERNAL UART BOX powered by +5V from the joystick port, which converts to MIDI DIN. To make the firmware faithfully BECOME that box, nail the exact parameters the emulated transport must match: (1) which PIA line carries serial OUT and which carries serial IN (believed PIA1 PA1 / $FF20 bit 1 out, PIA1 PB0 / $FF22 bit 0 in -- CONFIRM, do not guess); (2) the BAUD rate Lyra bit-bangs at, and the frame format (start/data/stop bits, parity); (3) CRITICAL: does Lyra bit-bang at MIDI rate (31250) DIRECTLY -- so the box just level-shifts and our firmware forwards bytes 1:1 -- or does it send at some other CoCo-friendly rate that the box's UART RECLOCKS to 31250 (so our firmware must decode at rate X and re-emit as MIDI)? This determines the decoder clock. (4) any handshake/flow-control lines the box used; (5) whether Lyra relies on interrupt or tight-loop bit timing (affects how cycle-accurate our tap must be -- likely very, like the audio DAC tap). METHOD: use the analyze-rom and trace-calls skills on Lyra's binary/driver to find the bit-bang routine and extract the timing constants + PIA addresses; cross-check against XRoar's serial handling and published CoCo bit-banger docs. Also document the external box's behavior for the record (and for anyone building real hardware, incl. the joystick-port +5V tap that conflicts with the PIZERO-50 joystick hat on real hardware only). OUTPUT: a short transport spec (PIA bits + baud + framing + reclock-or-not) that PIZERO-59 implements against. Cross-link PIZERO-59, PIZERO-60.

summary: GIME-compatible programmable timer + minimal interrupt registers (partial GIME; runs SOME unmodified CoCo3 timer software)
description:
Add a CoCo3/GIME-COMPATIBLE programmable interrupt timer so SOME unmodified CoCo3 software runs on this CoCo2 base -- without full GIME and without compromising CoCo2 (user goal 2026-07-19: a compatible LAYOUT, not our own ad-hoc device). CURRENT MODEL (recap): 6809 IRQ <- PIA0 (HS/FS sync, coco_machine.cpp:481), FIRQ <- PIA1 (CART line, :482); rates are FIXED. The scheduled-countdown needed for a timer ALREADY EXISTS as cart_toggle_remaining (:806-811) -- a cycles-to-next-pulse counter; the timer generalizes it to a register-loaded interval (no per-cycle hot-loop cost, fires only when it fires). IMPLEMENT (authentic GIME register layout, all in the $FF90-$FF95 block -- UNUSED on a CoCo2 so decoding is safe): (1) TIMER reload $FF94 (MSB, bits 11-8) / $FF95 (LSB) = 12-bit down-counter; on underflow raise the interrupt + auto-reload. (2) CLOCK SOURCE via INIT1 $FF91 TINS bit: fast 3.579545 MHz (~279 ns, = 4x the 0.895 MHz 6809 clock -> interval_cycles = reload*... convert) vs horizontal 15.734 kHz (~63.5 us); both convert cheaply to 6809-cycle intervals for the scheduler. (3) MINIMAL INTERRUPT CONTROLLER: $FF92 (IRQ enable) / $FF93 (FIRQ enable) with at least the TIMER source bit; read-to-clear status; route the timer to IRQ or FIRQ per the enable regs (OR into the existing MC6809_IRQ_SET/FIRQ_SET). Decode INIT0 $FF90 / INIT1 $FF91 as needed. (4) RELOAD QUIRK: match GIME period behavior (period = reload + 1 on the 1986 GIME, + 2 on the 1987 -- CONFIRM exact; matters for pitch-accurate music); pick a rev or make it a build option -- research item. COMPATIBILITY BOUNDARY (the honest 'some'): RUNS CoCo3 programs that (a) stay in CoCo2/VDG-compatible video, (b) install their OWN IRQ/FIRQ handler (we boot CoCo2 Extended Color BASIC, whose interrupt handler is PIA-based NOT GIME-aware, so ROM-handler-dependent GIME interrupt use won't work), (c) don't need the MMU / 512K / GIME hi-res modes, (d) don't hard-gate on full-GIME detection. SWEET SPOT = interrupt-driven MUSIC / timing / demo routines that just want a fast programmable tick. WON'T RUN: anything using GIME hi-res video, the MMU, 512K RAM, or the Super ECB ROM handlers. TIES to the music work: this is the guest-side programmable tick for a MIDI clock / sequencer / synth-envelope updates (PIZERO-17 synth, PIZERO-59 MIDI). HOST COST is proportional to fire rate; add a sanity FLOOR on the interval so a pathologically fast timer can't blow the ~5.3 ms core-0 headroom (PIZERO-48). Build-flag GATED; zero cost to a plain CoCo2 boot when off (only joins the IRQ/FIRQ OR when enabled). ALTERNATIVES: (B) our own non-GIME address block for the timer = simpler but runs ZERO existing CoCo3 software -> REJECTED in favor of the compatible layout per the goal; (C) FULL GIME (MMU, hi-res video, all interrupt sources, 512K) = OUT OF SCOPE, large lift and directly breaks CoCo2 purity. PRE-WORK: pick 2-3 candidate CoCo3 timer/music programs (VDG-mode, own-handler) to validate against; confirm the reload-quirk rev to emulate. VERIFY on hw: a candidate CoCo3 music/timer program runs unmodified at correct tempo; plain CoCo2 boot byte-identical with the timer disabled. Cross-link docs/ROADMAP.md, PIZERO-17, PIZERO-59.

[2026-09-16 DEFERRED in the PIZERO-107 triage. Not rejected, parked: it is an idea, not scheduled work, and leaving it open misrepresented intent. REVISIT TRIGGER: Revisit if a target title needs the GIME timer, or if CoCo 3 support becomes a goal.]

[2026-09-17 UN-DEFERRED and raised low -> high. It was parked in the PIZERO-107 triage on the grounds that nobody had asked for it; the PIZERO-111 decision asks for it directly. The revisit trigger recorded at the time was 'if a target title needs the GIME timer, or if CoCo 3 support becomes a goal', and the second has now happened in the affordable-features form: the GIME register layout at $FF90-$FF95 is free on a CoCo 2, and the scheduled countdown it needs already exists. This is one of the two features chosen precisely because it does NOT need the faster 6809 that full CoCo 3 would.]

[2026-09-17 IMPLEMENTED, flag-gated, not yet on hardware (the board is mid-soak).
lib/coco_machine/src/gime_timer.h holds the register behaviour and interval arithmetic, header-only and machine-free so it is testable on the host; coco_machine.cpp owns the instance and the wiring. New env pizero_gime = the product build plus -DGIME_TIMER.
SCHEDULING: rides XRoar's existing event queue rather than a new counter, so an idle timer costs nothing (the memory fast path already skips the queue when nothing is due, and a stopped timer is not queued at all). Both clock sources divide the 14,318,180 Hz event clock exactly: fast 3.579545 MHz = 4 ticks per count, horizontal 15.734 kHz = 910.
ROUTING: the timer ORs into the same IRQ/FIRQ lines as the PIAs, per the enable registers; status is read-to-clear and an unacknowledged status holds its line, as on real hardware.
SAFETY: GIME_MIN_INTERVAL_TICKS clamps a pathologically small reload (16 CPU cycles minimum) and counts how often it had to, so a guest running differently from real hardware is visible rather than silently eating the ~4 ms of headroom.
COST WHEN OFF IS ZERO, measured: the default build is byte-identical at 371,660 bytes; the GIME build adds 348.
TESTED: 15 host tests (pio test -e native), covering both clock sources, the 12-bit reload and its two register halves, reload 0 stopping the timer, the clamp, IRQ/FIRQ routing and independence, read-to-clear, the decode boundary (the CoCo 2's own PIA/SAM/cart addresses are explicitly NOT claimed), and that unimplemented source bits survive a read-modify-write. 44 tests total now pass.
STILL OPEN, both from the original ticket: (1) GIME_PERIOD_BIAS is a build option defaulting to 2 because the 1986-vs-1987 reload quirk is still unconfirmed by us, and it sets the tempo of any music written against it; (2) hardware validation against 2-3 real CoCo 3 timer/music programs that keep VDG video and install their own handler, plus a check that a plain CoCo 2 boot is unchanged with the flag off.]

[2026-09-18 TWO CORRECTIONS, found while writing a library proposal for the ~/github/coco Forth project, whose coco-guides/coco3-intro.md is a better authority on GIME quirks than anything we had here.
(1) THE RELOAD QUIRK WAS RECORDED BACKWARDS in this ticket and in the header. The guide states a count of 1 behaves as 3 on the 1986 part and as 2 on the 1987, i.e. roughly +2 on the 1986 and +1 on the 1987. We had the revisions swapped. The default GIME_PERIOD_BIAS of 2 therefore emulates the 1986 part, which is now what the code says.
(2) A ZERO RELOAD IS NOT 'STOPPED' ON REAL HARDWARE: it re-asserts the interrupt immediately, which is the root of the documented 'Arkanoid sound bug'. We treat zero as stopped on purpose, because a timer firing every tick would wedge the emulator, but the old comment claimed hardware behaved that way. Now recorded as a deliberate deviation so nobody 'fixes' it into a hang, and so a guest that depends on the real behaviour fails in an explainable way.
Neither changes the tests (15 still pass) or the build; both change what a reader believes.]

[2026-09-18 NOW IN THE DEFAULT BUILD, and the separate pizero_gime env is gone. Keeping a second build was the wrong call: it meant a board could silently lose the feature on an ordinary reflash, which is exactly what happened today mid-test. The justification for gating was that these were unproven on hardware; the palette is now proven, both blocks are unused on a CoCo 2, the decode claims no CoCo 2 address (asserted by host tests), and both are transparent until a guest writes to them: the palette holds the stock VDG colours, the timer stays stopped. Frame budget measured identical at 76.2%, RAM +484 bytes.]

[2026-09-28 CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE (user: 'i tested the GIME timer and it works').] Closed at ~80%. Left open and filed as PIZERO-170: which GIME revision's reload quirk to emulate (GIME_PERIOD_BIAS 2 = the 1986 part, the default), which sets the exact tempo of timer-driven music. The zero-reload deviation (treated as stopped, not an immediate re-assert) stays deliberate, as recorded above.
