summary: Say what is wrong instead of showing a black screen
description:
FOUND while drafting docs/kit.md 2026-08-17 by checking the failure path rather than assuming it. THE PROBLEM: if the SD card has no /coco/roms/bas12.rom, setup() prints 'ROM load FAILED (need /coco/bas12.rom [+extbas11.rom])' and RETURNS EARLY (src/main.cpp:1066); g_machine_running stays false and loop() just delay(1000)s (:1201). The message goes ONLY over USB-CDC serial. But multicore_launch_core1(core1_main) already ran at :1060, so libdvi IS running -- the monitor SYNCS and then shows a black frame.

WHY THAT IS THE WORST POSSIBLE FAILURE MODE: a monitor that syncs to a black picture is indistinguishable from a dead unit. The recipient of a gifted unit (PIZERO-91) has no serial console, no expectation of one, and no reason to suspect the ROM. They will conclude the hardware is broken. This is the single most likely first-run experience for anyone who plugs in before reading the card, because we deliberately ship NO ROMs (copyright) -- so EVERY unit fails this way on first power-up BY DESIGN.

SAME CLASS OF FAILURE, same silent result: SD mount failure ('SD mount FAILED -- no ROMs, idle.', main.cpp:1065) and coco_machine_init failure (:1070). All three return early to a black screen.

FIX: draw the diagnostic to the framebuffer instead of only to serial. The renderer needed already exists and is cheap -- coco_boot_blit_vdg_pizero_src(const uint8_t*, uint16_t*) (coco_boot.h:76) takes any VDG-format buffer, and font_6847t1 is available; PIZERO-81b is porting exactly this kind of small text-card renderer (coco_boot_card_clear / card_text / card_buffer from the AMOLED port). If PIZERO-81b lands first, reuse its card renderer verbatim -- this is the same 32x16 text card with different content. Otherwise this ticket justifies building it, and PIZERO-81b then reuses THIS.

MESSAGE CONTENT should be actionable, not an error code -- the reader is a non-technical recipient:
  * no SD card / mount failed -> 'NO SD CARD -- INSERT A FAT32 CARD'
  * card present, no bas12.rom -> 'NO ROM FOUND. COPY bas12.rom TO /coco/roms/ ON THE SD CARD. SEE THE CARD IN THE BOX.' Name the exact file and path; that is the whole fix for them.
  * machine init failed -> a distinguishable message so a real fault is not confused with a missing file.
Keep it legible on a TV at a distance: the existing 32x16 card at 8x12 glyphs is right, and it is the same look as the emulator so it does not appear to be a different device.

ALSO: keep the serial messages, do not replace them -- they are how WE debug. And ensure the screen keeps refreshing / the loop still pets the watchdog (PIZERO-33) so the board does not appear to hang while showing the message.

PRIORITY high, ahead of most of the video-mode work: it is small, it reuses existing code, and it is the difference between a gift that works and a gift that looks broken. Blocks nothing, but PIZERO-91 (kit.md) currently has to warn recipients in print that a black screen is expected -- which is a documentation workaround for a UX bug.

[2026-09-17 Summary rewritten in the PIZERO-107 triage, move 4, to say what this delivers rather than how. Previous summary: "On-screen boot diagnostics: a missing ROM currently shows a BLACK SCREEN with no explanation"]

[2026-09-18 IMPLEMENTED, not yet seen on a screen (the board is mid-soak).
A 32x16 text card in the machine's own 8x12 font and live palette, so a diagnostic looks like it came from the CoCo rather than from some other device: coco_boot_card_clear/_text/_center/_present in src/coco_boot.cpp, declared in coco_boot.h.
COSTS 512 BYTES, not the 24 KB a second VDG buffer would have: the card holds a character grid and renders straight into the framebuffer a glyph row at a time. PIZERO-81b can reuse it; it is the same card with different content.
All three pre-machine failures now draw as well as print (serial messages kept, as the ticket required): SD mount, ROM load, machine init. The idle loop already pets the watchdog every second, so the board holds the message instead of rebooting under it.
MESSAGES name the exact path, since that IS the fix for the reader: 'COPY BAS12.ROM TO /COCO/ROMS/ ON THE SD CARD'. Checked against the resolver rather than the old serial string, which said /coco/bas12.rom: coco_boot_resolve prefers /coco/roms/ and falls back to flat /coco/ (coco_boot.cpp:147), so the message quotes the preferred path. The init failure is worded differently on purpose so a real fault is not mistaken for a missing file.
REUSES TESTED CODE rather than re-deriving it: the glyph fold is vdg_alpha_glyph_index from vdg_pack.h, already covered by PIZERO-109's tests. The ASCII mapping and centring moved into src/text_card.h and got 8 host tests of their own, including that every one of the 256 possible bytes lands inside the font block, that unprintables become spaces rather than random glyphs, and that every real message fits 32 columns. 66 tests now pass.
REMAINING: see it on a screen. The natural check is to rename bas12.rom on the card and power on.]

[2026-09-18 TURNED INTO FULL PAGES, and the two gaps closed.
The card is 512 characters and we were using about 80 of them. A failure now gets a page: a centred title, a wrapped body saying what happened and what to do, and a detail block carrying the evidence. House style recorded in src/boot_messages.h: what happened then what to do, name exact files and folders, no error codes, no jargon, no blame.
GAP 1 CLOSED, a truncated ROM used to say NO ROM FOUND. coco_boot_load_rom_from_sd now records what it found (struct coco_rom_status: found flags and byte counts), so a present-but-wrong-size bas12.rom gets its own page, ROM FILE IS DAMAGED, with the actual byte count in the detail line. Someone is no longer sent hunting for a file that is sitting on the card.
GAP 2 CLOSED, a missing extbas11.rom was silent. It is not fatal, so the machine still starts, but it silently costs Extended and Disk BASIC and a recipient has no way to connect failing DISK commands to a file they never copied. A COLOR BASIC ONLY page now shows for 4 seconds before handing over.
MESSAGES MOVED OUT OF main.cpp into src/boot_messages.h so the tests can see what the reader will see. 8 more tests, 74 in the suite: every body fits its 7 rows and every detail its 3 at 28 columns, titles fit centred, wrapping always makes progress (a wrap bug that returned 0 would hang the boot path of the very feature meant to stop the machine looking broken), long paths hard-break instead of vanishing, every message is printable in the 6847 font, the two ROM failures do not read alike, and each names the exact path.
One test failed first time and the error was mine again, in the expected value rather than the code: the first 8 characters of /COCO/ROMS/BAS12.ROM are /COCO/RO.
Rendered all five pages as text on the host to check the layout by eye (.ref/preview_pages.cpp, not committed). Still to do: see one on a real screen.]

[2026-09-27 DONE: seen on a real screen. The user booted a CoCo Zero with no microSD card and photographed the NO SD CARD page on a TV: title centred, body wrapped as written in src/boot_messages.h, detail line at the foot, in the CoCo font and green, with no black screen. Only that page was photographed; the other four (NO ROM FOUND, ROM FILE IS DAMAGED, EMULATOR DID NOT START, COLOR BASIC ONLY) are filed as PIZERO-144.]

summary: docs/kit.md: power & keyboard section -- supply sizing, power-bank gotcha, keyboard selection criteria
description:
WHY: docs/kit.md tells a recipient to use "any phone charger" (kit.md:32) and "any simple wired USB keyboard" and says nothing more. Both are underspecified in ways that produce silent, confusing failures -- an undersized supply or a power bank that switches itself off looks exactly like a dead unit, and a keyboard with a built-in hub is the most likely "it just doesn't work" report the PIZERO-91 kit will generate. Add a POWER & KEYBOARD section to docs/kit.md.

WHAT THE SCHEMATIC ESTABLISHES (verified 2026-08-25 by reading docs/RP2350-PiZero-schematic.pdf; these are facts, not estimates):
  * Main rail is a TMI3112H synchronous buck (1uH / 3.5A inductor, FB = 0.6V) -> 3V3. Grossly oversized for this load; the regulator is not the constraint.
  * BOTH USB-C PORTS SIT ON ONE SHARED VBUS NET, reaching VSYS through an MBR230LSFT1G schottky. There is NO load switch and NO polyfuse on the host port -- a keyboard draws straight from the input supply, minus one diode drop. (Consistent with PIZERO-11b/PIZERO-51: VBUS is never switched, there is no software VBUS control.)
  * Each port has 5.1K CC pulldowns (Rd, sink config), so the board presents as a legitimate 5V sink and C-to-C from a modern PD charger works -- it will not be starved.
  * CONSEQUENCE WORTH PRINTING: because VBUS is one net, plugging power into the "wrong" Type-C still powers the board; it just leaves the keyboard nowhere to go. That is a friendlier failure than kit.md:120 ("The two USB-C ports are different") currently implies, and the gotcha card can say so.
  * There is also an ETA6096 Li-ion charger and a BAT pad (R15 selects 1A / 2A / 2.5A charge current), so battery operation is a latent hardware option. NOT in scope for the kit; mention only if it stops the reader from wondering what the 2-pin connector is.

WHAT IS NOT KNOWN: Waveshare publishes NO power-consumption figure for this board -- not on the wiki, not in the schematic. The figures below are ENGINEERING ESTIMATES for the pizero_stream_60 product build (252 MHz, both cores saturated, PIO+DMA shifting TMDS continuously). Label them as estimates in the doc until measured.

  Board @ 3V3: RP2350B both cores ~100-130mA; TMDS drive into 4x 100R differential pairs ~40-60mA; SD card 20-100mA in burst during autorun only; LEDs/quiescent ~10mA. Total ~150-250mA @ 3V3, which through the buck at ~88% is ~120-190mA @ 5V -- call it 1W steady.
  Keyboard @ 5V, added on top: basic wired membrane 20-50mA; 2.4GHz wireless dongle 30-100mA; unlit mechanical 50-100mA; white-backlit mechanical 150-350mA; RGB gaming board 300-500mA and spikier.
  Worst realistic total ~0.7A @ 5V (~3.5W). Typical with a sane keyboard ~0.3A (~1.5W).

RECOMMENDATIONS TO WRITE UP:
  * SUPPLY: 5V / 2A (10W) minimum, 5V / 3A ideal. Any decent phone charger or PD brick. 1A technically works but leaves no headroom for a hungry keyboard plus inrush.
  * POWER BANKS -- THE REAL GOTCHA. At ~1.5W many banks decide nothing is connected and shut off after 15-30 seconds. If battery operation is suggested at all, specify a bank with a low-current / trickle mode; otherwise do not suggest it. This belongs on the gotcha card, not buried in prose.
  * KEYBOARD SELECTION CRITERIA: wired, dumb, no lighting, and -- most important -- NO BUILT-IN USB HUB OR PASSTHROUGH PORT. Pico-PIO-USB's hub support is the weak spot in that stack; a keyboard that enumerates as a hub with a HID device behind it is the likeliest hard failure. A plain 60%/65% wired membrane or an unlit mechanical is the safe pick and keeps the whole unit pocketable. A 2.4GHz wireless mini-keyboard is attractive (one endpoint, low draw, tiny) but MUST be tested -- the dongle has to present as a boot-protocol HID keyboard. This sits alongside the existing USB 1.1 / full-speed-only constraint already recorded in kit.md and README.md.

MEASUREMENT LEFT AS A TODO FOR THE USER (hardware, cannot be done by an agent): put a USB-C inline power meter between the charger and the power port, boot the pizero_stream_60 build, and record three states -- idle at the BASIC prompt, running a game, and with the keyboard attached. That converts every estimate above into a measured figure. Write the section with the estimates and a clearly marked placeholder, then fill in the real numbers; do not block the doc on the measurement.

Related: PIZERO-91 owns docs/kit.md itself. This is filed separately rather than folded into it because PIZERO-91 is already large and its remaining scope is the case decision and the BOM.

summary: 3D-printable case: parametric OpenSCAD shell for the Waveshare RP2350-PiZero
description:
WHY: docs/kit.md sec.5 plans off-the-shelf Pi Zero CNC shells (~$6) and notes they do NOT match this board's ports: two USB-C instead of micro-USB, plus a 2-pin BAT connector and a 3-pin debug header. kit.md already lists 'publish an STL once a printed design exists' as a follow-on. This ticket is that design.

TOOLING: OpenSCAD 2021.01 is installed (/Applications/OpenSCAD-2021.01.app) and BambuStudio for slicing. Code-defined CAD, so the agent can author and render it headlessly and every dimension stays a named parameter. Files live in hardware/case/.

REFERENCE GEOMETRY (Waveshare wiki dimension drawing, 800x400 px, scaled off the 65.00 mm callout; +/- ~0.2 mm, to be confirmed with calipers on a real board):
  board outline 65.00 x 30.00 mm, same as a Raspberry Pi Zero
  mounting holes dia 3.00 mm, Pi Zero pattern: 58 x 23 mm, 3.5 mm inset from each edge
  bottom edge, measured from the left edge:
    mini-HDMI   6.3 - 18.4 mm  (width ~12.0, centre ~12.35)
    USB-C PIO   34.3 - 43.9 mm (width ~9.6,  centre ~39.1)  <- USB host / keyboard
    USB-C power 48.8 - 58.4 mm (width ~9.6,  centre ~53.6)
  left edge:  microSD slot ~9.0 - 19.2 mm from the top edge
  right edge: 2-pin BAT JST ~6.4 - 15.6 mm from the top edge
  top edge:   40-pin 2.54 mm header
A Pi Zero puts its micro-USB ports at ~41.4 and ~54.0 mm, so the USB cutouts genuinely move.

STILL NEEDED (not derivable from a top-down drawing): PCB thickness, connector heights above the PCB, how far each connector overhangs the outline, header height, and tallest top-side component.

SCOPE: parametric .scad source, rendered STLs, a fit-test coupon (ports and holes only, ~10 min print) before committing to a full shell, and a short hardware/case/README.md. Openings for BOOT and RUN, the microSD slot, and the 40-pin header are design decisions to settle with the user.

DONE 2026-09-12. Confirmed on hardware: base and lid both print clean and no supports, board seats without force, case closes, ports line up, both buttons reachable through the vent slots. Case is 69.8 x 34.8 x 20.6 mm, four M2.5 x 12 countersunk screws. Source is hardware/case/pizero_case.scad, 493 lines and 78 parameters; STLs and a fit-test coupon render from it. Fourteen revisions, 578a84a..09d3767. Remainder filed as PIZERO-95, 96 and 97.

summary: Case: countersink is 72.5 degrees, not the 90 a standard screw head wants
description:
FOUND while speccing fasteners for PIZERO-94. screw_head_h is 1.5 mm across a 5.0 -> 2.8 mm taper, which is a 72.5 degree included angle. A standard DIN 965 M2.5 head is 90.

EFFECT: the head seats 0.20 mm below the outer face, bearing on the rim of the countersink rather than across the cone face. It is flush, it does not rock, and it clamps fine, so the printed base is usable as it is. Line contact will dig into the plastic over many open/close cycles.

FIX: screw_head_h 1.5 -> 1.1 makes it a true 90 degree cone. One line. Deliberately not applied yet, because it changes the base that is currently confirmed on hardware; fold it in whenever a base is reprinted for another reason.

[2026-09-25 APPLIED IN THE MODEL at the user's go-ahead: screw_head_h 1.5 to 1.1. Measured on the rendered base mesh: countersink 4.98 mm across, 1.09 mm deep, 90.0 degree included angle (was 72.5). A 4.7 mm DIN 965 head now seats on the cone face about 0.15 mm below the surface instead of on its rim at 0.20, and there is 0.4 mm more floor under each seat. Base only: BASE v9 to v10; base.stl and plate.stl re-rendered, lid files untouched. The v9 base in use is fine and does not need replacing.
DONE WHEN: a BASE v10 is printed and the screw heads seat flush and flat.]

[2026-09-25 DONE: BASE v10 printed; the user reports it "screwed together much nicer", so the 90 degree seat is right. The heads stood just proud enough in the last turns to scrape a desk, so seat DEPTH is filed separately as PIZERO-127 rather than holding this open.]

summary: Case: [?] parameters are still estimates, never measured against a board
description:
PCB thickness, USB-C and microSD connector heights, plug overmould sizes and the base relief depth are all still marked [?] in hardware/case/pizero_case.scad: estimates that were never checked with calipers. Everything fits, so they are right enough, but nobody knows by how much margin.

WHY IT MATTERS: the margins are invisible until a supplier changes a connector or the case is adapted to another board, at which point a wrong estimate reads as a mystery fit problem. Measuring them converts luck into knowledge.

HOW: the base wall rim sits exactly at the PCB top surface by design, so with a board seated the rim is a z-zero datum to measure connector heights against. Re-mark each parameter [M] once measured.

summary: Prove it runs 25 hours unattended: freezes and video dropouts per hour
description:
WHY: this board is regarded as the most stable of the RP2350 XRoar ports in everyday use, but no long run has ever been recorded here. There is no soak, no video-dropout counter, and PIZERO-33's persistent freeze counter has never caught a real freeze. The sibling Fruit Jam port has a measured 25-hour baseline of 7.6 video dropouts per hour, each about 1 s of black (its README, FRUITJAM-56/58). Until this board is measured the same way, "more stable" is an impression rather than a figure, and it is the figure the friends-and-family kit (docs/kit.md) rests on. Raised by the 2026-09-14 cross-port comparison (xroar-adafruit-rp2350-fruit-jam/docs/rp2350-port-comparison.html).

DO:
(1) Flash the default pizero_stream_60 env and start from a COLD power-on. A dev-tool reboot can leave freezes=1 residue (PIZERO-33).
(2) Log serial for at least 25 hours with wall-clock timestamps. The Fruit Jam port's scripts/serial_logger.py survives reboots and can be copied. Kill any previous logger first: two readers on one port produce "device reports readiness to read but returned no data", which reads exactly like a board fault.
(3) Record freezes=N and last phase, fps and cpu from the [run] line. The watchdog only sees core-0 hangs, so also sample the frame count on a fixed interval (Fruit Jam uses 150 ms) to catch a video fault while the emulator keeps running. Log on an interval, never only on change, so a quiet log cannot be confused with a dead probe.
(4) Keep a USB keyboard attached, since PIZERO-11b/31 attribute earlier freezes to USB-host load. If any freeze appears, run a second arm without the keyboard.
(5) Confirm the probe strings are in the flashed binary (strings on firmware.elf) before believing a zero.

COMPLETION CONDITION: freezes per hour and video-fault episodes per hour over at least 25 h, recorded here and in the README, stated against Fruit Jam's 7.6/hr. Zero is a valid result and would let PIZERO-33 close. Run in the same session as PIZERO-88 so the re-baselined frame budget comes from the same build.

[2026-09-17 Summary rewritten in the PIZERO-107 triage, move 4, to say what this delivers rather than how. Previous summary: "25-hour soak of pizero_stream_60: freezes per hour and video faults per hour, comparable with Fruit Jam's 7.6/hr"]

[2026-09-17 19:51 SOAK RUNNING. 25 h logged by scripts/soak.py to docs/measurements/logs/2026-09-17-1951-pizero_stream_60.log, on the post-PIZERO-119 build (frame 12.5 ms, 75% of budget, audio short 0.0%), cold-booted with the keyboard attached so it enumerates, AUTORUN loading OPIL-EN.dsk. The watchdog reported a freeze in 'frame-pace' at that boot; it coincides with the power cut so it is treated as baseline, not as a freeze during this run (see PIZERO-33).]

[2026-09-18 AT 13 HOURS, and the headline changed once the analyser stopped lying.
  uptime   99.981% of seconds in band, 5 bad windows in 13.07 h
  sound    shortfall 0.0%, underruns 0; but 402,769 ring-overflow skips, the PIZERO-121 defect
  sync     0.38 short windows/h, no silences
  crashes  THREE freezes, all in 'emulate', 0.23/h -- see PIZERO-33
I reported this run as clean at 4.9 h and that was wrong: the analyser was misattributing real freezes. Two bugs, one in the firmware and one in the harness, and they hid each other. The firmware computed the uptime in the freeze message as frames/52, a leftover from the off-spec ~52 Hz build, which overstates it by 15% at 60 Hz; the harness then compared that inflated number against the session that had just STARTED rather than the one that died, and concluded every freeze belonged to somebody else. Fixed in both places: the firmware now divides by 60, and the harness attributes by structure (only the first banner in a log can describe a session that began before we attached) rather than by arithmetic on a number the firmware got wrong.
COMPARISON THE TICKET ASKS FOR: the Fruit Jam's baseline is 7.6 video dropouts/h. This board shows 0.38 short windows/h and no video dropouts of the second-long kind, so on video it is far better. On crashes it is not clean at all: 0.23 freezes/h, every one recovered by the watchdog.]

[2026-09-18 THE HOST SLEPT AND WE LOST 43% OF THE RUN. 45 gaps totalling 5.68 h of a 13.14 h span, in ~16-minute chunks: the laptop sleeping and briefly waking with the lid closed. The board kept running throughout (it is on its own power and the telemetry resumes mid-stream); what stopped was us listening.
CONSEQUENCES, both now corrected in the harness: per-hour rates were divided by wall clock rather than by time OBSERVED, understating everything by 43%; and freezes that happened inside a gap leave no watchdog message to count. The board's own counter moved 6 while we saw 3 messages, so the true freeze count is about SIX in 13 h, i.e. ~0.46/h, not the 0.23/h reported earlier.
The analyser now reports wall clock and observed hours separately, lists the gaps, computes rates per hour observed, and flags when the board counter disagrees with the message count.
FOR THE REST OF THIS RUN AND THE NEXT: keep the lid open, or the Mac awake. A soak measured through a sleeping host is a soak of the host.]

[2026-09-18 A UF2 FLASH WAS MANUFACTURING FAKE FREEZES. Flashing reboots THROUGH the watchdog, so 'timer reset plus surviving magic' was enough to be reported as a freeze, and the payload was uninitialised: 'stuck in loop-top after ~268435456 frames (~51 days)', which is 0x10000000. Since the analyser counts these messages, every flash would have seeded the next soak with a phantom.
FIXED by sanity-checking the payload as well as the magic: a real freeze carries a plausible frame count (a week at 60 Hz is 36.3 M) and a phase that is one of ours. An invalid one now prints 'scratch invalid after a timer reset -- treating as a fresh start, not a freeze' and drops the carried tally. Verified on the next flash, which printed exactly that instead of a bogus freeze.
This is the third time a measurement bug has hidden behind a plausible-looking number in this ticket: frames/52, the attribution rule, and now flash scratch. Distrust the summary; read the raw line.]

[2026-09-28 CLOSED at ~80% on the user's call ('haven't we done 98 enough?').] Delivered: the comparison the ticket was for. Video 0.38 short sync windows/h and no second-long dropouts vs Fruit Jam's 7.6 dropouts/h; freezes about 0.46/h, all in 'emulate', all watchdog-recovered (PIZERO-33 owns them). Three measurement bugs found and fixed on the way (frames/52 uptime, freeze attribution, UF2 flash faking freezes). Recorded in README ('Stability, measured'). NOT delivered: 25 h observed (13 h wall clock, ~7.5 h observed; the host slept). Not re-run on the old build because the firmware has changed a great deal since (key layers, fonts, gamepad, hub). Filed as PIZERO-168: soak the current firmware, 25 h observed, paired with PIZERO-121's first long run.

summary: Picture locks on other people's TVs, not just the one development monitor
description:
The default pizero_stream_60 timing is 800x525 at 25.2 MHz with horizontal blanking split 8/96/56 (front porch / sync / back porch), narrowed from the standard to make room for HDMI audio data islands (PIZERO-44/45). It has only been validated on the one development monitor, and that monitor ignores HDMI audio clock regeneration (PIZERO-32), so it is also a lenient test of the audio packets. docs/kit.md plans a batch of about ten units for other people, who will plug them into TVs and monitors nobody here has tried.

DO: try at least three further sinks, ideally including a TV and an HDMI capture device or cheap HDMI adapter, which tend to be the least tolerant of off-standard blanking. For each, record: does it lock, time to lock, any edge rolling or shimmer, whether audio plays, whether pitch matches desktop XRoar (the ACR question in PIZERO-32), and behaviour after a cold boot and after switching the sink's input away and back.

COMPLETION CONDITION: a compatibility table in docs/kit.md (or the README) listing every sink tried and its result. A sink that rejects the timing becomes its own bug naming the model; do not hold this issue open for it. Revisit trigger for PIZERO-32: any sink that honours ACR and plays at a different pitch. Raised by the 2026-09-14 cross-port comparison (xroar-adafruit-rp2350-fruit-jam/docs/rp2350-port-comparison.html).

[2026-09-17 Summary rewritten in the PIZERO-107 triage, move 4, to say what this delivers rather than how. Previous summary: "60 Hz timing (8 px front porch, 56 px back porch) has only been verified on one monitor: test more sinks before kits ship"]

summary: Renderer draws $0400 when the SAM display base is legitimately $0000 (bug shared by all four RP2350 ports)
description:
lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp:522 and :1077 compute 'const uint16_t base = g_m.sam_f ? g_m.sam_f : 0x0400;'. Zero is treated as "never set", so a program that clears every SAM F bit to put the display at $0000 has $0400 drawn instead.

The identical line is in all four RP2350 XRoar ports: the AMOLED port (filed as AMOLED-70, open, high, inferred from source and not yet confirmed on hardware), the Fruit Jam (FRUITJAM-108) and the 4.3B (flagged by its uncommitted COCO-68 diagnostics). This glue descends from the AMOLED port.

IMPACT: probably rare, since BASIC and most software never place the display at $0000. The fallback presumably exists because SAM F reads 0 before BASIC initialises it, so a fix must not show a frame of $0000 garbage at boot: track whether F has been written, or start sam_f at the reset state desktop XRoar uses.

COMPLETION CONDITION: confirmed on hardware (clear the F bits with POKEs to $FFC6-$FFD3 in a graphics mode) and fixed, or shown not to occur, with the result noted in AMOLED-70 so the other ports can take the same fix. Found during the 2026-09-14 cross-port comparison (xroar-adafruit-rp2350-fruit-jam/docs/rp2350-port-comparison.html).

summary: Case style pass: base vents, 5 mm corners, rounded port openings, 2 mm groove loop on the lid

User feedback on the PIZERO-94 case, which works on hardware; changes are stylistic.

1. BASE VENTS: same slots as the lid (3 mm wide, 3 mm rib, 6 mm pitch, rounded ends) cut through the floor, running front to back. Two banks of four, 6 mm gap between banks, centred on the board.
2. CORNERS: outer vertical corner radius 4 -> 5 mm. Inner cavity radius stays 2 mm so board fit cannot change. Top edge stays a chamfer (a 5 mm fillet would break through the wall/roof).
3. PORT CORNERS: round the visible corners of the front port openings and plug pockets (HDMI, both USB-C).
4. GROOVES: widen from 0.5 to 2 mm (depth stays 0.6). Instead of running off the side walls, join front and back grooves with front-to-back legs near the left and right edges, just inside the top chamfer, with rounded corners: one closed loop outlining the top (user chose option (a)).

DONE WHEN: rendered, printed, and user confirms on hardware.

[2026-09-15 REV 2 after viewing rev 1 in the slicer: user happy with vents, port corners and vertical corners. Two changes. (a) Groove: legs move off the top onto the left and right side walls; front and back grooves wrap over the edge and down the sides, joined by a front-to-back leg with the rounded corners on the side face. (b) Top edge: the 1 mm chamfer becomes a 5 mm round matching the vertical corners; the cavity top is rounded 3 mm to keep the shell about 2 mm thick. Print note: roof-down, the bottom ~1.5 mm of the round is a shallow overhang at the bed.]

Battery connector opening (right wall, opposite microSD) tightened: right edge seen from outside pulled in 1 mm (bat_y1 23.6 -> 22.6), top lowered 0.5 mm (bat_oh 6.0 -> 5.5). No pitch centres both buttons with a centred grille; 5 mm gives each 0.65 mm of plunger under open slot (was 1.25). Paperclip test needed on the print. Base floor vents unchanged.]

summary: Alternate case lid with an opening over the 40-pin header, plugged by a printed cover when unused
description:
An alternate top for the PIZERO-94/101 case that exposes the 40-pin GPIO header, so a 2x20 female connector can be pushed on without a struggle. The base and the standard lid stay as they are; this is a second lid variant rendered from the same pizero_case.scad (part="top_header"). summary: A microSD card goes in easily, stays in, and can be pulled back out
description:
User report on the printed case: inserting a microSD card is unreliable. Sometimes the card goes right inside the case and misses the reader entirely; other times it will not enter the reader because it catches on the sides. The thumb dish cut into the base (sd_scoop straddles the split line) is unnecessary. The lid's slot and dish need to line up better with the actual socket.

DO: (1) re-derive the socket's card-entry position (y extent and height above the PCB) from the Waveshare dimension drawing, schematic/socket part, and board photos, replacing the sd_y0/sd_y1/sd_oh estimates; (2) remove the dish from the base; (3) resize and re-centre the lid slot on the socket mouth; (4) add internal guides between the wall and the socket, a funnel that narrows to the socket mouth in width and height, so the card cannot ride over the socket or catch its edges.

DONE WHEN: rendered, printed, and a card inserts and ejects reliably, confirmed by the user on hardware. Applies to both the standard lid and the PIZERO-102 header lid.

[2026-09-15 FINDINGS: socket is XunPu TF-110 (LCSC C266613): housing 11.95 W x 11.55 D x 1.32 H, latched card tail 3.90 mm out of the housing. Waveshare drawing puts the housing at y 10.9..22.9, front x 0.5; card y 11.4..22.4. Old slot y 9.8..21.5 was 1.2 mm forward (card caught on the back edge) and 2.5 mm tall (card could ride over the socket). FIX: channel 11.6 x 1.3 centred y 16.9, guide block on the inner wall face to 0.4 mm short of the housing, flared outer mouth, dish lid-only. Base no longer cut.]

[2026-09-16 PRINTED: card now goes in easily and stays in; user credits the side/bottom guide block. Two things left: the card latches FLUSH with the outer wall, and the round dish is too shallow to grip it. REV 2: (a) sd_front_x corrected 0.5 -> 1.5 [M] (flush card + 3.90 mm tail means the housing sits 1 mm further in than the drawing), so the guide block grows from 0.5 to 1.5 mm long; (b) finger relief 18 x 5 x 1.2 deep cut into the outer wall around the mouth in BOTH halves, replacing the dish, leaving the card 1.2 mm proud with a recess to pinch. Considered and rejected: shortening that edge, which caps at 1.0 mm on a 2 mm wall and shortens the channel.]

[2026-09-17 Summary rewritten in the PIZERO-107 triage, move 4, to say what this delivers rather than how. Previous summary: "microSD fit in the case: drop the base dish, re-align the lid slot to the socket, add card guides"]

[2026-09-25 DONE: confirmed on the TOP v12 print, which has the rev 2 channel and guide block plus the taller PIZERO-123 relief: "the microsd works well now."]

summary: Verify paperclip access to RUN and BOOT through the 1 mm roof vent slots
description:
Left over from PIZERO-101. The roof grille went from 3.0 mm slots to 1.0 mm slots on a 3.33 mm pitch (rev 5), which is what lets five rows fit between the grooves. Geometrically both buttons are well covered: rows 2 and 5 land within 0.07 mm of BOOT and RUN, with 1.18 mm of each 1.5 mm plunger under open slot (the model echoes this, _check_button in hardware/case/pizero_case.scad). But a 1 mm slot prints nearer 0.8 mm, and the 1.5 mm plunger diameter is itself inferred, not measured. Nobody has tried to press either button through a printed lid.

DO: with the case assembled, press RUN and BOOT through the grille with a paperclip or similar. If they cannot be reached, options in order of preference: widen just the two rows over the buttons; raise vent_w for the whole grille; or re-enable buttons_open for two 3 mm holes.

summary: Engrave a per-part version inside each case STL so a printed part maps to a revision
description:
Printed parts accumulate and become indistinguishable: several revisions of the lid look alike in the hand. Each part now carries its own version string, engraved on a face that is inside the assembled case, so it is readable before assembly and hidden after.

WHERE: base, on the floor between the two banks of floor vents (x 32.5, y 15, the 6 mm gap). Lid, on the roof underside, centred on the two USB ports (x 46.35) at y 2.2, in front of the groove loop; mirrored in the model so it reads correctly when looking up at the inside.

summary: Backlog triage: group every issue under one of seven themes and park the idea-stage work
description:
The tracker had grown to 106 issues, 69 of them live, with no structure: 225 free-form tags, summaries written for the implementer rather than the owner, and no statement of what 'done enough' means. At a glance it was impossible to tell a two-hour fix from a multi-month programme, so verification work competed with new features and lost.

MOVE 1 (this issue): every issue carries exactly one theme field from a fixed vocabulary, and issues.html filters and labels by it. Themes: trust (does it work, provably), kit (handing it to other people), input, experience (how the machine feels to use), storage (the VFS/hypercall replatform), devices (new video/audio hardware the CoCo never had), platform (the core port and its plumbing).

MOVE 2 (this issue): idea-stage low-priority issues move to status deferred, each with an explicit revisit trigger, so the live list states intent honestly. Deferring is reversible and loses nothing: the ticket and its reasoning stay.

STILL TO DECIDE (moves 3 and 4, deliberately not done here): a vetting milestone with a declared finish line, a ranked roadmap.jsonl, and rewriting the summaries of the issues that stay visible in terms of what the user gets. Free-form tags are left alone for now; theme is the new axis.

[2026-09-17 DONE. Moves 1 and 2 shipped in 2f946eb: all 107 issues themed, 17 idea-stage issues deferred with revisit triggers, issues.html filtering by theme. Move 4 done in part here: the eleven issues that stay visible on the roadmap were rewritten to say what they deliver, with the previous wording preserved in each description. Move 3 (a declared vetting milestone) is now expressed as the ranked roadmap.jsonl rather than a separate ticket.]

summary: Soak harness and a permanent measurement archive, so runs can be compared build to build
description:
The [run] telemetry line already carries everything the reliability goals need (fps, per-phase cpu/render/blit/audio times, USB line state and report counts, freeze count and the phase it froze in, audio ring fill/skips/underruns), but nothing captures it. Measurements live in issue comments and die there.

DO: (1) scripts/soak.py reads the serial port, timestamps every [run] line, survives board reboots, and writes raw CSV plus a summary; kill any previous reader first, two readers on one port produce a fake fault. (2) It computes the rates the goals are stated in: fps windows outside 59.9-60.1, audio underruns and skips per hour, freeze count and last phase, USB disconnect events. (3) docs/measurements/*.jsonl keeps one record per run: date, git hash, PlatformIO env, metric, value, plus a README describing the schema. Benchmarks may be deleted later; their numbers must not be.

WHY FIRST: PIZERO-98 cannot start without it, and every performance argument after this one wants a baseline to compare against.

COMPLETION CONDITION: a 30-minute trial run produces a record in docs/measurements and a readable summary.

[2026-09-17 BUILT: scripts/soak.py (record | analyse | ports) and docs/measurements/ with a README describing the schema. Record mode is the Fruit Jam logger's shape (timestamps, self-reconnecting, silence notices) plus a --hours stop and a git-state header. Analyse mode is separate on purpose, so a log can be re-read later by a better analyser, and it groups metrics by reliability goal rather than by source line. Cumulative board counters (freezes, skips, under, rfail) reset on reboot; the analyser sums increments across resets and counts banners as reboots_seen. VERIFIED against a synthetic 2.5 h log with a mid-run freeze and a reboot: duration, window count, bad windows, underruns summed across the reset (4+3=7), skips, freezes and reboots all came back exactly as constructed. NOT yet verified against a real board: no hardware attached this session. Remaining before this closes: one real 30-minute trial run, which is also the first archive record.]

[2026-09-17 FIRST REAL RUN, 3 minutes against the board on /dev/cu.usbmodem101. The harness worked end to end: it logged, survived the board rebooting under it, parsed, summarised and archived. It also earned its keep immediately by capturing the freeze PIZERO-33 has waited three months for. One weakness found in the metrics themselves, filed as PIZERO-118: the audio underrun counter climbs continuously at idle, so it cannot currently distinguish silence from a dropout, which is what goal 2 needs it to do.]

[2026-09-17 DONE. scripts/soak.py (record | analyse | ports) and docs/measurements/ with its schema README are in use and have proven themselves four times over: they caught the PIZERO-33 freeze in a 3-minute shakedown, exposed the audio shortfall behind PIZERO-118/119, measured the render fix before and after, and are now logging the 25-hour soak. Two analyser bugs were found and fixed by using it: cumulative counters must be summed across reboots, and a counter already non-zero when logging starts is a baseline rather than an event. Nothing outstanding.]

[2026-09-18 A THIRD ANALYSER BUG, and the most serious: freeze attribution. Real freezes were being reported as predating the log. The rule now is structural rather than arithmetic: a watchdog message describes the session that just died, so only the FIRST banner in a log can describe one that began before we attached; every later message is ours, and the first is flagged ambiguous rather than guessed at. The metric also stopped doing arithmetic on the board's freeze counter, which resets on reboot and can carry across a power cycle: one watchdog message is one freeze, and the counter delta is kept only as a cross-check. Lesson worth keeping: this harness has now found three of its own bugs by disagreeing with the log, and each one was found by reading the raw lines rather than trusting the summary.]

[2026-09-18 FOURTH HARNESS FIX: host-side gaps. A sleeping laptop loses telemetry the board still emitted, so rates must be per hour OBSERVED, not per hour of wall clock, and a freeze inside a gap leaves no message to count. The analyser now subtracts gaps from the span, reports both figures, and prints the board's freeze counter whenever it disagrees with the number of messages, which is the signal that something happened while we were not looking.]

summary: Unit tests on the laptop for the logic we wrote, so a bad edit fails in seconds
description:
XRoar's own core is trusted as-is; what needs tests is the glue this port added. No tests exist today and there is no native build.

DO: a PlatformIO [env:native] with Unity, running on the development machine, no board. First targets, chosen because they are pure functions with checkable outputs: (1) HDMI packet builders, ACR N/CTS pairs, AVI and audio InfoFrames, BCH parity and TERC4 encoding, against golden vectors from the spec; (2) the cross-core audio ring's fill/skip/underrun accounting, including wrap and overflow; (3) HID usage to CoCo matrix mapping, which PIZERO-49 is about to extend; (4) VDG address arithmetic, including the SAM display base case that is PIZERO-100 (that bug is four lines of test).

COST, STATED HONESTLY: this logic currently lives inside src/main.cpp (68 KB) and coco_machine.cpp. Testing it means extracting it. Extract only what a test touches, one module at a time; do not start with a refactor.

COMPLETION CONDITION: `pio test -e native` runs green in CI-less local use, with at least the four targets above covered.

[2026-09-17 FIRST SLICE DONE: [env:native] with Unity, 12 tests, `pio test -e native` green in 4 s on the laptop with no board.
Extracted lib/coco_machine/src/vdg_pack.h (header-only, no Arduino/Pico) and pointed coco_machine.cpp at it, so the tests exercise the code the firmware runs rather than a copy. Firmware still builds, RAM 70.9%.
Covered: pack8 nibble order (getting it backwards mirrors every glyph); SG4 across all 128 characters x 12 sub-rows against the original put2 reference; RG6 mono, RG6 artifact in both PIZERO-43 phases, and the colour-clock-spans-two-pixels rule; alpha in both colourings and the T1 glyph fold; and the SAM display base.
The reference implementations in the test file ARE the per-pixel versions PIZERO-119 replaced, kept on purpose so the fast tables are always checked against something readable.
PIZERO-100 is now pinned by a test: test_display_base_legacy_loses_address_zero asserts the CURRENT wrong behaviour, so whoever fixes it gets a failing test pointing at the fix, and vdg_display_base(sam_f, written) next to it is the intended version.
REMAINING on this ticket: the HDMI packet builders (dvi_data_island.c already has a DVI_DI_HOST_TEST path, so it should be cheap), the audio ring accounting, and HID-to-matrix mapping. lib_ignore keeps the board libraries out of the native build; extract further modules as tests need them.]

[2026-09-17 SECOND SLICE: 17 more tests for the HDMI data-island builders, 29 in total, still about a second on the laptop. dvi_data_island.c compiles straight into the test through its own DVI_DI_HOST_TEST path, so this is the firmware's encoder rather than a re-implementation. Covered: ACR field layout with the CTS=25176/N=6144 pair PIZERO-32 turns on, and that a 20-bit value keeps its top nibble; both InfoFrames' type/version/length plus the spec's sum-to-zero checksum rule, including the PB7 spill into the second subpacket; GCP mute bits; audio sample packet header, the 192-frame IEC block-start bit, little-endian sample bytes and frame-count clamping; BCH parity zero case, sensitivity to every header bit, and determinism; TERC4 symbols distinct and within 10 bits, pair packing, and the guard band not colliding with a data symbol.
One test failed on the first run and the bug was MINE, in the test's expected values, not the encoder's: 0xFDCBA >> 16 is 0x0F, not 0x0D. Worth recording because it is the ordinary case for a new suite, and the encoder came out clean.
REMAINING: the audio ring accounting and HID-to-matrix mapping, both of which need extraction work first.]

[2026-10-11 CLOSED at ~80% in the tracker clean-up. All four first targets now have host tests: VDG address arithmetic and PIZERO-100 (test_vdg_pack), HDMI packet builders (test_data_island), HID to CoCo matrix mapping (test_key_translate, from PIZERO-163), and the audio ring's fill dynamics through the servo simulation (test_audio_servo). The suite has grown to 237 cases across 18 suites (lockstep 6809, settings, text editor, catalogue, PNG, GMC and more); `pio test -e native` ran green on 2026-10-11 (236 pass, 1 skipped) in about 9 s. NOT covered: a direct test of coco_machine_audio_read's skip and underrun accounting branch; filed as PIZERO-207.]

summary: A self-test build the board runs on demand, printing PASS or FAIL for each check
description:
Unit tests on the laptop cannot see timing, DMA, or hardware. The goals that matter most (60 Hz uptime, continuous audio, no sync drops, no crash) are properties of the running board.

DO: [env:pizero_selftest], a firmware build that runs a fixed sequence and prints machine-readable results over CDC, driven by a host script so it can be repeated per build: ROM load from SD; SD read-back integrity; DVI lock and measured fps over a window; audio ring health after N frames (no underruns once primed); watchdog fires and recovers; USB enumerate, and replug if a device is present. Each check prints PASS or FAIL with the measured number, never just PASS.

DEPENDS ON PIZERO-108 for the measurement record format, so self-test results land in the same archive.

COMPLETION CONDITION: one command flashes, runs and reports, and its output is archived like a soak run.

summary: Decide which CoCo 3 graphics modes this chip can actually drive, before promising any
description:
CoCo 3 support is a stated goal, but the honest answer to 'can it?' is mode by mode, and nobody has done the arithmetic. The 6809 and the MMU are not the question; RAM and scanout bandwidth are.

DO: for each GIME mode, work out the framebuffer bytes at 512 KB guest RAM, the per-frame blit cost into the 320x240 RGB565 buffer this port scans out, and whether libdvi at 252 MHz can carry it at 60 Hz. Compare against the measured core-0 budget from PIZERO-88. Say plainly which modes are reachable, which are reachable only at reduced refresh or colour depth, and which are not reachable at all.

EXPECTATION TO TEST, NOT ASSUME: the 320-wide 16-colour modes look reachable and 640-wide 16-colour looks like the wall. That is instinct, and instinct is what this ticket exists to replace.

COMPLETION CONDITION: a table in docs/ of GIME mode against verdict and the numbers behind it, and a decision on whether CoCo 3 becomes a programme or stays an aspiration. Depends on PIZERO-88.

[2026-09-17 ANALYSIS DONE: docs/coco3-feasibility.md, with the numbers behind every verdict.
THE EXPECTATION IN THIS TICKET WAS WRONG, which is what it was for. Video is not the binding constraint; the 6809 is. A CoCo 3 runs at 1.79 MHz, double what we emulate today at a measured 10.4 ms per frame, so emulation alone would need ~20.8 ms of a 16.67 ms frame: about 80% of real speed before the GIME's MMU, timer and interrupts cost anything. docs/cpu-speed.md reached the same number from the SAM high-speed side.
RAM: 520 KB on-chip and the PSRAM pad is UNPOPULATED (README.md), so 512 KB CoCo 3 is not reachable on this board at any speed: it needs +448 KB and even deleting the whole framebuffer frees ~150 KB. 128 KB fits today with ~23 KB spare.
VIDEO: 320-wide GIME modes drop straight into our 320-wide framebuffer; 640-wide modes cannot use a framebuffer at all (640x240 RGB565 is 307,200 bytes) and need per-line generation into libdvi's scanline queue, which is libdvi's own supported path and would incidentally free 153,600 bytes. Per-mode table in the doc. Conversion cost for every mode lands in 0.3-3.0 ms, inside the ~4 ms headroom, so video is affordable once the scanout changes.
RECOMMENDATION: stays an aspiration, scoped 128 KB ONLY if ever taken up, and the first step is a 6809 dispatch experiment proved with the soak harness at an emulated 1.79 MHz. If that fails, no GIME work is worth starting.
REMAINING for this ticket: the user's decision on programme vs aspiration.]

[2026-09-17 DECIDED by the user: ASPIRATION, not a programme. Full CoCo 3 is not attempted; instead the port adopts GIME-compatible FEATURES it can afford on the CoCo 2 base, taking the register layouts from the real machine so unmodified software has a chance of working. First two chosen: palette customisation (PIZERO-55 for the classic 6847 modes, PIZERO-85 for the CoCo 3-style register file) and the programmable timer (PIZERO-62, un-deferred by this decision). Both were already costed as cheap here: the palette is a const-to-writable change on a LUT the blit already reads per pixel, and the timer generalises a countdown that already exists (cart_toggle_remaining). Neither needs the 6809 to get faster, which is what ruled the full machine out.]

summary: Prove a card survives power loss mid-write, before anything writes to it
description:
Goal 5 is no data loss. Today nothing writes to the card, so the goal is vacuously met and completely untested. The moment PIZERO-64/65 land, it stops being vacuous.

DO, alongside the write path rather than after it: a write-integrity corpus (write known files, checksum them back across remount and reboot) and a power-cut test (pull power during a write, repeatedly, and verify the filesystem and the untouched files survive). Record failures per hundred cuts in the PIZERO-108 archive.

WHY IT IS FILED NOW: writing the test with the write path is cheap, and retrofitting it after a corruption report is not. This ticket is the acceptance gate for PIZERO-64 and PIZERO-65, not an afterthought.

COMPLETION CONDITION: the corpus passes, and a hundred power cuts during writes leave no corrupted filesystem.

summary: Assign four drives from the overlay, the way a real disk system works
description:
Taken from the Fruit Jam implementation, which does this well and which the PiZero launcher tickets do not cover at all. Its picker shows four columns, one per drive, and keys 0-3 toggle the highlighted image into or out of that drive; it opens with the cursor on whatever disk sits in the drive DSKREG last addressed, and its status line reads NAME IN DRIVE d / DRIVE d EMPTY / LOAD FAILED.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE: this board is presented as a computer rather than a console, so multi-drive work (copying between disks, a system disk plus a work disk) is exactly the use case. PIZERO-81 as written is a single-selection launcher.

NEEDS: a runtime mount/eject API per drive. Fruit Jam has coco_machine_mount_dsk_drive(drive, ...) and coco_machine_fdc_drive() (coco_machine.h:122,126); this port mounts once via coco_boot_attach_dsk() with a sector-read callback and cannot swap at runtime. That API is the substance of this ticket.

COMPLETION CONDITION: four drives can be filled and emptied from the overlay, the machine sees the changes, and the screen opens on the drive last used.

[2026-09-26 PART OF THE CURRENT MILESTONE: four drives from the F12 overlay. Keys 0-3 toggle the highlighted .dsk in that drive (hot swap, no reset; see PIZERO-115). Disk data stays on the SD card read a sector at a time (no PSRAM here; Fruit Jam's whole-image loads dropped HDMI, FRUITJAM-97). One read-only FIL per drive; coco_boot_disk_read_sector serves drives 0-3 and an empty drive reports NOT READY; the FDC already decodes drives 0-3 from $FF40 (coco_machine.cpp:369-372). autorun.txt @DISK and the default disk still go to drive 0. The overlay opens on the drive last selected. Writes stay write-protected (PIZERO-66).]

[2026-09-26 LOWER HALF BUILT (no UI yet): src/coco_boot.cpp keeps one read-only FIL per drive; coco_boot_mount_drive(d, path), coco_boot_eject_drive(d), coco_boot_drive_path(d). coco_boot_attach_dsk() now mounts drive 0, so autorun behaves as before. coco_boot_disk_read_sector serves drives 0-3 and returns COCO_DISK_NOT_READY for an empty drive, which the FDC turns into WD279x status 0x80 (other errors stay 0x10). The reader is now installed whenever the Disk BASIC cart loads, not only when a disk was found, so drives filled later work. coco_machine_fdc_drive() reports the drive last selected at $FF40. RAM 73.1%. The overlay keys (0-3) come with PIZERO-81c.]

[2026-09-26 UI BUILT, not yet on hardware: keys 0-3 in the F12 overlay mount the highlighted image in that drive, or eject it if that drive already holds it; the list shows which drives hold each disk. The overlay opens with the cursor on the disk in the drive DECB last selected. RAM for the whole milestone: product build 71.1% to 73.1% (+10.5 KB, mostly the 128-entry catalogue); the double-buffered fallback env 'pizero' is now at 99.4% static RAM, so its headroom is thin. CHECK ON HARDWARE: F12 over running BASIC, 1 mounts, DIR 1 lists it, 1 again ejects and DIR 1 reports an error, ESC closes without a BREAK, audio silent while open and clean after, no picture drop.]

[2026-09-27 DONE: confirmed on hardware by the user: keys 0-3 in the F12 overlay put the highlighted disk in that drive and take it out again. Writes remain read-only (PIZERO-66).]

summary: Decide what ENTER does: cold boot the selection, or swap the disk under a running machine
description:
The two ports disagree, and Fruit Jam is inconsistent with itself (FRUITJAM-67): its button path mounts and cold-boots, its keyboard path hot-swaps under a running DOS. PIZERO-81d currently says cold-boot only.

THE TRADE: cold boot is predictable and always correct, but it throws away whatever is in memory, which is wrong when someone is mid-session and just wants the next disk of a two-disk program. Hot-swap is what a real drive does and is what makes the four-drive work in PIZERO-114 meaningful, but a swap under a DOS that has cached directory sectors can corrupt the guest's idea of the disk.

PROPOSAL TO TEST: ENTER swaps (a real drive door), SHIFT+ENTER or a second key cold-boots, and the status line says plainly which happened. Only adopt this if a swap mid-session is demonstrably safe with DECB.

COMPLETION CONDITION: one documented behaviour, consistent between every input path, with the reasoning recorded here.

[2026-09-26 PARTLY DECIDED: for DRIVE ASSIGNMENT (keys 0-3 in the overlay, PIZERO-114) the answer is hot swap with no reset, as Fruit Jam's keyboard path does. This board has no buttons, so FRUITJAM-67's two-paths-disagree problem cannot arise. The LAUNCH question (what ENTER does, PIZERO-81d) stays open here.]

[2026-09-27 DECIDED by the user, and IMPLEMENTED with PIZERO-81d: the overlay has three lists switched with Left/Right (disks, programs, cartridges). In every list ESC goes back to the running session untouched. DISKS: keys 0-3 hot-swap drives (no reset); ENTER cold-boots with the highlighted disk in drive 0 and runs its first program. PROGRAMS: ENTER cold-boots and loads and runs the .bin directly. CARTRIDGES: ENTER installs the cart and cold-boots into it (the cart FIRQ jumps to $C000). So: hot swap for drive assignment, cold boot for launching, one behaviour per key in every list.]

summary: RUN button cold-starts straight to the BASIC prompt, skipping AUTORUN
description:
USER DECISION 2026-09-25: pressing RUN is a cold start that skips AUTORUN and lands at the BASIC prompt. Predictable every time, and a way out if an AUTORUN title misbehaves. Power-on and every other kind of restart keep running AUTORUN as now.

HOW THE BUTTON WORKS (docs/RP2350-PiZero-schematic.pdf): RUN is Key2 on the RP2350's RUN pin, a hardware reset. Firmware never sees the press; it only sees that the chip restarted. So the whole feature is a decision at boot: read the reset reason and, if it was the RUN pin, take the no-AUTORUN path.

WHERE: the boot strategy is at src/main.cpp:1168-1206. coco_boot_load_autorun() reads /coco/autorun.txt; without it, the code already falls back to Disk BASIC (disk11.rom) with the default disk attached (coco_boot_find_default_dsk) and no autotype. A RUN press should take exactly that fallback, as if autorun.txt were absent. The AUDIO_WAV_DUMP build already skips autorun at line 1171, which shows the shape.

RESET REASON: RP2350 POWMAN CHIP_RESET has HAD_RUN_LOW (POWMAN_CHIP_RESET_HAD_RUN_LOW_BITS, 0x00040000, pico-sdk hardware/regs/powman.h:675). Check on hardware how it behaves across the other restarts this firmware sees, and that each of them still autoruns: cold power-on, the PIZERO-33 watchdog freeze recovery, the PIZERO-51 deliberate USB-replug watchdog reboot (scratch[4] sentinel, main.cpp:850-855), a picotool/UF2 flash (see the PIZERO-98 note on flashes rebooting through the watchdog), and BOOT+RUN into BOOTSEL. Also check whether the bits are sticky across a later non-RUN reset, and clear them if so.

DISCOVERABLE: print on serial and on the boot screen that AUTORUN was skipped because of RUN, so it is not folklore. Update AUTORUN.md and docs/kit.md (RUN is reached through the case vents with a thin wire, PIZERO-126).

DROPPED from the 2026-09-17 version of this issue, by the user: RUN as a WARM restart restoring the last state, with a double-tap within ~2 s for cold. That depended on PIZERO-82 (SD write) and on a press counter in watchdog scratch. A single, always-cold behaviour replaces it. A long hold was already ruled out because the chip is in reset while RUN is held.

SPLIT OUT: the BOOT-button half of this issue is now PIZERO-128.

DONE WHEN: on hardware, a RUN press with an AUTORUN title on the card lands at the BASIC prompt with no title loaded, while power-on still runs AUTORUN, and the restarts listed above each behave as before.

[2026-09-25 IMPLEMENTED, not yet on hardware.
src/main.cpp setup(): reads powman_hw->chip_reset first thing, sets g_run_button_reset from POWMAN_CHIP_RESET_HAD_RUN_LOW_BITS, and prints '[boot] chip_reset=0x........' on EVERY boot (with '(RUN button)' when set), so the hardware check of the other restart kinds is just reading that line.
Autorun block: if g_run_button_reset and autorun.txt loaded, it prints '[autorun] skipped: RUN button reset (PIZERO-116)', shows an AUTORUN SKIPPED boot page for 2.5 s, then clears have_autorun so the existing no-autorun fallback runs (Disk BASIC, default disk, no autotype). With no autorun.txt on the card nothing is skipped, so no page and no delay.
Message text in src/boot_messages.h (MSG_RUNSKIP_*), added to all the layout and printable-character checks in test/test_text_card; 84/84 host tests pass. pizero_stream_60 builds (RAM 71.1%); the new strings are confirmed in firmware.elf.
Docs: AUTORUN.md section E (the anti-kiosk interrupt it asked for) and the boot decision tree; docs/kit.md button paragraph.
TO TEST ON HARDWARE, card WITH an autorun.txt: power on (should autorun, chip_reset without RUN); press RUN (AUTORUN SKIPPED page, then the BASIC prompt); power cycle again (autorun). Also note the chip_reset value after a flash and after a USB-replug reboot, and that BOOT+RUN still enters BOOTSEL.]

[2026-09-27 DONE: confirmed on hardware by the user: pressing RUN lands at the BASIC prompt. The serial check of the restart cause across other restart kinds (flash, USB-replug reboot, power-on) was not captured, so it is filed as PIZERO-137 rather than holding this open.]

summary: After mounting a disk, offer to run what is on it
description:
Fruit Jam does this and it removes the last piece of ceremony: after a mount and cold boot it reads the RSDOS directory, finds the first runnable program, waits for the OK prompt and autotypes RUN"NAME" or LOADM (dsk_first_program(), autotype_task() in its coco_main.cpp).

THE REFINEMENT WORTH MAKING: Fruit Jam only does this on its button path, so the behaviour depends on how you got there. Here it should be a property of the selection, shown on screen before it happens (the overlay can name the program it found), and skippable. Nothing should type into a BASIC session without the user having seen what it was going to type.

DEPENDS ON PIZERO-81d for the cold-boot path. COMPLETION CONDITION: selecting a disk that has an obvious program runs it without the user typing anything, and the overlay says what it is about to run.

summary: The audio ring runs empty all the time, so nothing can tell silence from a dropout
description:
Found by the first PIZERO-108 harness run, 2026-09-17, on the default pizero_stream_60 build with a disk autorunning. Every [aud] line in three minutes read ring fill=0 or 1, and the underrun counter climbed steadily by roughly 400 to 500 per second, through 77,934 underruns across the run. The audio phase time was 0 to 2 us throughout.

TWO SEPARATE PROBLEMS, AND BOTH MATTER.

(1) THE METRIC IS USELESS AS IT STANDS. Goal 2 is continuous sound, and the number meant to prove it counts the same whether the machine is silent or the audio has genuinely broken. Any soak result for goal 2 is currently unreadable, including the 25-hour run in PIZERO-98.

(2) THE BEHAVIOUR ITSELF NEEDS EXPLAINING. The expected design after PIZERO-41 is an event-driven integrate-and-dump resampler keyed to PIA writes, so a machine making no sound produces no events and the ring legitimately drains, with the consumer repeating the last sample as DC. If that is what is happening, the fix is in the accounting, not the audio. But a permanently empty ring also describes a consumer starved of a stream it is supposed to receive, and the HDMI sink is locked to that stream: it cannot be assumed benign without checking.

DO: determine which it is, on hardware, with something audible playing (the PIZERO-18 ascending-tone test is the obvious source). If the ring fills and underruns stop while sound plays, this is accounting: count underruns only while the source is producing, or feed silence continuously and keep the counter meaning what it says. If the ring stays empty while sound plays, it is a real defect in the streaming audio path.

COMPLETION CONDITION: an [aud] reading that distinguishes 'nothing to play' from 'failed to deliver', and a soak record whose goal-2 number can be read at face value. Blocks the audio half of PIZERO-98.

[2026-09-17 DIAGNOSED, and the first reading of it was wrong. The producer is NOT event-gated: audio_integrate() runs from the per-memory-access path and emits a sample every 1/48000 s of emulated time regardless of whether the machine is making sound (coco_machine.cpp:732). So an empty ring never meant 'nothing to play'. Measured from the trial log: underruns run a median of 321/s against a 48 kHz stream, which is a 0.67% DELIVERY SHORTFALL, sustained, with fill pinned at 0-1. The consumer reads one sample per call from the per-line IRQ (main.cpp:610) and holds the last sample when the ring is dry, so roughly 320 times a second the stream carries a repeat instead of a sample. That is a real defect, not an accounting artefact, and it is a plausible contributor to the buzz in PIZERO-41.

METRIC FIXED: coco_machine now counts samples produced and how many were audible (coco_machine_audio_counters), and the [aud] line reports RATES: fill, prod/s, want/s, under/s, short=%, tone/s, plus the cumulative totals. A silent machine now shows prod == want with short=0.0%; a broken stream shows the shortfall directly. scripts/soak.py reads both shapes and says explicitly when a log predates this change and therefore cannot answer goal 2.

REMAINING, and the reason this stays open: the underlying rate mismatch. The source produces ~47,680 samples/s where the consumer asks for 48,000. Prime suspect is the same one as PIZERO-32: the consumer is paced by the real pixel clock while the producer is paced by emulated CoCo time, and the two do not agree. Next step is to read prod/s on hardware with the new build and see whether it is steady (a fixed clock ratio, fixable by deriving the sample rate from the pixel clock) or ragged (a scheduling problem).]

[2026-09-17 ROOT CAUSE FOUND, and it is not in the audio path. Measured on hardware with the new telemetry (docs/measurements/logs/2026-09-17-1742-pizero_stream_60.log, 61 windows):
  frame work    16,821 us median against a 16,667 us period = 100.9% of budget
  producer      47,534 samples/s median against 48,000 = 99.03%, i.e. emulated time runs 0.97% slow
  correlation   -0.64 between frame work and samples produced
Those two deficits are the same deficit. Audio is paced by emulated cycles (audio_integrate runs off the memory-access path), so when a frame does not fit in 16.67 ms the machine runs slow and about 1% of samples are never made. The ring primes to ~3,900, drains to empty in ~25 s, and from then on the consumer holds the last sample 250-650 times a second.

SO THE AUDIO ACCOUNTING IS NOW CORRECT AND THE AUDIO PATH IS NOT AT FAULT. Fixing this is either (a) get frame work under 16.67 ms, which is PIZERO-88's territory, or (b) decouple delivery from emulated time so a slow frame borrows from a buffer instead of starving the stream. Filed as PIZERO-119.

This ticket now needs only the tone counter confirmed on hardware: the first version counted absolute level and so read tone == prod exactly, because the DAC rests far from zero. It now counts sample-to-sample change instead. Built but NOT yet flashed.]

[2026-09-17 VERIFIED ON HARDWARE after flashing (docs/measurements/logs/2026-09-17-1757-pizero_stream_60.log). The line now reads what it should on a silent machine: prod=47,534-47,723/s, want=48,000/s, short=0.4-0.9%, tone=0/s, and the analyser reports 'audible in 0/61 windows'. Silence and shortfall are now separately legible, which is what this ticket asked for. CAVEAT, stated rather than glossed: only the tone=0 case is proven. Nothing on the board was making a sound during the run (no keyboard attached to type a SOUND command), so the tone>0 path is still unverified. The obvious check is the PIZERO-18 ascending-tone program once a keyboard is attached, or any disk title with audio.]

[2026-09-17 DONE. The [aud] line reports rates (fill, prod/s, want/s, under/s, short=%, tone/s) and a silent machine is now distinguishable from a short stream, which is what this asked for. The shortfall it exposed turned out to be PIZERO-119 (the frame not fitting) and is fixed: 0.9% -> 0.0%. The tone>0 path is still unproven, since nothing has made a sound during a measured run; that check rides along with the audible test in PIZERO-41 rather than holding this open.]

summary: The machine runs about 1% slow, because a frame does not fit in 16.67 ms
description:
Measured 2026-09-17 on the default pizero_stream_60 build, idle at an autorun disk with no keyboard attached (docs/measurements/logs/2026-09-17-1742-pizero_stream_60.log, archived in docs/measurements/2026-09.jsonl).

  cpu 10,383 us + render 4,862 us + blit 1,580 us = 16,821 us of work per frame
  frame period at 60 Hz                            = 16,667 us
  emulated time therefore advances at 99.03% of real time

EVIDENCE IT IS REAL, not an artefact of overlapping timers: the audio producer, which is paced by emulated cycles, delivers 47,534 samples/s where the stream asks for 48,000, and frame work correlates -0.64 with samples produced across 61 windows. Two independent measurements of the same 1%.

WHAT IT COSTS: the HDMI audio ring drains to empty about 25 s after boot and stays there, so the stream carries a repeated sample 250-650 times a second for as long as the machine runs (PIZERO-118). A CoCo running 1% slow is also 1% flat in pitch and 1% slow in every timing loop a program depends on.

TWO WAYS OUT, and they are not exclusive:
(a) SPEND LESS PER FRAME. render at 4.86 ms is the obvious target: it regenerates the whole VDG buffer every frame regardless of what changed. blit is 1.58 ms. Either could plausibly find the 154 us needed, and more.
(b) STOP COUPLING DELIVERY TO EMULATED TIME. Give the ring enough depth and a rate adaptation so a frame that runs long borrows from the buffer rather than starving the consumer. This hides jitter but cannot hide a sustained deficit, so it is a complement to (a), not a substitute.

DO NOT close this by lowering the audio sample rate to match the deficit: that fixes the symptom the telemetry reports and leaves the machine running slow.

COMPLETION CONDITION: frame work median under 16,667 us with a keyboard attached, and prod/s within 0.1% of want/s across a soak run. Relates to PIZERO-88 (the budget), PIZERO-118 (how it was found), PIZERO-40 (pool depth).

[2026-09-17 FIXED, measured on hardware. The hot path was NOT a graphics mode: it was SG4 semigraphics, which lives inside render_alpha_frame, so the mode bits read 'alpha' and the cost hid behind the text path. An SG4 screen did 8 put2 read-modify-writes per cell, 49,152 a frame. It now indexes a 32-entry table (colour x two block bits) for one packed 32-bit store per cell.
  render      4,883 us -> 478 us
  frame total 16,589 us (99.5% of the period) -> 12,902 us (77.4%)
  audio       prod 47,5xx/s, short 0.9% -> prod 48,005/s, short 0.0%, ring stable at ~4,060
Verified byte-identical to the put2 version across all 1,536 cases (128 SG4 characters x 12 sub-rows) with .ref/sg4check.cpp. Log: docs/measurements/logs/2026-09-17-1942-pizero_stream_60-sg4lut.log.

REMAINING before this closes: (1) the same measurement with a keyboard attached, since USB cost is still not in any of these numbers; (2) a real graphics mode (RG6/PMODE) measured, as those paths were LUT'd in the same work but never exercised; (3) user confirmation on hardware.]

[2026-09-17 WITH A KEYBOARD, cold-booted so it enumerates (usb=1): frame 12,504 us median = 75.0% of the period, p99 13,443 us, cpu 10,475 us, render ~470 us, blit ~1,550 us. USB and keyboard cost about 350 us. Audio steady: prod 48,010/s, short 0.0%, ring holding ~4,130. Log: docs/measurements/logs/2026-09-17-1944-pizero_stream_60-keyboard.log. Note the keyboard had to be present at boot: attaching it later leaves usb=0 and rpts=0, which is PIZERO-11b.]

[2026-09-17 RG6 ARTIFACT PATH EXERCISED at last, via a BASIC loop parked in PMODE 4 (10 PMODE 4,1:SCREEN 1,1:PCLS / 20 GOTO 20). Telemetry reads mode=gm7c, so this is the artifact LUT, not the mono one. render 211 us, frame total ~12.9 us thousand (77% of the period), audio prod 48,009/s short 0.0%, ring stable at ~4,550, keyboard attached (usb=1, rpts=284). Log: docs/measurements/logs/2026-09-17-1948-pizero_stream_60-pmode4.log. All three render paths are now measured on hardware and none of them threatens the budget: SG4 478 us, RG6 artifact 211 us, alpha text ~430 us. Nothing remains on this ticket except the user's word to close it.]

[2026-09-17 CLOSED by the user after hardware measurement. Delivered: the SG4 and RG6 render paths converted from per-pixel put2 read-modify-writes to packed 32-bit stores from small tables, verified byte-identical across 2,304 cases, and the graphics row packer no longer re-packs a row for each display line it repeats. Frame work went from 16,589 us (99.5% of the period) to 12,504 us (75.0%) with a keyboard attached, and the audio delivery shortfall from 0.9% to 0.0%. NOT done, deliberately: nothing was attempted on the cpu phase itself (10.5 ms, the XRoar core, which we trust as-is), and no dirty-region tracking was added because the budget no longer needs it.]

summary: A vertical band of fuzz down the centre of the picture on one LCD monitor
description:
User report 2026-09-17: a band of fuzz runs down the centre of the screen on one LCD HDMI monitor. The rest of the picture is correct. The same monitor is clean when driven by a MacBook Pro, so it is not a monitor defect.

RULED OUT BY EXPERIMENT, not by reasoning:
- Audio data islands. dvi_setup_active_audio_line() places every island inside the horizontal BACK PORCH, before the video preamble and guard band, so it never touches active pixels. Confirmed by flashing pizero_60hz (no audio, no data islands): band still present.
- The narrowed 60 Hz blanking (8/96/56). pizero_60hz uses HDMI_60HZ_TEST, i.e. standard 16/96/48 blanking: band still present.
- Buffer tearing. pizero_60hz is double-buffered, and the band appears on a STATIC green BASIC screen where the blit writes identical pixels every frame.
- A seam in the encoder. _dvi_prepare_scanline_16bpp encodes each channel of a line in ONE call (dvi.cpp:129), so there is no mid-line chunk boundary to explain a centred band.

REMAINING SUSPECTS: libdvi's TMDS encoding (its fast table does not track running disparity the way a full encoder does, and a flat colour field is the most repetitive symbol pattern a sink can be given), board-level signal integrity, or this scaler's response to a 320x240-doubled 640x480 source.

NEXT TEST: the stock vendor demo (env waveshare_demo, Waveshare's own libdvi example). If the band appears there too, nothing in this port causes it and the question becomes libdvi or the board. If it does not, the difference is in our scanout path.

WHY IT MATTERS: kits are meant to go to other people's screens (docs/kit.md), so a flat-field artefact on an ordinary LCD is a shipping blocker, not a curiosity. Related: PIZERO-99 (timing on other sinks).

[2026-09-17 KEY OBSERVATION from the user: the band is visible only when the picture is in COLOUR. Black and white content does not show it.

WHY THAT MATTERS: it moves the suspicion from timing to signal levels. Pure black and white are the cheapest patterns a TMDS link carries; mid-range colours produce many more transitions per line. Combined with the band being fixed in position and present on a STATIC screen, the shape of the fault is 'marginal signal, revealed where the panel is most sensitive' rather than anything frame- or content-timed.

SUPPORTING GUESS, not yet tested: many LCD panels drive the screen as two halves with separate source drivers, and a seam at dead centre is where a marginal input shows first. That would explain why this monitor shows it and others do not, without the monitor being faulty (it is clean from a MacBook, which has a full TMDS encoder and a different cable).

NEXT TESTS, cheapest first, none needing a reflash: (1) a different and ideally shorter HDMI cable; (2) a different input port on the same monitor; (3) the same board on other screens (PIZERO-99).
THEN, if those do not settle it: libdvi's encoder does not track TMDS running disparity the way a full encoder does, and its 16bpp path maps each RGB565 value through a fixed table (lib/libdvi/tmds_table_fullres.h). A colour-only artefact is consistent with particular table entries being poorly balanced. Testing that means changing a palette entry and seeing whether the band changes with it, which needs the board free.]

[2026-09-17 CABLE RULED OUT by the user, who reads it as a data or monitor issue. Source read, and the mechanism is now understood well enough to stop guessing.

WHAT OUR ENCODER DOES: the product path is tmds_encode_data_channel_16bpp (lib/libdvi/tmds_encode.cpp:67), the pixel-doubling scheme. Its table turns each 6-bit channel value into a PAIR of symbols whose net DC balance is zero (lib/libdvi/tmds_table.h header). Two things follow.
(1) Running disparity cannot accumulate along a line, so a band partway across CANNOT be DC drift. That rules out the theory this ticket was heading toward.
(2) The pair is a symbol and its near-complement, so a FLAT COLOUR FIELD alternates symbols every pixel for the whole line: the highest transition density the link can be asked to carry. Black and white map to benign low-transition symbols, which is exactly the reported pattern of when the band appears.

CONCLUSION: our data is spec-legal but is the worst case for a receiver's equalisation, and this monitor appears to fail on it in one region (a panel's two driver halves meeting at centre is the usual reason a fault sits there). It is a real interaction, not a defect in the port, and a second screen showing no band would settle it.

OPTION IF IT EVER MATTERS: libdvi's full-resolution encoder does true per-pixel running disparity and does not force alternation, but its own comment calls it 'barely possible, utterly impractical' on CPU cost, and we have ~4 ms of frame headroom, not 4 ms to burn on this. Do not attempt it for one monitor.

PRIORITY DROPPED high -> medium: one monitor, understood mechanism, no evidence yet that any other sink is affected. Re-raise immediately if PIZERO-99 finds a second screen with it.]

[2026-09-18 REPRODUCED ON A SECOND BOARD, same monitor, freshly flashed with the current product build. That rules out the one thing that would have made this a non-issue: a marginal individual unit, a bad joint, one chip's drive strength. It follows the DESIGN, so every unit we hand out will do this on a monitor like that one. PRIORITY BACK TO HIGH (it was dropped to medium on 2026-09-17 when it looked like one board plus one fussy screen).

WHAT IS NOW ESTABLISHED, all by experiment: not the cable, not the audio islands, not the narrowed blanking, not tearing, not an encoder seam, not a single unit. What remains is our symbol stream meeting this panel: the pixel-doubling encoder emits each pixel as a symbol and its near-complement, so a flat COLOUR field alternates symbols every pixel, the densest transition pattern the link can carry, while black and white land on benign symbols. The band is where that panel is least tolerant.

NEXT EXPERIMENT, now cheap because there are two boards and one is free: flash pizero_gime on the spare and POKE individual palette entries ($FFB0-$FFBF) to walk a colour through the RGB565 space while watching the band. If the fuzz tracks specific colour VALUES, it is the symbol pattern and we can pick friendlier palette entries as a mitigation; if it only tracks 'not black or white', it is broader and the honest answer is a compatibility note. Either way it is the first test that can distinguish them, and it needs no new code.
STILL WANTED: PIZERO-99, other screens, to bound how many sinks are affected.]
