summary: Two watchdog recoveries in frame-pace after an unexplained power-on during the PIZERO-168 soak
description:
From the first card-logged soak (PIZERO-168, docs/measurements/logs/2026-10-09-1153-pizero_stream_60-card.log). Product build of 2026-10-09 (fw v0.7.2-292-gd3ec182-dirty, soak_log on), powered from a monitor's USB-C port, keyboard and pad through the simple hub, no laptop. 22.8 h with no freeze; then a power-on (file soak-002, 'boot=power-on') of unknown cause; then watchdog recoveries 1 h 39 min and 3 h 36 min after it, both recorded in phase frame-pace (WP_PACE, src/main.cpp ~1995 onward: the 1 Hz telemetry block and the pacing wait). Not the soak logger: both hangs began mid-minute (about 18 s and 33 s after its last write, and those writes reached the card), with WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT_MS 3000. PIZERO-98's freezes were all in emulate, so this is a different place. LEADS: (1) everything after wd_phase(WP_PACE) that can block for 3 s: Serial printf over USB CDC if a host holds the port open without reading (was the monitor's USB-C port a hub on a computer?), the pacing loop if micros() and next_us diverge, any SD access there; (2) whether the power-on was the monitor (standby, or its USB port resetting) and whether the board's state after a brown-out differs; (3) add the watchdog's stuck-phase detail at finer grain inside WP_PACE (a sub-phase marker before telemetry, before pacing) so the next occurrence names the line. DONE WHEN: the next soak shows no frame-pace freezes, or one is pinned to its line. 2026-10-10, from the user: nobody touched the power; the restarts came after they opened the F12 overlay, not immediately. So the 10:40 'power-on' was most likely a crash: the header writes power-on for any reset that is not the watchdog, and a HardFault or assert resets through __NVIC_SystemReset (crash.c), which looks the same. The log confirms the overlay was open three minutes into boot 2 (cpu=0us at 17:54:22 board time) and shows nothing unusual in the minutes before the restart (steady cpu, full audio ring). LEAD FOR THE FRAME-PACE FREEZES: the WP_PACE section is only the pacing delay and the 1 Hz telemetry (Serial prints, then soak_log_tick). arduino-pico SerialUSB::write (cores/rp2040/SerialUSB.cpp) spins while tud_cdc_connected() and the buffer is full, until a second passes with no progress, and any progress restarts that second; so a host that holds the port open and reads slowly stalls each print, and the telemetry is several prints (PIZERO-201 split [run] and [aud] into two each). That needs the port open on some host, which fits if the monitor's USB-C port is a hub on the Mac. PLAN: (1) the soak header records rp2040.getResetReason() (PWRON, BROWNOUT, SOFT, WDT, RUN_PIN, GLITCH), so a crash and a supply dip are told apart; (2) sub-phases inside WP_PACE (pace delay, serial telemetry, soak log) so the watchdog names the line; (3) telemetry never waits on USB: skip a line when Serial.availableForWrite() cannot take it, as the Fruit Jam port does; (4) re-soak with deliberate overlay use, noting whether the monitor's USB-C is a hub on a computer. 2026-10-10 user: the monitor's USB-C port IS a hub on the Mac, so the board's USB serial port was on the Mac all along. BUILT: (1) [boot] reset reason line and reset=<power-on|software|watchdog|brownout|run-pin|glitch|debugger|unknown> in the soak header (rp2040.getResetReason); soak.py reports reset reasons and counts a software reset after the first boot as a crash, not a power-on; (2) phases WP_TELEM ('telemetry') and WP_SOAKLOG ('soak-log') after WP_PACE, WP_LAST for the scratch sanity check; (3) tprintf/tele_write: the 1 Hz block prints only if the previous second drained (availableForWrite >= 192 of 256), each line gets 10 ms to find room, else the rest of the second is dropped and counted as tdrop= on the [run] line. Builds: pizero_stream_60 75.8%, pizero_stream 75.7%, pizero_wavmeas 99.5%; native 236 pass. NEXT: reproduce on the board by holding the port open without reading, old firmware then new. TESTED 2026-10-10 on the board, plugged into the Mac directly, soak firmware rebuilt from 995b5ec: a host holding the port open without reading for 60 s and then 540 s, and one draining 16 bytes every 0.5 s for 120 s, caused no slow second (badfps unchanged) and no freeze. macOS keeps accepting CDC data and drops what nobody reads, so it never back-pressures the board: the serial-stall theory does NOT explain the soak's frame-pace freezes. The guard (0b3166c) stays, as protection against hosts that do push back. The finer phases and the reset reason are now on the board (current firmware, from HEAD plus the clock diagnostics); a reflash reads as reset=software, so the analyser would count a reflash mid-run as a crash. NEXT: re-soak with the overlay used on purpose (the user's observation: the restarts followed overlay use, not immediately) and read the phase and reset reason of whatever happens. Side note: after the card was swapped this afternoon the board was silent on serial with its USB device unchanged since 14:36, i.e. it seems to have stayed powered while its card was removed and reinserted; it was restarted by flashing. RE-SOAK 2026-10-10 (firmware b952ed7, board on the Mac's port): clean at 1 h 35 min (freezes 0, badfps 4, tdrop 0, audio ring full, no underruns). The user then opened the overlay and launched a game; read at 16:56 local, uptime 1 h 43 min (sof 6,185,731 ms), still clean (badfps 6 counts the launch's own seconds). Watch the 1.5 h to 4 h after that launch: last soak's freezes came 1 h 39 min and 3 h 36 min after overlay use.

[2026-10-12 END OF THE RE-SOAK, partial evidence. The soak board is unit 10 (USB serial 8DEF17616A6EA5F1, sticker 234220, qc/qc-log.csv). The user moved it to the Mac's USB port this morning; about 39 s after that boot its telemetry read freezes=1 last=emulate badfps=1, fps 60, cpu ~10.7-11.1 ms, audio clean, keyboard and pad attached (usb=2), a game in gm7c. A power-on should clear the tally, so either it froze in emulate within a minute of the move and the watchdog recovered it, or the tally survived the move. Note emulate, not frame-pace: if real, it is the PIZERO-98 phase again, which the runaway guard should have turned into a [runaway] line instead.]

Unit 10 then went to the PIZERO-209 profile builds for ~10 minutes (their boots also log to the card, env=pizero_cpuprof*) and back to the product build; the soak continues from there.] [2026-10-13 BENCH BOARD C58D06257AE30E85 FREEZES TOO, ON EVERY BUILD. Its card (/coco/log/soak-001..027, the relevant ones copied to docs/measurements/logs/bench-card-2026-10-13/) shows watchdog recoveries before any PIZERO-131 code: frame-pace twice (d3ec182, soak-003/004), emulate twice and VDG-render once (0b3166c, soak-010/011/012), about 5 in 45 h. Since PIZERO-131 (soak-013..027, about 17.6 h): blit (soak-020, 3 min into a played game at 55 fps, 4ed9fe4-dirty cpu179), emulate (end of soak-021 after 7 h 46 min unattended overnight, same build), emulate (soak-024, 16 min, after the Daggorath bench, 05956c5 cpu179), frame-pace (soak-026, 45 min idle at the BASIC prompt with no keypresses, product build 4cc400b). 4 in 17.6 h is about twice the earlier rate, but on 4 and 5 events that is not a meaningful difference, and the phase mix (frame-pace, emulate, blit, VDG-render) is the same before and after. Read: one fault that lands in whatever phase is running, not something PIZERO-131 introduced. Unit 10 (pre-131 build) had its first frame-pace recovery at about 17.5 h. summary: Board clock seeded hours ahead: NOS9L1.DSK copied to the card at ~14:45 carries a FAT time of 22:39
description: Found 2026-10-10. The board seeds its always-on clock at power-on from the newest file time on the card (PIZERO-201). After NOS9L1.DSK was copied from the Mac (cp, ~14:45 EDT), the board reported '[clock] newest in 0:/coco/dsk: NOS9L1.DSK 2026-10-10 22:39:58', about 8 h ahead, while other Mac-written files on the card (zork1.dsk, the cart ._ files) read as sensible local times; the board's later files then carried the wrong time forward because the clock is kept across reboots when no file is newer. The firmware now prints the newest file in each scanned folder at boot ('[clock]   newest in ...'), which is how this was found. DO: with the card on the Mac, read NOS9L1.DSK's raw timestamps (stat, and the exFAT/FAT directory entry, including exFAT's UTC offset field if the card is exFAT) and find whether macOS, cp, or FatFs's reading is the cause; then either fix fat_to_time (e.g. apply the exFAT UTC offset) or drop implausible outliers from the seed. Until then, deleting the board's soak logs dated in the future and re-touching NOS9L1.DSK puts the clock right at the next power-on.

summary: Measure where the 185 host clocks per emulated 6809 cycle go: hook versus core, dummy cycles, cycles per instruction
description:
First step of PIZERO-131, agreed with the user 2026-10-12. PIZERO-130 measured 185.4 host clocks per emulated cycle as a whole; nobody has measured the split, and the PIZERO-131 plan rests on a guess (hook ~60-70, core ~115). That split decides whether 131 is plumbing (batching the per-cycle bookkeeping, inlining RAM/ROM) or a core rewrite. Dummy cycles alone were estimated at only ~3 clocks per cycle of saving.

DO: a profiling build using the Cortex-M33 cycle counter (DWT CYCCNT via m33_hw), never micros(), which is far too coarse per cycle (the old AMOLED-52 PROFILE_MEM_CYCLE used micros and is replaced). Count per second: emulated bus cycles, dummy (NVMA, address $FFFF) cycles, opcode fetches; time the bus path (interrupt latch stores + call + coco_mem_cycle) as one window in the 6809's fetch/store helpers, and the whole run with CYCCNT. Calibrate the cost of a timing window at boot and subtract it. A second build splits the hook into its sections (decode, data, events and audio, irq and budget). Print a [prof] line once a second. Report: total clocks per cycle (check against 185.4), bus path per cycle, core = the rest, % dummy cycles, cycles per instruction, and the hook sections.

DONE WHEN: both builds measured on the board on the PIZERO-130 workload (BASIC prompt after autorun DIR), numbers archived and written into PIZERO-131 with a revised plan.

Also possible later: instruction-level attribution in the cocozero emulator (~/github/cocozero-emulator), which has no profiler today; that would be a change in that project, by its own session.

[2026-10-12 BUILT, not yet run on the board. lib/xroar_core/include/cpu_prof.h: DWT CYCCNT by its architectural address (the SDK's m33.h pulls in stdbool.h, which breaks XRoar's token-pasted delegate names). mc6809_common.c times fetch_byte_notrace and store_byte from before the latch stores to after the hook returns, counts $FFFF (dummy) accesses; mc6809.c counts each next_instruction; coco_machine_run_cycles times the whole run; CPU_PROF=2 reuses the old AMOLED-52 section points inside coco_mem_cycle with CYCCNT instead of micros() (that profiler is gone). coco_machine_cpu_prof() enables the counter, calibrates one timing window (cost inside a window and in total) and hands main the counters for a [prof] line a second. CAUGHT BEFORE MEASURING: with the timing added, the compiler stopped inlining fetch_byte_notrace and store_byte and put them in FLASH (0x1001xxxx), which would have measured a slower machine than the product; CPU_PROF_INLINE forces them inline in the profile builds only (empty otherwise). Checked with nm: in all three builds coco_mem_cycle and mc6809_run are in SRAM and the helpers have no out-of-line copy; the product's mc6809_run and coco_mem_cycle sizes are unchanged (0x39ec, 0xb74). Side observation, confirming a PIZERO-131 suspect: in the product, op_sub, op_sub16, op_add16 and word_immediate are in flash. 237 host tests pass, lockstep included. Envs pizero_cpuprof and pizero_cpuprof_hook, RAM 76.5%.]

[2026-10-12 MEASURED on unit 10 and archived (docs/measurements/2026-10.jsonl, logs 2026-10-12-1338-pizero_cpuprof-unit10.log and 1341-pizero_cpuprof_hook-unit10.log), firmware ab1cc7e, BASIC prompt workload as PIZERO-130.
RESULT, and it reverses the guess this issue started from (hook ~65, core ~115):
- The BUS PATH (latch stores, call, coco_mem_cycle and everything it dispatches: VDG and PIA events, audio, IRQ lines) is about 150 of the 185 host clocks per emulated cycle, roughly 80%. The 6809 core proper (decode, execute, flags) is about 35. Exact bounds, because the instrumentation itself costs ~34 clocks per cycle and the calibration does not say where: bus 121-155, core 30-64. Either way the bus path dominates.
- Dummy (NVMA) cycles are 36.5% of all cycles, not the ~25% assumed. 4.05 cycles per instruction.
- Inside the hook (CPU_PROF=2, raw, each section including about one counter read): decode 23.5, data 33.7, events+audio 55.9, irq+budget 25.8; latch stores, call and return ~16.
KNOWN FLAW, left as is: the window calibration is unreliable (CPU_PROF=1 reads in=1, CPU_PROF=2 read 716), so the [prof] line's derived bus/core figures are approximate on CPU_PROF=1 and invalid on CPU_PROF=2; the raw window and section figures are the trustworthy ones. Revised plan written into PIZERO-131.]

summary: Win back some of the 13 KB of RAM PIZERO-131 step (c) added to mc6809_run
description: Remainder of PIZERO-131. Step (c) (commit 05956c5) put the inline deadline check (coco_fastbus_advance, lib/xroar_core/include/coco_fastbus.h) into every bus access of mc6809_run, which is HOT_FUNC in RAM, growing it from 15.8 to 23.4 KB; the product build went to 79.6% RAM. Not urgent (every env still builds), but the CoCo 3 (PIZERO-133) needs 128 KB of emulated RAM plus GIME state, so RAM will be tight. Ideas: keep only the hottest opcodes' bus helpers inline and call one out-of-line copy for the rest, or move rarely used opcode paths of mc6809_run out of RAM. Measure clocks per cycle before and after; anything costing more than about 1% speed is not worth it.

summary: Configurable low-pass filter on the sound output (default about 8 kHz)
description:
User 2026-10-13: a low-pass filter on the audio output, around 8 kHz, configurable. The 6-bit DAC's hard steps give a harsh top end; the real CoCo's output went through analog filtering, so this is both an improvement and arguably closer to the original. Design: a two-pole (biquad) low-pass on the 48 kHz samples after the integrator (lib/coco_machine/src/audio_integ.h produces them; the filter goes where finished samples are pushed to the audio ring in lib/coco_machine), so it runs once per sample, not per emulated cycle: about 5 multiply-adds per sample, well under 1% CPU. A one-pole was considered and rejected: its 6 dB/octave roll-off does little at 8 kHz. Setting in settings.txt and per game in NAME.TXT, e.g. audio_lowpass = 8000 (Hz) or off; coefficients computed once when the setting is applied (fixed-point, Q14 or similar, to keep integer maths). Defaults ON (project rule: improvements default on). Host test: a step input settles to the same level, and a tone above the cutoff is attenuated by the expected amount. Document in docs/BUILD.md or the settings doc alongside volume (src/settings.h). Needs a listening check on hardware before done. [2026-10-13 BUILT, NOT YET HEARD. lib/coco_machine/src/audio_lowpass.h: RBJ Butterworth biquad, Q28 coefficients worked out in floating point when the setting is applied (audio_lp_set), integer per sample (audio_lp_run). The fed-back outputs are kept in Q8 with error feedback: without the extra bits a 20 kHz cutoff rang by +-2 forever on a held level (the first version failed the host test that way). b1 is derived from the others so DC gain is exactly 1. audio_emit (coco_machine.cpp) runs it before the clamp, since a band-limited edge overshoots. It replaces PIZERO-30's fixed AUDIO_OUTPUT_LPF two one-poles (alpha 14/16), which no build used; that flag is gone. NOTE for the listening check: PIZERO-30 built that older, gentler filter out because it dulled the tone against desktop XRoar, so 8 kHz may sound duller still; the cutoff is the knob. Setting: audio_lowpass = 1000-20000 | on (8000) | off, default 8000, in settings.txt and a game's own .TXT; coco_machine_set_lowpass from settings_apply (src/main.cpp), logged in the [settings] line. Coefficients use the nominal 48 kHz; the servo moves the real rate by under 0.3%. Host tests: test/test_audio_lowpass (off is identity, held levels exact at 1-20 kHz, -3 dB at the cutoff, below -12 dB an octave up, full-scale square safe) and test_settings. 245 host tests pass. RAM: product 79.6 -> 79.8%. NEEDS: the user's listening check at 8000 and with off, to compare.]

[2026-10-15 DONE] The user's listening check: '8000 sounds fine'. The default stays 8000; off and other cutoffs remain available in settings.txt.

summary: CoCo 3: MMU fast path so the CoCo 3 runs at full speed
description: Remainder of PIZERO-133. In env pizero_coco3 every 6809 cycle goes through tcc1014_mem_cycle and the coco3_cpu_cycle call-back, because fastbus_deadline() sets the deadline to now when g_c3 (lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp, fastbus_deadline, the 'no skipping yet' line) and fastbus_sync sets every window top to 0. MEASURED on hardware 2026-10-13 (bench board, BASIC idle at OK, 0.89 MHz): [run] fps=29 cpu=~35000us per frame against a 16.7 ms budget, so the machine runs at about half speed and [aud] is 52% short. The user called it sluggish but not terrible. 1.79 MHz will be about twice as slow again. DO: give the CoCo 3 the PIZERO-131 treatment: let RAM and ROM cycles skip the GIME call-back when nothing time-critical is due (event queue head, GIME timer, the next scanline), mapping each 8 KB logical page through the MMU registers ($FFA0-$FFAF, task select in $FF91, ROM map mode in $FF90) into fast-bus windows, and invalidate the windows on any write to the MMU, $FF90/$FF91 or the SAM-subset registers. Use upstream ~/github/xroar src/tcc1014/tcc1014.c and the xroar skill's gime-tcc1014.md for the decode. Lockstep against the slow path with a host test like test_coco3_boot. DONE WHEN: on hardware BASIC at OK runs at fps=60 at 0.89 MHz with [aud] short near 0, and the 1.79 MHz cpu time is reported. [2026-10-13 STARTED, built and host-tested, not yet measured on hardware. DESIGN: flat windows cannot describe the MMU, so the 6809 core gets a page table instead, under COCO_FASTBUS_PAGES (lib/xroar_core/include/coco_fastbus.h; -DCOCO3 implies it, every other env is unchanged and the product build is byte-identical at 418204 B RAM). Below page_top ($FE00, so MC3's constant page and all I/O stay slow) a read of A comes from rd[A>>13][A&$1FFF] and a write goes to wr[A>>13][A&$1FFF] when set (mc6809_common.c fetch_byte_notrace/store_byte); a cycle is coco_fastbus.ticks long (8 at 1.79 MHz). Two small functions added to the vendored tcc1014.c (noted in PROVENANCE.md): tcc1014_decode_page (one page's S and bank, as tcc1014_mem_cycle decodes it) and tcc1014_cycle_ticks. coco3_bus.h's coco3_bus_page turns that into the page's pointers: internal ROM by logical address, cartridge ROM only when it is at least 8 KB, RAM by bank; anything else NULL. coco_machine.cpp: fastbus_sync builds the table for the CoCo 3 (and, in a paged build, for a CoCo 2 from its windows); coco3_cpu_cycle calls it after writes to $FF90/$FF91, $FFA0-$FFAF and $FFC0-$FFDF; init and cold reset call it after tcc1014_reset; coco_mem_tick on a CoCo 3 repeats the whole cycle through tcc1014_mem_cycle (the byte is moved again, which changes nothing); fastbus_deadline is the CoCo 2's (next event, next audio sample, budget end) with the cycle length from ticks. The GIME's IL1 keyboard edge is now sampled only on full-path cycles, at least once per audio sample. pizero_coco3 RAM and flash both fell about 7 KB (one lookup instead of three window checks in every inlined fetch). TESTS (test/test_coco3_boot, needs coco3.rom in COCO_ROM_DIR): boots to OK on the fast path; boots with and without it and compares tick, registers and all 128 KB at fields 1-8, 16, 32, 64, 128; and runs a program after boot that sets 1.79 MHz and keeps mapping bank $30 into $4000-$5FFF, filling it and mapping $3A back (8 passes in 30 fields) with the same comparison. The first run found the host glue set the IRQ lines at the start of each cycle (as upstream), which left a stale line across fast cycles after a $FF92 acknowledge and caused a spurious interrupt at field 83; the host now sets them at the end of the cycle, as the firmware's mem_cycle_tail always has, which is identical for the full path. 249 host tests pass. NEXT: flash pizero_coco3 and read [run] fps and cpu at OK, then at 1.79 MHz (POKE 65497,0).] [2026-10-13 HARDWARE, bench board, BASIC idle at OK, 0.89 MHz. Before (PIZERO-133): fps=29, cpu ~35000us, [aud] short 52%. With the page table (141c51b): fps 52-55 at cpu ~19000us, settling to fps=44 at ~22900us after about 12 s; the user said 'that's definitely faster'. WHERE THE REST GOES, by two throwaway builds (not committed): with the GIME's render_scanline and our scanline copy both returning at once, cpu=8300us at fps=60, so the emulation itself is now well inside the frame; with only our copy off, cpu=15900us. So the GIME's renderer costs about 7.6 ms a frame and our copy into g_fb 3.5-7 ms (writing the framebuffer core 1 is scanning out). Putting tcc1014_mem_cycle, render_scanline and the per-line GIME events in SRAM (HOT_FUNC) changed nothing (19-23 ms), so it was reverted: flash is not the cost. FIX FOR THE COPY: coco3_bus_render_line keeps a 32-bit hash per framebuffer row of the 640 GIME pixels it last showed and skips a row whose hash matches (coco3_bus_line_sum, word reads); coco3_bus_invalidate clears them, called by coco_machine_set_framebuffer and by main.cpp on every overlay frame (the overlay draws into g_fb). Host test test_row_skip. Result: fps=58, cpu ~17450us, [aud] short 4.6%. Product build unchanged (418204 B).] [2026-10-13 DONE. The user checked on hardware: the picture looks right and the BASIC screen redraws fully after the menu closes. 1.79 MHz (the user typed POKE 65497,0 at OK): fps=48, cpu ~21100us, [aud] short ~21%; a later stretch read fps=60 at ~16150us with short 0%, cause not identified (screen contents or what was typed). Not reached: fps=60 at 0.89 MHz idle (58, 17.4 ms) and 1.79 MHz in budget. The emulation itself is 8.3 ms; what is left is video, filed as PIZERO-218.]

summary: CoCo 3: check WIDTH 40, palette, GIME timer and HSCREEN on hardware
description: Remainder of PIZERO-133, which closed on boot-to-OK. Its other DONE criteria were not checked on hardware: WIDTH 40 text, a palette POKE recolouring the screen (e.g. POKE &HFFB0,n or PALETTE), a GIME timer program (timer IRQ/FIRQ via $FF94/$FF95 and $FF92/$FF93), and HSCREEN 1 and 2 (320-wide graphics) drawing. Run them in env pizero_coco3 and record what each shows. Expect slowness until PIZERO-213. File any defect found as its own issue; 640-wide modes (HSCREEN 3/4, WIDTH 80) are PIZERO-134. PROGRESS 2026-10-15: all four checks pass on the host CoCo 3 (test/test_coco3_boot, which now has a keyboard matrix and a typist: COCO3_TYPE, COCO3_FRAMES, COCO3_DUMP, COCO3_RAM). WIDTH 40 text with ATTR colours, underline and blink; PALETTE and direct POKE &HFFBx (32-column screen's palette 12/13); HSCREEN 1 (4 colours) and HSCREEN 2 (16 colours, all bars matching the CMP default palette 18,36,11,7,63,31,9,38,0,18,0,63,0,18,0,38); and the GIME timer: reload 10 on the 63.5 us line clock gives 23.9 IRQs per field at 0.89 and 1.79 MHz, i.e. 263/11, the 1987 GIME's N+1 (upstream master XRoar with -vdg-type gime1987 counts the same). Pitfall found: BASIC's TIMER loses about a quarter of its 60 Hz ticks under 1,400 timer IRQs a second, in upstream XRoar too (473 of 627 expected), so it cannot time the test; the check counts the GIME's own VBORD IRQ as the field clock instead. The hardware run: docs/coco3-checks/pizero214.bas, typed in by scripts/serial_type.py (too long for autorun.txt, PIZERO-229), with Print Screen on each screen. FIRMWARE RUN 2026-10-16: the pizero_coco3 firmware itself, run in the CoCo Zero emulator (~/github/cocozero-emulator, an RP2350 emulator, driven from a scratch Rust program through its library API with Disk BASIC on the virtual card), typed the listing through the keyboard matrix with all 18 lines matching the source in the CoCo's RAM (read out and detokenized), and ran all six screens right: WIDTH 40 with ATTR colours, underline and blink; PALETTE 0,36; HSCREEN 1; HSCREEN 2 with 16 bars; palette POKEs; timer 23.9 per field at 0.89 and 1.79 MHz; vector restored. ON THE BOARD the typed listing gave ?SN ERROR: first because scripts/serial_type.py paced 5 fields a key when the firmware takes 6 (fixed), then because a stopped run left $FEF7 hooked to code that NEW overwrote (line 80 now restores it; start from a cold boot), and on a third, cold-booted try still ?SN ERROR, cause not found. Serial typing on the board is the open question, not the CoCo 3. SOUND CHECK 2026-10-19 (pizero_coco3 on the board, with the PIZERO-232/233 audio delivery, typed over serial): PLAY "T3;O2;CDEFGAB;O3;CDEFGAB;O4;C" at 0.89 MHz, SOUND 89,60, then POKE 65497,0 and the same scale at 1.79 MHz. The user heard all three as right. Telemetry: under=0/s and skips=0 throughout; tone/s stepped up with the scale; at 1.79 MHz fps held 60 with cpu about 15.7 ms of the 16.7 ms frame and prod dipped to about 47,830/s with the servo covering it. Still to do on the board: the pizero214.bas screens (serial typing ?SN ERROR). BOARD RUN 2026-10-19: PASSED. The listing typed one key at a time (6.3 fields a key, 1.5 s after each ENTER) ran with no ?SN ERROR, so the earlier failures came from sending each line to the serial port in one burst; scripts/serial_type.py now writes key by key. Ctrl-P screenshots SCR0001-0006 checked: WIDTH 40 black on green with ATTR 3,0 white on green, ATTR 1,2 green on blue and the underline (blink not checkable in a still); PALETTE 0,36 red background; HSCREEN 1 red circle, full box (edges at x 0 and 319, rows 0 and 191) and bars green, red, blue, grey; HSCREEN 2 red background, blue-painted circle, white box and 16 bars matching the CMP default palette; POKE &HFFBC/&HFFBD white on red; GIME timer 24 at 0.89 MHz and 23.9 at 1.79 MHz against 23.9 expected. The 24 is within the method's error: counting starts mid-field, so N/V reads up to about 24/300 = 0.08 high. fps held 60 except brief dips (43-59) while screens redrew.

summary: CoCo 3: ALT, CTRL, F1, F2 keys and the second fire buttons
description: Remainder of PIZERO-133. In env pizero_coco3 the keyboard uses the CoCo 2 matrix, so the CoCo 3's extra keys are unmapped: ALT, CTRL, F1 and F2 sit on PIA1 PB2's column 6 rows (upstream ~/github/xroar src/keyboard.c and coco3.c; the xroar skill's io-mc6821.md). Map them from the USB keyboard in CoCo 3 mode only. Check PIZERO-205's F1 caveat (the overlay's F1 key vs a real CoCo 3 F1). Also the 'fire2' pad action from the PIZERO-164 note in PIZERO-133: the second fire button of each stick reads on PIA0 PA2 (right) and PA3 (left) (upstream coco3.c:1361); it must not exist in CoCo 2 mode, where those bits are keyboard rows. KEYS DONE 2026-10-20 (decided with the user: F1 and F2 go to the CoCo 3, INFO comes off F1 on both machines and stays reachable as the overlay page Left of disks). src/key_translate.h: K_ALT/K_CTRL/K_F1/K_F2 = dscan 0x33-0x36 (row 6, columns 3-6, as upstream dkbd.c); kt_state.coco3 (set in main.cpp from coco_machine_is_coco3 at machine start) maps HID F1/F2 (0x3A/0x3B) to K_F1/K_F2 and either Ctrl (mods 0x11) / Alt (0x44) to K_CTRL/K_ALT in kt_keys (KT_KEYS_MAX = held + SHIFT + CTRL + ALT); F1/F2 never auto-repeat; on a CoCo 2 all four press nothing. src/overlay_keys.h: HK_F1 removed from ovk_fkey_list, INFO legend 'ESC TO CLOSE'. Host tests: test_key_translate (+3 cases), test_overlay_keys updated, 40/40 pass. ON THE BOARD (pizero_coco3): docs/coco3-checks/pizero215.bas, which reads row 6 in machine code (BASIC's BREAK check rescans the keyboard between statements, so a POKE/PEEK in BASIC reads the wrong column), shows each of ALT, CTRL, F1 and F2 alone while held (user). Pitfall on the way: the first version stored its readings at $7F30, the routine's own last byte (RTS), and crashed BASIC; the CoCo 3 host harness (COCO3_TYPE) reproduced it before the board did again. LEFT IN THIS ISSUE: the second fire buttons (fire2 pad action). SECOND BUTTONS DONE 2026-10-20: pad actions fire2 / fire2_right (gamepad.h PAD_ACT_FIRE2 0x43, PAD_ACT_FIRE2_RIGHT 0x44; settings.h parses and writes them); defaults R2 = fire2 and L2 = fire2_right (improvements on by default); coco_machine_set_joystick_fire2 sets g_joy_fire bits 2-3, pulled onto PIA0 PA2/PA3 only when g_c3 (upstream coco3.c: buttons & 15), so on a CoCo 2 they do nothing. ON THE BOARD: BUTTON(0..3) at rest 0 0 0 0; A = 1 0 0 0, X = 0 0 1 0, R2 = 0 1 0 0, L2 = 0 0 0 1 (user): BUTTON(0)/(1) the right joystick's first and second, (2)/(3) the left's. BUG FOUND AND FIXED ON THE WAY: the GameSir in Android (HID) mode sets its digital R2 bit at rest with the trigger's analog byte at 3, so R2 read as held; once R2 meant fire2 it held PA2 low, i.e. the keyboard row P-W, which stalled autorun after 'LOAD' and broke typed tests. pad_decode_hidgp now reads L2/R2 from the analog bytes (b9, b8) at >= 0x80, as the XInput decoder does; test_hidgp_trigger_bit_at_rest_is_not_a_press covers the captured report. The [pad] telemetry line now also prints buttons= and the first 10 raw bytes. README and SETTINGS.md updated. Not checked by the user: F1 no longer opening the overlay, and INFO via F12 then Left (host-tested in test_overlay_keys).

summary: CoCo 3: LOADM and BIN loading under a non-default MMU map
description: Remainder of PIZERO-133. coco_machine.cpp's loadm_write writes a CoCo 3 program to physical 0x70000+addr, which is right only while BASIC's default MMU map (task 0, pages $38-$3F) is in place. A program loaded after something remapped the MMU lands in the wrong place. DO: translate each address through the current MMU registers ($FFA0-$FFAF and the task bit in $FF91) as tcc1014.c does, or through the same mapping PIZERO-213 builds. Test with a host case that remaps a page and loads into it.

summary: CoCo 3: tearing, and double-buffer builds
description: Remainder of PIZERO-133. In env pizero_coco3 the GIME draws each scanline straight into g_fb while libdvi scans it out, so moving pictures can tear; the CoCo 2 builds render a whole frame at the frame boundary instead. The double-buffer envs are not supported with -DCOCO3. DO: measure whether tearing is visible (a scrolling or animated program) once PIZERO-213 brings the speed up; if it is, render into a line buffer and copy at frame end, or support a double-buffer env within the RAM left after the 128 KB (check free heap from the [mem] boot line).

summary: CoCo 3: get the GIME's video under the frame budget
description: Remainder of PIZERO-213. With the MMU fast path, the CoCo 3 at BASIC's OK prompt takes 17.4 ms of CPU per frame at 0.89 MHz (fps=58, [aud] short 4.6%) and about 21 ms at 1.79 MHz (fps=48, short 21%), against 16.7 ms. MEASURED on the bench board with throwaway builds (PIZERO-213 notes): emulation without video is 8.3 ms; the GIME's own render_scanline (lib/xroar_core/src/tcc1014/tcc1014.c, inlined into do_hs_fall, called per active line and before every register write) about 7.6 ms; our coco3_bus_render_line about 1.5 ms now that unchanged rows are skipped by hash (it was 3.5-7 ms writing the scanned-out g_fb). Placing the GIME code in SRAM made no difference, so the cost is the work, not flash. IDEAS, measure each: (1) a port-side renderer that turns VRAM straight into RGB565 for the framebuffer row, per mode, skipping upstream's 912-byte 6-bit pixel line (it draws borders too, and writes up to 16 bytes per 4 bits at resolution 0); keep upstream's for modes not yet handled; (2) skip rendering a line whose VRAM bytes, registers and palette are unchanged since that row was last drawn; (3) render every other frame at 1.79 MHz if nothing else fits; (4) hash cost: hash only the shown bytes. PIZERO-178 (render cost per mode) is the benchmark for this; 640-wide modes are PIZERO-134. DONE WHEN: on hardware BASIC at OK runs fps=60 with [aud] short near 0 at 0.89 MHz and at 1.79 MHz, and a 320-wide HSCREEN mode's cost is reported. [2026-10-13 STEP 1, a port renderer. tcc1014.c (port addition, PROVENANCE.md): public flag port_render; port_render_scanline draws each active line once, the first time the beam is found past the active area's start, with render_scanline's own fetch and colour decode, straight into the 320 pixels the port shows (the 640 GIME pixels centred on the active area, halved); do_hs_fall passes those to render_line with npixels=320, or a border/sync fill for other lines. A change of state inside the active area now shows from the next line instead of mid-line. coco3_bus_render_line takes either form. test_coco3_boot test_port_render boots both ways and requires identical framebuffers for BASIC's screen and eight CoCo 3 modes set by a program over pseudo-random VRAM (40-column text with and without attributes; 320, 256, 128 and 640 wide graphics at 2, 4 and 16 colours). HARDWARE at OK, 0.89 MHz: fps=60, cpu ~13300-14000us, [aud] short 0. Cycle counters (a temporary build): the port renderer about 70 M clocks/s (4.7 ms a frame, ~6100 clocks a line for 32 characters), the sink 12 M clocks/s (0.8 ms). One run stepped to ~17.8 ms after about 12 s, as earlier builds had, when the HDMI audio stream started (fill stopped rising, the servo engaged); a later run held 14 ms for 40 s, so the step is not deterministic; watch it. NEXT: hoist the mode state out of the loop (byte stores make the compiler reload every GIME field), read VRAM without the delegate, and skip the decode when a line's inputs match last frame's.] [2026-10-13 STEPS 2-3. 35f3e95: the port renderer gathers each line's VRAM bytes (directly from public port_vram[2], the two 64 KB halves; fetch_vram if NULL), hashes them with every piece of state the decode reads, and skips a line matching the same scanline's last frame (render_line gets NULL; port_redraw clears the per-scanline hashes, set by coco_machine_video_invalidate and when the active area moves). Then a table-driven decode: each VRAM byte becomes eight colours in one 64-bit word (two-colour patterns through a 256-entry bit-to-byte mask table in flash, four- and sixteen-colour ones by pairs and quads), emitted by resolution; a contiguous gather is one memcpy. MEASURED with DWT cycle counters (a temporary build, scratch script xp_measure.sh): the old upstream-style decode was ~4500 clocks a line; hoisting state, SRAM placement and a RAM font each changed nothing; the cost was port_sel's 64-bit multiply, a call to __aeabi_lmul through a veneer, twice a byte. With 32-bit halves, worst case (every line decoded every frame) render 34 M clocks/s = 2.25 ms a frame plus sink 0.8 ms, versus ~9 ms before; at OK with skipping, cpu ~8.5-9 ms a frame at 0.89 MHz. test_port_render now covers 17 modes (CoCo 3 text, attributes and graphics; VDG-compatible alpha/SG4 with both CSS, CG1, RG1, CG2, RG3, CG6, RG6) against upstream, after a VRAM change, through both fetch paths.] [2026-10-13 DONE on hardware (bench board, build 9997d63). BASIC at OK: 0.89 MHz fps=60 at ~8.5-9 ms; 1.79 MHz (the user typed POKE 65497,0) fps=60 at ~13.5 ms, [aud] short 0. HSCREEN 2 with HCIRCLE in a running program: the user saw the circle; fps=60 at ~9.5 ms, short 0 (a static picture, so most lines skip). Not measured, filed as PIZERO-219: a full-screen animation at 1.79 MHz (the worst case, every line redrawn: about 3 ms of video on top of ~12 ms emulation, by the cycle counters), and the occasional +4 ms step some runs showed about 12 s after boot.]

summary: CoCo 3: measure a full-screen animation at 1.79 MHz, and the step after boot
description: Remainder of PIZERO-218. The CoCo 3 build (pizero_coco3) runs BASIC at OK at fps=60 at 0.89 MHz (~9 ms CPU a frame) and 1.79 MHz (~13.5 ms), and a static HSCREEN 2 picture at ~9.5 ms. Those screens are mostly static, so the port renderer skips most lines. The worst case, every line changing every frame, was measured only at 0.89 MHz with skipping forced off (scratch instrumentation: renderer 34 M clocks/s = 2.25 ms a frame, sink 0.8 ms); at 1.79 MHz that predicts ~15 ms, inside 16.7 ms but with little margin. DO: run a CoCo 3 program that redraws the whole screen every frame at 1.79 MHz (a scrolling HSCREEN 2 picture, or a game) and read [run] cpu and [aud] short. Also: several runs in PIZERO-213/218 stepped up by about 4 ms around 12 s after boot, when the HDMI audio stream began (the ring stopped filling, the servo engaged); others did not. Find out whether that step is real load (core 1 contention) and whether it survives the 218 renderer. DONE WHEN: both numbers are recorded, and if the animation misses 60 fps, the next optimisation is filed with its measurement. [2026-10-13 FIRST READING: a running program with HSCREEN 2 and one HCIRCLE (static picture). At 0.89 MHz, apparently after a reboot: fps=60, cpu ~9500us, short 0. After the user POKEd 65495 and ran it again it was evidently at 1.79 MHz: fps=60, cpu ~14650us, [aud] short ~1% (fill near 0, servo at its 48064 limit), so 1.79 MHz graphics is already at the edge even with most lines skipped: the per-frame work outside cpu (USB, audio encode, pacing) is what tips it. Note 65495 is $FFD7, the SAM R0 bit, which the GIME ignores; only $FFD8/$FFD9 (R1) set the CoCo 3's speed, so the speed probably came from an earlier POKE 65497. NEXT: measure the rest of the frame (main.cpp's per-frame phases) at 1.79 MHz to see what the margin really is.] [2026-10-13 DONE. f87e4a1 added slack= (least spare time a frame had that second) and late= (frames that missed their slot) to [run]. At OK at 0.89 MHz: cpu ~8.5 ms, slack 5.2-6.2 ms, late 0, so the work outside emulation in the worst frame is ~2.7 ms. WORST CASE, user ran 10 POKE 65497,0 / 20 HSCREEN 2 / 30 FOR C=0 TO 15:HCLS C:NEXT C / 40 GOTO 30 (every line changes every frame): fps=60, cpu ~14.1 ms with spikes to 17.7-18.7 ms, slack -2.4 to -3.5 ms, late 3-5 frames a second, [aud] short 0.4-0.8% (servo pinned at 48064, fill near 0). Compare BASIC at OK at 1.79 MHz, ~13.5 ms: full-screen redraw adds only ~0.6 ms, so video is no longer the cost; the 6809 plus per-cycle GIME work at 1.79 MHz is. The +4 ms step after boot was not chased separately; it moves to the remainder. REMAINDER: PIZERO-220.]

summary: CoCo 3: cut per-cycle emulation cost at 1.79 MHz so a full-screen animation has slack
description:
Remainder of PIZERO-219. On pizero_coco3 at 1.79 MHz a program that HCLSes the whole HSCREEN 2 every frame runs at fps=60 but with [run] late=3-5 a second, slack -2.4 to -3.5 ms, cpu ~14.1 ms (spikes 17.7-18.7 ms) and [aud] short 0.4-0.8%. The per-frame work outside emulation (USB, audio encode, pacing) is ~2.7 ms, so emulation must come down to about 13 ms with margin, i.e. ~1.5-2 ms off. BASIC idle at 1.79 MHz is already ~13.5 ms and the full-screen redraw adds only ~0.6 ms (PIZERO-218 renderer: worst case 2.25 ms render + 0.8 ms sink), so the cost is the CPU side: mc6809 core plus the per-cycle coco_mem_tick / tcc1014_mem_cycle path (lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp, lib/xroar_core/src/tcc1014/tcc1014.c). DO: profile emulation at 1.79 MHz with the DWT instrumentation in scratchpad xp_measure.sh style (cycles per frame in the CPU loop vs in per-cycle GIME/SAM work vs line events), then attack the largest. Candidates: batch the per-cycle tick (count cycles and settle the GIME timer and line events at deadlines instead of every cycle); skip the sink-side line hash for lines the GIME already flagged changed (port_sum makes it redundant). ALSO: several PIZERO-213/218 runs stepped up ~4 ms about 12 s after boot when the HDMI audio stream started; check whether that is core 1 contention and whether it is part of this budget. DONE WHEN: the HCLS loop at 1.79 MHz shows late=0 and short ~0 over a minute on hardware. [2026-10-13 WORK. Profiled with a new env pizero_coco3_prof ([prof3] lines). The board autoruns TEST1 from drive0.DSK (the HCLS loop), so it boots into the worst case. Findings, per frame at 1.79 MHz: the late frames were not the loop outside emulation (wmax is cmax + ~40 us; the earlier ~2.7 ms estimate was wrong) but emulation spikes to ~19 ms, in the frames where all 192 active lines change. The port renderer's decode cost ~7,900 clocks a line (~49 a byte) on HSCREEN 2 because its loop tested the mode for every byte. THREE CHANGES: (1) a CoCo 3 fast-path cycle that reaches the deadline no longer runs the whole cycle through the GIME again: coco3_tick does the GIME's IL edge detect (new port function tcc1014_poll_lines) and the tail; dummy cycles likewise. (2) The deadline no longer includes the next audio sample boundary: audio_integ_run (audio_integ.h) emits every sample a run of cycles crossed, exactly as stepping each access would (test_audio_integ checks it sample for sample); slow ticks fell ~1,800 -> ~1,040 a frame. Affects the CoCo 2 too. The catch-up is one noinline RAM function (inlined everywhere it cost 4 KB of RAM). (3) The port renderer gives each bitplane mode and resolution its own loop (PORT_LOOP, port_emit, port_quads): decode 7,900 -> 2,500 clocks a line; test_port_render still matches upstream. Also: [run] gains cmax= and wmax=; tele_write sends in 64-byte pieces (the [run] line had stopped appearing). RESULT on hardware (bench board, pizero_coco3, HCLS loop at 1.79 MHz, 66-75 s): fps 60, late 0, slack min 1.4-1.5 ms, cmax 15.1-15.2 ms, cpu median ~12.9 ms (was ~14.1), [aud] short 0.0%, under 0. CoCo 2 product (pizero_stream_60) checked on the same board: cpu 6.07 ms, short 0.0%, late 0. RAM: pizero_stream_60 418,216 -> 419,364 bytes. Awaiting the user's look and listen on hardware.]

[2026-10-15 DONE, user's call] The pending sound check is settled: the questionable sound heard during this work came from one of the user's monitors (the test TV), not the code or the hardware. The same board and build play the SN76489 jukebox cleanly on a second Samsung (PIZERO-224). Reopen if another display shows sound problems.

summary: Docs: bring ROADMAP, coco3-plan, coco3-feasibility, pipeline, README and cpu-speed up to date with the CoCo 3 work
description:

summary: SAM rate-transition cycles (15, 17, 25 ticks) not modelled at CoCo 2 high speed
description: Remainder of PIZERO-132 (done 2026-10-14), which made the CoCo 2 honour POKE 65495/65497 with a flat 8 ticks for a fast cycle and 16 for a slow one (sam_ticks in lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp). The real SAM, and XRoar's mc6883_mem_cycle (lib/xroar_core/src/mc6883.c, its running_fast / extend_slow_cycle state), spend 15 ticks on a slow-to-fast change and 17 or 25 on fast-to-slow while it re-interleaves with the VDG. That only happens at address-dependent speed (POKE 65495), where RAM and ROM cycles alternate. Measured effect of leaving it out is unknown; expected within a few percent of the guest's speed over a frame. Fixing it would mean tracking the previous cycle's speed on every bus cycle, including the 6809 core's fast path (coco_fastbus.ticks/rom_ticks in lib/xroar_core/include/coco_fastbus.h), which costs host time on the hot path. DONE WHEN: a timing loop at POKE 65495 matches upstream XRoar's jiffy count, or the difference is measured and judged not worth the cost. Also note in lib/xroar_core/PROVENANCE.md that mc6809_common.c carries the port's fastbus path (PIZERO-131, 132), which it does not yet say.

summary: SN76489 jukebox music garbled on HDMI TVs: generation cleared, HDMI audio packets fixed to IEC 60958, exact 48 kHz, louder and AC coupled
description:
The user reports SN76489 music (their jukebox demo, ~/github/coco/src/jukebox/build/songs.dsk, which plays .SNG songs on the GameMaster chip at $FF41) sounds garbled on at least two HDMI TVs, with the three voices hard to tell apart, while it sounds right in desktop XRoar. Question: our generation, or delivery over HDMI / the TVs?

Established 2026-10-14 on the host: INVENT08.SNG fed through our own csg_sn76489.h, sn_render averaging, volume and the 8 kHz audio_lowpass, driven exactly as lib/sn76489.fs drives it (envelope included), differs from an alias-free box-averaged render of the same chip output by an error 26 dB below the music overall (33 dB in 500 Hz-2 kHz): mild square-wave aliasing, the same class as upstream XRoar's (a 3rd-order Butterworth at Nyquist). No writes are lost (Forth is far slower than the 32-clock ready gap). Output is quiet (peak about 1,200 of 32,767). So generation alone should not smear the notes. Not yet checked: the machine running the real program on the board, and HDMI delivery.

Plan: env pizero_wavmeas_boot, pizero_wavmeas (no video, the WAV dump drains the ring) but booting normally with the card's autorun, and recording 20 s when Ctrl-W (0x17) arrives on USB serial instead of at attach. With songs.dsk as drive 0 the jukebox autoruns; type a song letter over serial, trigger, and compare the WAV with the host render (scratchpad sngrender.c). Match: our side is cleared, look at delivery and the sinks (PIZERO-41, 120, 99). Mismatch: the difference points at the machine.

Also noted: the jukebox switches the analog sound mux to the cartridge (PIA0 CA2/CB2) and expects the DAC to be cut; we always mix the DAC in. Harmless while the DAC is held, but not faithful.

[2026-10-14 RESULT] The board's own audio matches the host render. pizero_wavmeas_boot on the new board (50D37286DD1820A6), songs.dsk as drive 0, the jukebox autoran (csg writes=4 at the menu, dropped=0); 'D' (INVENT08) and Ctrl-W over serial gave 20 s at 48 kHz. Sample-for-sample comparison is meaningless (square-wave phases start differently), so windows were compared by spectrum (8192-point Hann, 60 Hz-5 kHz): magnitude correlation median 0.974 against the host render through the same low-pass; the strongest frequencies agree within a few Hz window by window (at 4 s both 328, 439, 990, 1318 Hz). Level: peak about 2,100 of 32,767 with a DC offset of about -1,650 (the DAC held at 0, mixed in although the program selected the cartridge on the sound mux). Conclusion: the garbling is not in what the emulation generates. Remaining suspects: HDMI data-island delivery (the 48 kHz stream with the rate servo, PIZERO-121) or the TVs. Not yet compared with desktop XRoar's actual output (XRoar here has no WAV audio module); the user can play scratchpad ours_lp.wav on the Mac to judge that by ear.

[2026-10-14] The user listened to the host render (ours_lp.wav, our chip code and low-pass) on the Mac in QuickTime: "that sounds great". With the board capture matching that render, generation is cleared end to end up to the audio ring. Next: HDMI delivery or the TVs (TV sound processing off, volume = 15, then our data-island path and rate servo).

[2026-10-14] Still mushy on a TV with its sound processing off, so delivery is the suspect. Found in dvi_di_set_audio_samples (lib/libdvi/dvi_data_island.c), FRANK's packet: V=1 on every sample (IEC 60958: not reliable, a sink may conceal or mute), no channel status (all zero = 44.1 kHz, against ACR N 6144 / CTS 25200 at 25.2 MHz and the InfoFrame, both 48 kHz), and the B block-start flag set only when a packet began on frame 0 (g_aud_framectr advances 1-4 a packet in stream_audio_cb, src/main.cpp), so most block starts were skipped. Fixed to the spec: V=0, a consumer channel status (linear PCM, copying permitted, channel 1/2, 48 kHz, 16-bit) sent one C bit a frame, B on whichever subpacket starts a block; the table is in RAM for the core-1 IRQ (PIZERO-37). Flashed on the new board (pizero_stream_60, telemetry normal). The previous image is kept as scratchpad sng/product_before_iec.uf2 for an A/B. DONE WHEN: the user hears the jukebox's chords clearly on a TV that was mushy, or the change is shown not to help.

[2026-10-14] After the IEC fix the user heard it as "still a bit fuzzy": one note fairly clean, several notes distorted. Asked to turn the volume up. Done: AUDIO_DAC_GAIN 60 -> 180 and the SN76489 by the same factor (AUDIO_GAIN_X 3, +9.5 dB; volume 0-15 keeps its scale relative to the default), and a DC blocker (audio_dc_run in audio_lowpass.h, one-pole high-pass at about 5 Hz, settling exactly to 0) ahead of the low-pass, as the real CoCo's output is AC coupled: the parked DAC put a -32 step offset on the output and the SN76489 only adds positive levels, wasting headroom. Host test test_dc_blocker; 256 tests pass. RAM pizero_stream_60 422,296 bytes (80.5%). A capture of the jukebox menu with the new code is exact digital silence. SETTINGS.md notes the louder default.

[2026-10-14] Louder + DC blocker: still fuzzy with several notes. Mac-to-TV comparison impossible (the Samsung plays no sound from the Mac over HDMI). pizero_chord (C4 E4 G4, sines then squares, no CoCo in the path): user hears both fuzzy, squares more (the test squares are naive and alias, so only the sines are a fair test). Per-line IRQ timing checked and safe: dvi_dma_irq_handler runs after all three lanes load the line's last block and repoints entries for the next line. Found and fixed a rate error: the 16.16 meter (800/480 truncated) delivered 47,999.7 samples/s against the declared 48,000; now exact (g_meter_acc in 480ths, src/main.cpp). User after the fix: 'seems a little fuzzy i think'. Acoustic measurement with the user's go-ahead (Achtung mic near the TV, ffmpeg avfoundation): the sine chord from the TV and a control (a perfect chord from the MacBook speakers, same mic, TV silent) both show the same mic/room artefacts (G read at 394.1, E with side peaks near 323/337), so those are not the link. The TV adds tones at 123, 450 and 573 Hz that are not harmonics: intermodulation, consistent with 'one note clean, several fuzzy', which could be the TV's amp and speakers or the link; an acoustic recording cannot separate them without a second source through the same TV. Open: an HDMI capture device would settle it (record exactly what we send); a second HDMI source with sound on the same TV playing a chord; meanwhile audio_lowpass = 4000 softens square-wave chords on a TV that intermodulates.

[2026-10-14] HDMI capture attempt: the Elgato HD60 S+ shows a black frame and records all-zero audio from the board (it reports 640x471 at 24.05 fps, red LEDs pulsing). It is built for console/TV formats (720x480, 720p, 1080p) and does not accept the 640x480 VGA timing (CEA VIC 1); a generic MS2109-class capture stick accepts PC timings. The user does not have one.

[2026-10-15 CLOSED at about 80%, user's call] Delivered, all on main and on the new board (pizero_stream_60): generation proven correct end to end (board capture matches the host render, which the user heard as 'sounds great'); IEC 60958 sample packets (V=0, 48 kHz consumer channel status, B on every block start; lib/libdvi/dvi_data_island.c dvi_di_set_audio_samples); exactly 48,000 samples/s (src/main.cpp g_meter_acc); 3x louder default with a DC blocker (audio_lowpass.h audio_dc_run); diagnostics pizero_wavmeas_boot and pizero_chord (docs/BUILD.md). The user's hearing went from 'mushy' to 'a bit fuzzy' / 'a little fuzzy' with several notes. Not done: deciding whether the remaining fuzz (TV intermodulation at 123/450/573 Hz on a sine chord) is the link or the TVs' amps and speakers. Filed as PIZERO-224, which waits on a capture device that accepts 640x480. Also not done: honouring the jukebox's analog-mux selection of cartridge audio (we always mix the DAC; harmless while the DAC is held).

summary: Residual fuzz on multi-note HDMI audio: capture what the board sends to tell the link from the TV
description:
Remainder of PIZERO-223 (closed 2026-10-15). After the IEC 60958 packet fix, the exact 48 kHz meter, the louder default and the DC blocker, the user still hears chords as 'a little fuzzy' on Samsung TVs, while one note is clean. The source is cleared: the board's own ring audio (pizero_wavmeas_boot) matches a host render the user heard as clean on the Mac. A mic recording of the pizero_chord sine chord (C4/E4/G4, no CoCo in the path) from the TV shows intermodulation tones at 123, 450 and 573 Hz absent from a Mac-speaker control, but an acoustic recording cannot tell the HDMI link from the TV's amp and speakers, and the Samsung plays no sound from the Mac over HDMI so no second source could be compared.

Blocked on hardware: the Elgato HD60 S+ does not accept 640x480 (black frame, all-zero audio). Needs a generic MS2109-class USB capture stick (accepts PC timings), or another TV/monitor whose HDMI audio can be compared against a known-good source.

Plan when a capture device is available: flash pizero_chord, record the HDMI audio with ffmpeg, and compare with the ideal sines. Bit-exact or near-exact means the link is clean and the fuzz is the TVs (close as theirs, recommend audio_lowpass = 4000 for square-wave chords). Intermod in the capture means the data-island path: look at packet timing across the frame, the rate servo (PIZERO-121) and the sample sequence at packet boundaries. Related: PIZERO-99 (other screens), PIZERO-41.

[2026-10-15 ANSWERED, no capture needed] The user took the CoCo Zero (new board 50D37286DD1820A6, pizero_stream_60 with all of PIZERO-223's fixes) running the jukebox to an older 48" Samsung upstairs: 'it played the music perfectly. no complaints whatsoever.' Same board, same build, same music, a clean result on a second TV, so the link is fine and the residual fuzz belongs to the test TV (its amp, speakers or processing). No code change. If a user reports fuzzy chords on their own TV, suggest audio_lowpass = 4000 in settings.txt.

[2026-10-17 Later note: PIZERO-232 changed the HDMI audio delivery (audio on vblank lines, full 4-sample packets, trailing guard bands, ACR on every 8th vblank line) and the user reports the TVs that were fuzzy before now play clearly, so the residual fuzz here was most likely the old delivery, not the TV.]

summary: Watchdog post-mortem: record where core 0 really was when it froze (for PIZERO-203)
description:
For PIZERO-203. Today a watchdog recovery records only the phase marker (scratch[1]), a frame heartbeat (scratch[2]) and a running tally (scratch[3]), src/main.cpp around WD_MAGIC. The five recoveries so far landed in five different phases (blit, emulate, emulate, emulate, frame-pace), which suggests core 0 is not stuck in loop() code at all but in an interrupt handler (Pico-PIO-USB's 1 ms SOF timer runs on core 0) or on a stalled bus, with the phase being whatever was interrupted.

Plan: (1) an early-warning interrupt at top priority on core 0 (a spare timer0 alarm, every 200 ms) that, once the watchdog has less than 1 s left, saves the interrupted PC, LR and exception number (which IRQ, if any, core 0 was inside) from the exception frame; if it never runs, core 0 had interrupts masked or was in a higher-priority handler, which is itself an answer. (2) A HardFault handler that records the fault frame and fault status registers and lets the watchdog reset, so a crash is told apart from a hang. (3) Context at the warning and at the last capture: core 1's line count (is core 1 alive), the USB SOF frame number (is the USB timer IRQ still running), the guest 6809 PC and emulated tick, USB device count, uptime in ms, heartbeat and phase. PC, LR and the exception number also go in watchdog scratch[5..7], which survive any watchdog reset; the rest goes in a small .uninitialized_data block with a magic. The next boot prints a [watchdog] post-mortem line and the soak log header carries it. Test with pizero_wdtest (wedge in loop(), and a variant with interrupts off). Symbols resolve with arm-none-eabi-addr2line against the build's firmware.elf.

Deploying to unit 10 (the PIZERO-203 soak board) needs the user's go-ahead.

[2026-10-15 BUILT AND SELF-TESTED on the new board 50D37286DD1820A6] src/wd_post.cpp/.h. A timer0 alarm claimed with hardware_alarm_claim_unused, priority 0, every 200 ms; once the watchdog has under 1 s left it saves the interrupted frame. The HardFault vector is overwritten in the RAM vector table at boot (shared by both cores) because no-OS-FatFS's crash.c already links a strong isr_hardfault (breakpoint, then lockup; its record was never read). FINDING: .uninitialized_data RAM does not survive a watchdog reset on this board: the record at 0x20000188 came back holding Thumb code (b5104b05...), so the boot reuses low SRAM. The record therefore lives only in registers: watchdog scratch[5..7] (PC, LR, kind/core/saves/exception number) and powman scratch[0..7] (uptime, warning span and core 1 line delta, 6809 PC/USB devices/EXC_RETURN, NVIC active+pending or CFSR/HFSR/BFAR/MMFAR, magic WDP1); powman scratch is unused elsewhere and needs no password. pizero_wdtest now cycles four freezes; results, PCs resolved with arm-none-eabi-addr2line: (0) spin in loop(): 'hang, core 0 at pc=10021e62 in thread mode; 5 warnings over 800 ms, core 1 running (+19,973 lines)', pc = loop; (1) interrupts off: 'the early warning never ran'; (2) spin in an alarm callback: 'in TIMER0_IRQ_3', pc = the lambda, lr = alarm_pool_irq_handler, active bit 3; (3) udf: 'HARD FAULT on core 0', cfsr=00010000 (UNDEFINSTR), hfsr=40000000 (FORCED), pc = loop. The next boot prints a '[watchdog] post-mortem:' line; the soak log writes it under the header; scripts/soak.py analyse lists them. Product (pizero_stream_60) back on the board: fps 60, short 0.0%, freezes 0. RAM: pizero_stream_60 423,308 (80.7%), pizero_stream 422,704, pizero_wavmeas 406,104, pizero_coco3 402,424. 256 host tests pass. NEXT: put the product build on unit 10 (8DEF17616A6EA5F1) for the PIZERO-203 soak, with the user's go-ahead; the first recovery's post-mortem line answers loop vs interrupt vs masked vs fault.

summary: CoCo 3: run a list of real CoCo 3 titles and record a result for each
description: Filed 2026-10-15 so that a CoCo 3 compatibility statement rests on software, not just on BASIC booting. As of today no CoCo 3 game or program has been run on the board: what is proven is Super Extended Color BASIC booting to OK at 60 fps at 0.89 and 1.79 MHz (PIZERO-133, 213, 218), HSCREEN drawing, and a full-screen HCLS animation at 1.79 MHz with no late frames (PIZERO-219, 220). DO: pick a handful of titles that between them cover the CoCo 3's features: a few disk games using the 320-wide 16-colour modes, something whose music runs off the GIME timer (also feeds PIZERO-170), something using 40-column text, and NitrOS-9 Level 2 (which will show 80-column limits, PIZERO-134). Run each in env pizero_coco3 on hardware and record per title: loads, plays, picture right, sound right, keys needed (ALT/CTRL/F1/F2 are PIZERO-215), and whatever goes wrong, each defect as its own issue. Write the list and results into a doc (docs/coco3-titles.md or a section of docs/coco3-feasibility.md) that the README's CoCo 3 paragraph can point to. DEPENDS ON: PIZERO-214 (basic features checked first) and ideally PIZERO-215 (keys). DONE WHEN: at least six titles have a recorded result and the README states CoCo 3 compatibility from them, with the 80-column caveat. RUN 2026-10-19 on the board (pizero_coco3), titles from the user's card. TEST LIST: montrev.dsk, galactus-2.dsk, STARCAST.DSK, SPACE-RAID.DSK, nos9l2.dsk, and GOLAXIAN.DSK and sinistar.dsk (both state 512K; expected to refuse). 1 MONTEZUMA'S REVENGE (montrev.dsk): title screen right; ENTER gave ?IE ERROR IN 18026.5994. Cause read from the disk, not the firmware: MONTREV.BAS line 100 LOADMs LOADDATA.BIN, whose segments write $FFA2 (the MMU slot for $4000-$5FFF) with pages $36, $08-$0C, $10, $11, $3A and load up to 8 KB into each. Pages $08-$11 exist only on a 512K CoCo 3; on 128K the page number wraps to $38-$31, so the first data segment lands on page $38, BASIC's own $0000-$1FFF, which wrecks Disk BASIC mid-load (hence the ?IE and the nonsense line number). This copy needs 512K, which this board cannot have (docs/coco3-feasibility.md). Result: needs 512K, fails as a real 128K CoCo 3 would; not a CoCo Zero defect. Not yet confirmed in desktop XRoar at -ram 128 vs 512. Note GALACTUS.BIN also loads $08 into an MMU register, so it may be 512K too. 2 SPACE RAID (SPACE-RAID.DSK, RUN"START"): loads and plays fine, per the user on the board. 3 STARCAST (STARCAST.DSK): works, per the user on the board. 4 GALACTUS (galactus-2.dsk): works, per the user; its LDA #$08 into an MMU register is not a 512K requirement. 5 GOLAXIAN (GOLAXIAN.DSK): refuses cleanly with its own memory check (the disk holds the messages '512K REQUIRED' and '128K DETECTED'); the right result on a 128K machine. 6 SINISTAR PREVIEW v0.02 (sinistar.dsk, RUN"SINI"): readme says 512K minimum. SINI.BAS line 10 sets WIDTH 80, so its opening AI-consent question shows at half width and cannot be read (PIZERO-134, a real finding apart from 512K). Answered Y and 3 over serial; it stalled loading M4TAIL.BNK. Cause read from the disk: each .BNK is LOADMed then EXEC &H3000, and that stub maps MMU pages $26 and $1E (512K-only; on 128K they wrap to $36 and $3E) to copy the bank, so on 128K it overwrites live memory. Result: needs 512K, as stated; no memory check of its own, so it hangs rather than refusing. 7 NITROS-9 LEVEL 2 (nos9l2.dsk, DOS): prints NITROS9 BOOT then FAILED. Not a CoCo 3 defect: the image is the 30 MB CoCo SDC distribution (LSN0 says 'NitrOS-9 3.3.0 6809 Level 2', 122,868 sectors), and its OS9Boot's disk driver is llcocosdc, for CoCo SDC hardware the board does not emulate; nos9l1.dsk is the same kind of image, which is why Level 1 needed scripts/mkos9disk.py (PIZERO-199). A Level 2 boot floppy is filed as PIZERO-236. Screenshots SCR0007-0009 on the card: SCR0008 is Sinistar's WIDTH 80 consent screen, SCR0009 the Level 2 boot message, both through the half-width 80-column path (PIZERO-134). CLOSED 2026-10-19: seven titles recorded in docs/coco3-titles.md (3 work, 3 need 512K, NitrOS-9 Level 2 needs PIZERO-236), and the README's CoCo 3 paragraph now states compatibility from them, with the 80-column caveat. Not done here: a GIME-timer music title, a 40-column program and ALT/CTRL/F-key games, listed under 'Still to try' in the doc.

summary: Autorun typing drops keys after a long line, and its buffer stops at 1,024 bytes
description: Found 2026-10-15 while preparing PIZERO-214. (1) BASIC at 0.89 MHz takes over a third of a second to store a long program line (about 190 characters, with CoCo 3 BASIC; seen in the host CoCo 3 in test/test_coco3_boot, where 20 fields after ENTER were not enough and 60 were), and keys typed meanwhile are lost. Autotype in src/main.cpp pump_keyboard waits only its usual 4-field gap after ENTER, so an autorun.txt with long numbered lines would lose the start of the next line. Not yet seen on the board; the CoCo 2's BASIC may be quicker. Workaround today: a '~' after a long line. FIX: wait longer after '\r' in autotype, scaled by the line's length or a flat 1 s, or wait until BASIC polls the keyboard again. (2) coco_boot.h autotype[1024]: a longer autorun.txt is truncated with a serial warning only. A typed-in BASIC program easily passes that (PIZERO-214's check listing is 1,600 bytes, so scripts/serial_type.py types it over USB serial instead). Consider a larger buffer, or reading autorun.txt a line at a time. AUTORUN.md should mention whatever limit remains.

summary: Audio output level is low: music peaks around -13.5 dBFS, SOUND around -11 dBFS
description:
Found while closing PIZERO-41. Measured off the HDMI stream with the capture stick (2026-10-16): DAC music peaked at 6921 of 32767 (-13.5 dBFS) with RMS about -28 dBFS; SOUND 159,255 swung -8922..+9253 (about -11 dBFS). That leaves 11 to 13 dB of unused headroom, so a TV is turned up further and its own noise comes up with it. Nothing clips today. To do: find where the DAC and SN76489 mix is scaled (lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp audio output path, and the PIZERO-202 volume setting), pick a gain that puts the loudest realistic case (full DAC swing plus the sound chip) just under full scale, and confirm with a capture that nothing clips. Capture caveat: the stick drops 512-sample blocks (see PIZERO-41), so judge level and clipping, not continuity.

[2026-10-16 Gain doubled (+6 dB): AUDIO_DAC_GAIN 180 -> 360, AUDIO_GAIN_X 3 -> 6 (lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp), docs/pipeline.md updated. Reasoning: at 180 a full 0-63 swing is 11,340 p-p, so a square wave sat near -15 dBFS at the default volume 10; AC coupling lets a narrow-pulse waveform push one side to nearly the whole swing plus about 5% low-pass overshoot, so 360 (22,680 p-p) leaves about 3 dB in the worst case. Volumes 11-15 may clip on such waveforms; a program driving the DAC and the SN76489 both at full scale at once clips at any useful gain. Note: the board captured for PIZERO-41 was likely at volume 15 (SOUND swung 18,175 p-p, 1.5x the volume-10 figure). Flashed to board 50D37286DD1820A6; needs a capture to confirm the level and no clipping.]

[2026-10-16 DONE, user confirmed it sounds good on the stream. Capture of SOUND 159,255 at volume 15 after the change: -17,848..+18,343 (36,191 p-p, exactly twice the 18,175 before), peak -5.0 dBFS, no samples at full scale. That also confirms the board's card is set to volume 15; at the default 10 the same tone would peak near -8.5 dBFS. Whether lopsided waveforms clip at volumes above 10 is untested and filed as PIZERO-231.]

[2026-10-17 Doc follow-up: the volume entry in SETTINGS.md still described only the PIZERO-223 tripling. Now it says each number is six times its pre-PIZERO-223 level (x3 on 2026-10-14, x2 on 2026-10-16) and that volumes above 10 may clip on hard-driven music (PIZERO-231).]

summary: Check whether hard-driven DAC music clips at volume 11-15 after the PIZERO-230 gain doubling
description: Left over from PIZERO-230, which doubled the output gain (AUDIO_DAC_GAIN 360, AUDIO_GAIN_X 6 in lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp). A symmetric SOUND tone at volume 15 peaks at -5.0 dBFS with no clipping. The output is AC coupled (audio_dc_run), so a waveform of narrow pulses can push one side out to nearly the whole peak-to-peak swing: at volume 15 a full 0-63 DAC swing is 34,020 p-p, which would clip, and a program driving the DAC and the SN76489 at full scale together clips even at volume 10. To do: capture a game or music program that drives the DAC hard (and one using the SN76489 with the DAC) at volume 15 with the HDMI capture stick, count samples at +-32767. If clipping is real and audible, options are a soft limiter in audio_emit or capping the gain above volume 10. Capture caveat: the stick drops 512-sample blocks (PIZERO-41), so judge level and clipping only.

summary: HDMI audio sounds garbled and fuzzy on the main monitor, and did before the PIZERO-230 gain change
description:
Reported by the user 2026-10-16: audio from the board over HDMI sounds garbled and fuzzy on their main monitor, and it already did before PIZERO-230 doubled the gain, so the extra level (and the volume 11-15 clipping question in PIZERO-231) is not the cause. Before PIZERO-230 the stream peaked near -13.5 dBFS, far from full scale.

What is already established about the stream: a MacroSilicon capture stick decodes the board's HDMI audio exactly (PIZERO-41, PIZERO-230), and the same board and build played the jukebox cleanly on an older 48" Samsung (PIZERO-224). So the samples the board sends are right; what is left is how this sink receives them, or the monitor's own amp and speakers.

Candidates on the link side: (1) the product build sends AVI + Audio InfoFrame + ACR on every vblank line, about 45 ACR packets a frame and roughly 2,700 a second bunched into vblank (audio_vblank_info_cb in src/main.cpp, see PIZERO-32), where sinks normally see about one ACR per millisecond spread evenly; a sink that regenerates its audio clock from ACR could be disturbed by that. (2) audio sample packet spacing across the frame, nothing in active video during vblank. (3) 640x480 at 25.2 MHz with CTS=25200 N=6144 (correct by spec, PIZERO-32).

To do: (a) find out whether this monitor plays clean audio from another HDMI source (the Mac); if not, it is the monitor. (b) note whether it is every sound or only some (single SOUND tone vs. DAC music vs. SN76489 chords) and try audio_lowpass = 4000. (c) if the link is suspect, build a variant that sends ACR once per frame (or at a spec-like rate) and compare by ear on this monitor. Unknown so far: which monitor this is, and whether it is the dev monitor from PIZERO-32 that ignores ACR. Related: PIZERO-32, PIZERO-99, PIZERO-224, PIZERO-231.

[2026-10-16 The Mac's HDMI audio plays cleanly on this monitor, so the monitor's speakers are fine and the problem is in how it receives the board's stream. Test build pizero_vblank_audio (-DAV_VBLANK_AUDIO, src/main.cpp audio_vblank_info_cb and the stream_meter/stream_encode helpers split out of stream_audio_cb): the sample meter now spreads the 800 samples a frame over all 523 non-sync lines instead of the 480 active ones, so the ~1.4 ms gap every frame is gone; each vblank line carries one island in its ACTIVE block (audio, or on every 8th line AVI + Audio InfoFrame + ACR), so ACR drops from about 2,700 to 360 a second. A first version put the vblank audio in the back porch, which PIZERO-34 had already found blanks the dev monitor; it was rewritten to the active block, where the info island has always worked, before the user tried it. Built (RAM 83.0%), the IRQ code confirmed in RAM, flashed. The product build pizero_stream_60 is unchanged in behaviour (the refactor only) and still builds at 80.7%. Noticed while reading, not acted on: dvi_setup_scanline_for_vblank_island (lib/libdvi/dvi_timing.cpp) lays a leading guard band before each vblank island but no trailing one, which HDMI requires; a strict sink might mis-parse those islands. A candidate if this build does not help. Next: the user listens on the main monitor. Clean means the gap or the ACR flood was the cause, and the fix moves into the product build (watch PIZERO-34's sync problem on the dev monitor and the upstairs Samsung). If it still garbles, try the trailing guard band.]

[2026-10-16 Result of pizero_vblank_audio on the main monitor: picture fine, audio still garbled, 'possibly not quite as bad'. So the per-frame gap and the ACR flood are at most a minor part. Next step in the same env, -DAV_HDMI_STRICT_FRAMING: (1) a 2px trailing guard band after each vblank island (lib/libdvi/dvi_timing.cpp dvi_setup_scanline_for_vblank_island), which had none; (2) horizontal timing 4/96/60/640 instead of 8/96/56/640 (src/main.cpp dvi_timing_640x480p_57hz_240mhz), because at bp 56 the control period between each active-line audio island's trailing guard and the video guard is only 10px (one control word plus the 8px video preamble) against HDMI's 12px minimum; at 60 it is 14px. h_total stays 800, so 60.0 Hz. Built (RAM 83.0%) and flashed; waiting on the user's ear.]

[2026-10-16 Result with AV_HDMI_STRICT_FRAMING: picture good, sound very similar to the previous build. Playing three-note music: 'I can hear each of 3 notes, but there's a lot of fuzzy buzzing and warbly distortion.' Strict framing kept in the test env (harmless, spec-correct) but it is not the cause. Next, -DAV_AUDIO_FULL_PACKETS in the same env (stream_meter in src/main.cpp): only full 4-sample audio packets, one every 2.4-2.6 lines, as an ordinary source sends, instead of 1-2 samples on nearly every line. Built (RAM 83.0%) and flashed. If that does not help, the next step is pizero_chord-style pure sines over this build to separate the link from anything CoCo-side.]

[2026-10-17 Result with AV_AUDIO_FULL_PACKETS: 'sounds similar. it's the clearest i've heard it.' The user then reported that the MS2109 capture stick does not capture this build's video. Likeliest cause: the 4px front porch from the strict-framing step. The 4/96/60 timing moved to its own flag AV_HDMI_WIDE_BP (left off), so pizero_vblank_audio is back to 8/96/56 with vblank audio, the trailing guard and full packets. Rebuilt and flashed; to check: does the stick capture again, and does the monitor sound the same. The 10px control period before video (HDMI asks for 12) stands; a later fix could shorten the sync pulse instead of the front porch.]

[2026-10-17 With the timing reverted the stick captures again, and the monitor sounds the same as with 4/96/60. Decisive test: recorded 20 s of this build's HDMI audio with the MS2109 stick (lossless WAV, ffmpeg avfoundation device 'Guermok USB3 Video'; peak -25.6 dBFS, RMS -43.7, so no clipping) and played it from the Mac with afplay. The user heard it 'same', the same fuzz and warble as the board direct. So the HDMI link is cleared: the fuzz is in the samples the board generates (or is how this monitor renders that content), and the pizero_vblank_audio changes are not the fix. The 'clearest yet' impression from those builds is not supported by this test. Caveat: afplay plays to the Mac's selected output; the user did not say whether that was the monitor or the MacBook's own speakers. Open question for the next step: what reference 'the right sound' is (desktop XRoar playing the same program, or a real CoCo), and which program was playing (three-note music, likely SN76489 chords). If desktop XRoar sounds clean through the same monitor, the board's sound generation differs from XRoar's and that is the bug; if it is fuzzy too, it is the emulated sound itself (try audio_lowpass = 4000, or a band-limited SN76489).]

[2026-10-17 Correction: the user pointed out the same board played cleanly on the upstairs TV earlier, so the samples are fine; and the Mac-playback test was not clean evidence anyway, because the MS2109 stick drops 512-sample blocks and each drop is a click. audio_lowpass: 4000 changes it, off sounds best, but the fuzz stays, described as 'almost a popping at a specific frequency'. Serial telemetry on pizero_vblank_audio found a bug in the test build: fill pinned near 7,780 of 8,192, skips climbing ~150/s, servo clamped at 47,936. The vblank info lines skipped stream_meter, so a frame carried ~791 samples, not 800; the producer outran the consumer and the ring discarded samples, a steady pop. Fixed (info lines now add their share to g_meter_acc). So the pizero_vblank_audio results above were heard through that bug. Product build pizero_stream_60 flashed back and measured: fill ~4,170 (half), prod 48,006/s, srv 47,997, under 0/s, skips 0. Its ring is healthy, so the product's fuzz is not dropped or repeated samples. Next: the user listens to the product build on the main monitor (audio_lowpass off and default) and describes it against the popping heard on the test builds.]

[2026-10-17 Product build listened to on the main monitor: 'less popping, and also less discernable tones'. Then the fixed pizero_vblank_audio (meter bug gone, telemetry clean: fill ~4,140, skips 0, under 0/s): 'oh that's nice sounding now!' So the fix is the delivery: audio on the vblank lines (in the vblank active-block island), full 4-sample packets, and the trailing guard band, with the info/ACR island on every 8th vblank line. Which of these matters most was not isolated. Promoted into the product: AV_VBLANK_AUDIO, AV_HDMI_STRICT_FRAMING and AV_AUDIO_FULL_PACKETS now in pizero_stream_60 (platformio.ini), the pizero_vblank_audio env removed, docs/BUILD.md and docs/pipeline.md updated. RAM: pizero_stream_60 83.0%, pizero_coco3 79.0%, pizero_chord 83.2%, pizero_videobench 87.3%, pizero_cpuprof_hook 84.5%; pizero_stream 80.6% and pizero_wavmeas 77.5% unaffected. Flashed; telemetry fill ~4,120, prod 48,000/s, skips 0. The MS2109 capture stick captured this signal (8/96/56 timing). Waiting on the user to confirm the product build on the main monitor before closing; checking the dev monitor and the upstairs Samsung is the follow-up.]

[2026-10-17 DONE. The user confirmed the product build on the main monitor: 'dungeons of daggorath is sounding right'. Not done here, filed as PIZERO-233: checking the new delivery on the dev monitor and the upstairs Samsung, and the 10px control period before video (HDMI asks for 12), whose 4/96/60 fix (AV_HDMI_WIDE_BP) broke the capture stick.]
