summary: Buzzy HDMI audio on the PIZERO-120 LCD monitor, unchanged by picture content and by the PIZERO-232/233 delivery fixes
description:
Found 2026-10-17 after PIZERO-232 and PIZERO-233 fixed garbled audio on two other screens (the main monitor and a Samsung TV). On the LCD monitor from PIZERO-120 (the one with a band of fuzz down the centre of colour pictures), the sound is still fuzzy with the current product build (pizero_stream_60 with AV_VBLANK_AUDIO, AV_HDMI_STRICT_FRAMING, AV_AUDIO_FULL_PACKETS, AV_HDMI_WIDE_BP).

Ruled out by experiment: the picture. The user played a plain BASIC tone (SOUND 100) over the green text screen, where the band shows, and over a black PMODE 4 screen (10 PMODE 4,1:PCLS:SCREEN 1,1 / 20 SOUND 100,30 / 30 GOTO 20), where it does not: 'the tone is buzzy regardless'. So this is not the marginal-colour-signal mechanism of PIZERO-120; the two defects are separate.

Known about the stream: the board's ring is healthy (telemetry fill ~4,100 of 8,192, skips 0, under 0/s), and the same build is clean on two other screens and decodes on the MS2109 capture stick.

Open: whether a square wave is simply buzzy on this monitor's speakers (needs a reference: the same kind of tone, or desktop XRoar, played from the Mac through this monitor), and if not, what this sink wants that the others do not (ACR at 360/s now vs about 1,000/s from a normal source, channel status or Audio InfoFrame fields, the monitor's own clock recovery).

[2026-10-17 Reference test: the Mac (default output 'U29I', this monitor, confirmed with system_profiler) played a 300 Hz sine and a 300 Hz naive square wave at about -12 dBFS through this monitor with afplay: 'both were cleaner' than the board's SOUND tone. So it is not the monitor's speakers with square waves; it is how this monitor receives our stream. Already varied tonight without fixing this monitor: ACR ~2,700/s then 360/s, packet fill, vblank gap, trailing guards, blanking 8/96/56 then 8/92/60. Never varied: the AVI InfoFrame's VIC, always 0 (unknown). Test env pizero_vic1 (-DAV_AVI_VIC=1, CEA 640x480p60; macro in src/main.cpp at the AVI setup) built (RAM 83.0%) and flashed. Waiting on the user's ear.]

[2026-10-17 pizero_vic1: 'still a bit raspy' (at most a slight improvement). Kept VIC 1 and stacked two more in env pizero_aif: AV_AIF_REFER_STREAM (Audio InfoFrame SF and SS 0, as CEA-861 asks for L-PCM over HDMI) and AV_VBLANK_INFO_EVERY=3 (info/ACR island on every 3rd vblank line, ~840 ACR/s, near a normal source's ~1,000; tonight's builds had only tried ~2,700 and 360). Two changes at once to save a round; bisect only if it helps. Built (RAM 83.0%), flashed, telemetry clean (fill ~4,115, skips 0).]

[2026-10-17 pizero_aif: 'still raspy. maybe cleaner but it's hard to tell.' By-ear judgement exhausted, so measured acoustically with the MacBook mic near the monitor (ffmpeg avfoundation ':0', pure-Python Goertzel scan, scratchpad tone.py). Board, BASIC 10 SOUND 100,30:GOTO 10 typed over serial (Esc = BREAK): fundamental 275 Hz, mic peak -35 dB; strongest peaks 825, 770, 275, 330, 1320, 550 Hz. Mac, a naive 275 Hz square via afplay through the same monitor at -29 dBFS: mic peak -44 dB, clean, 275 dominant then 820/825 and 1370, nothing at 330 or 770 (at -9 dBFS also clean). Fine scan of the board: sidebands at 330 and 769.5 Hz, i.e. every peak is a multiple of 55 Hz (275 = 5x55). The board's tone repeats only every fifth cycle; that structure is the candidate for the rasp. Not 60 Hz, so not frame-rate modulation. Next: capture the same tone digitally with the MS2109 stick to tell source from reception. In the capture: the board generates it (emulation, or authentic CoCo SOUND behaviour; compare desktop XRoar). Not in the capture: this monitor's reception adds it.]

[2026-10-17 DIGITAL CAPTURE of the same tone (pizero_aif, MS2109 stick): peak -7.4 dBFS, clean. Relative to the 275 Hz fundamental: 330 Hz -42.7 dB, 550 -39.6, 770 -32.0, 825 -11.0, 1375 -17.8. Mic of the Mac's square through the monitor: 330 -42.3, 770 -38.5, 825 -13.7. Mic of the BOARD through the monitor: 330 -5.6, 550 -6.5, 770 +0.2, 825 +2.7. So the board's samples are clean and this monitor adds the 55 Hz-spaced rasp to our stream only. Also: the board's tone (-7 dBFS) reached the mic 9 dB quieter than the Mac's -29 dBFS square at the same monitor volume, so the monitor loses much of our audio. Hypothesis: the receiver drops corrupted audio packets and conceals the gaps (quieter, periodic rasp), the same marginal-signal weakness as PIZERO-120. libdvi drives the TMDS pads at 2 mA with slew limiting (dvi_configure_pad, lib/libdvi/dvi_serialiser.cpp). Added DVI_PAD_DRIVE / DVI_PAD_SLEWFAST; test env pizero_drive8 (pizero_aif + 8 mA, fast slew) built (RAM 83.0%), flashed, telemetry clean. Next: mic-measure on the monitor, and look at the PIZERO-120 band.]

[2026-10-17 pizero_drive8 (8 mA, fast slew) on the monitor: 'quieter now. barely making a sound', the user turned the monitor to 100%. The PIZERO-120 band looked the same. So this monitor's audio does depend on the electrical signal, and a stronger, faster edge makes it worse. Next, separating the two: pizero_slew2 (2 mA, fast slew) built and flashed; 4 mA with the slew limit kept is the other half.]

[2026-10-17 pizero_slew2 (2 mA, fast slew), mic: peak -33.4 dB; relative to 275 Hz: 330 -3.1, 550 -7.4, 770 -5.0, 825 +3.0, 1375 -3.7. Against pizero_aif at 2 mA slew-limited (peak -35; 330 -5.6, 770 +0.2): the same rasp, within mic noise. Slew alone does not move it; 8 mA made it much quieter. The monitor's volume setting between the two mic takes is not known exactly, so absolute levels are only roughly comparable.]

[2026-10-17 PARKED. Summary for whoever picks this up: the board's audio is clean at the source (MS2109 digital capture), the Mac's audio is clean through this monitor, and the board's audio through this monitor is quieter than it should be and carries a rasp with peaks on a 55 Hz grid (275 Hz tone: strong 330 and 770). Tried without a fix: AVI VIC 1 (pizero_vic1), Audio InfoFrame refer-to-stream plus ~840 ACR/s (pizero_aif), 8 mA + fast slew (pizero_drive8, much quieter), 2 mA + fast slew (pizero_slew2, unchanged); plus everything in PIZERO-232/233. Not a picture effect (black vs colour screen the same). Untested: whether this monitor handles audio at 640x480 from any source (the Mac cannot output a mode that low; a Raspberry Pi or another small computer forced to 640x480p60 would answer it), 4 mA slew-limited drive, and sending stereo with real L/R channel status rather than mono duplicated. The board is back on the product build pizero_stream_60. The test envs (pizero_vic1, pizero_aif, pizero_drive8, pizero_slew2) and flags (AV_AVI_VIC, AV_AIF_REFER_STREAM, DVI_PAD_DRIVE, DVI_PAD_SLEWFAST) stay for this work; none is in the product. Related: PIZERO-120 (same monitor's band, a separate defect).]

summary: NitrOS-9 Level 2 boot floppy for the CoCo 3 build
description: Filed 2026-10-19 from PIZERO-228. The card's nos9l2.dsk is the 30 MB CoCo SDC distribution image (NitrOS-9 3.3.0 6809 Level 2); its boot track loads REL, Boot and Krn and prints NITROS9 BOOT, then FAILED, because OS9Boot's disk driver is llcocosdc and the board emulates the WD1793 floppy controller, not a CoCo SDC. Level 1 had the same problem and was solved by scripts/mkos9disk.py (PIZERO-199), which builds a 35-track floppy from the distribution image. DO: the same for Level 2: a boot floppy whose OS9Boot uses the floppy driver (rb1773 with D0/D1 descriptors, from the Level 2 distribution's modules), built by extending mkos9disk.py. Consider a 32-column VDG term (CoVDG with a VDG Term descriptor) or 40 columns so it is readable before PIZERO-134 lands. DONE WHEN: DOS boots NitrOS-9 Level 2 to a shell prompt in pizero_coco3 on the board, and dir works. DONE 2026-10-20: scripts/mkos9disk.py --level 2 builds it from the 3.3.0 nos9l2.dsk (CoCo SDC image), following SCRIPTS/mb.floppy: track 34 rel_80 + boot_1773_6ms + krn (4,608 bytes); OS9Boot is standard.bl with krnp2/ioman/init, rb1773 and the 35-track ddd0/d0/d1/d2 descriptors, vtio + keydrv_cc3 + snddrv_cc3 + joydrv_joy, cowin with term_win80 and /w to /w7, vrn/vi/ftdd, pipes, clock_60hz + clock2_soft, sysgo_dd (28,738 bytes); CMDS has 77 commands with grfdrv and shell kept (b09utils, edit and the Level 1 exclusions left out); a plain startup (echo, link shell, load utilpak1) replaces the distribution's, which merges SYS fonts and opens windows the disk has no room for; about 11 KB free. The Level 1 output is unchanged (66 commands, 52 KB free). ON THE BOARD (pizero_coco3, 640-wide): DOS boots to the 80-column shell prompt and dir works, per the user. MISHAP: copying it to the card as NOS9L2.DSK replaced the card's 30 MB nos9l2.dsk, because FAT and macOS ignore case; the same file is in ~/Downloads/Coco SDC Image (2025-08-28)/NITROS9/, to be restored, with the floppy renamed L2BOOT.DSK. README now warns about the clash.

summary: Documentation sweep: the CoCo 3 as a first-class machine
description: User request 2026-10-20: 'now that the coco3 is well supported, it will need to become the focus.' Since PIZERO-135 one firmware is a CoCo 2 or a 128 KB CoCo 3 (machine setting, per-game switching), 80 columns show whole (PIZERO-134), the CoCo 3 keys and second buttons work (PIZERO-215), real titles are recorded (PIZERO-228, docs/coco3-titles.md) and NitrOS-9 Level 2 boots (PIZERO-236). summary: AY chips cost about 1.6 ms a frame each: render by events, and measure on the CoCo 3
description:
Left over from PIZERO-149. ay_render (lib/coco_machine/src/psg_ay8910.h) steps every chip tick (clock/8) and averages per audio sample. Measured on the board (cocozero, docs/ay-checks/sym12.bas): 6.5 ms a frame idle, 8.3 ms with one chip, 12.9 ms with four, so about 1.6 ms per chip per frame (800 samples, roughly 500 host cycles a sample a chip). A CoCo 2 has room; a CoCo 3 at 1.79 MHz already peaks at 15.2 ms (PIZERO-220), so symphony12 = on there would overrun. Idea: compute the next tick at which any output can change (the nearest tone count, noise step or envelope step) and add level times duration in one go, instead of looping per tick; most samples then cost a few operations. Also check that AY_LEVEL and the hot path run from RAM, not flash. Done when four chips cost well under 1 ms a frame, measured on both machines, with test_psg_ay8910 still passing. Related: the SN76489's sn_render has the same 64-bit division that cost the AY 2 ms a chip; fix it the same way.

[2026-10-22 Measured on hardware with docs/ay-checks/allvoice.bas (product build 6d46534, CoCo Zero at 0.89 MHz): all four Symphony-12 chips (12 tones), the SN76489's three tones and noise, stereo on. The emulation took 15.4-16.7 ms of each 16.7 ms frame for about 23 s (9.9 ms before the music, so the chips cost about 5.6 ms). Every frame was late (late=60/s), the machine ran about 1% slow (47,550 samples/s against 48,000), the audio ring drained from 4,160 to 0 in about 10 s, and then underran at 350-3,650 samples/s (0.7-7.6%), heard as crackle. Video held 60 fps, and everything recovered on its own once the voices faded (late 0, underruns 0, the ring refilling). So a CoCo 2 can NOT carry every voice at once today; this issue, not only the CoCo 3 case, is what stands in the way. The stereo filters (PIZERO-250) are a small part: the four-chip figure before stereo was about 6.4 ms.]

[2026-10-22 BUILT, awaiting the user's ears.] What the cost was, measured with pizero_cpuprof (its [prof3] line now prints the audio samples' clocks on the CoCo 2 too): about 400 CPU clocks per chip per sample, and it was NOT the tick loop. Three steps, each measured on the board with docs/ay-checks/sym12.bas and allvoice.bas:
1. RAM, not flash: ay_tick and (since PIZERO-250) audio_emit had been compiled as out-of-line functions in flash, and AY_LEVEL/SN_LEVEL lived in flash. SOUND_HOT / SOUND_TABLE (defined in coco_machine.cpp, empty on the host) put the render path and the tables in RAM, and audio_emit is HOT_FUNC. sn_render's 64-bit divide became 32-bit, as the AY's had. This took about 0.9 ms off every frame (the filters), not the chips.
2. Skipping quiet ticks alone did nothing, and at first made things WORSE (17 ms, the distortion the user heard in SYM12 after the 4th chip): sym12.bas leaves tones B and C at period 0, which toggles every tick, so the skip stopped every tick. Fixed by running only the parts that can be heard (ay_heard: a tone on in the mixer with a level above 0, the noise if such a channel takes it, the envelope if a channel is under it and it still moves). A part no one hears is left behind (since[]) and caught up exactly in ay_sync, which every register write calls first.
3. The per-sample fixed work (loops, mix, two divides) was still about 375 clocks. Each chip now keeps what the last render found (valid, parts, out, quiet, pending): a sample in which nothing heard changes counts down and returns the cached output. Four chips in SYM12 went from 1.46 M to 0.64 M clocks a frame of audio work (idle 0.26 M), so about 1.6 ms for four chips including stereo's second filter chain.
Result, product build, allvoice.bas (12 AY tones in stereo + 3 SN tones + SN noise + the DAC): 9.3-9.7 ms a frame, 10.8 ms at the peak, against 15.4-16.7 ms before; no underruns, ring never below 2,900. Exactness: test_render_skipping_matches_every_tick (test_psg_ay8910 and test_csg_sn76489) compares against stepping every part every tick under random writes, sample for sample and in the final state; each was checked by breaking the code on purpose (5 AY mutations, 4 cache mutations, 2 SN mutations, all caught). RAM 84.6 percent product (pizero_stream 84.4, wavmeas 81.2, coco3 84.6). Code: commit 518bb23.
Not done here, filed as PIZERO-252: the SN76489 still runs every part every sample while active, about 0.85 ms a frame even when silent once a program has touched it; and the CoCo 3 at 1.79 MHz with symphony12 on is not yet measured.

[2026-10-22 DONE: confirmed on hardware by the user ("it all sounds wonderful now"): sym12.bas clean through the fourth chip, allvoice.bas without crackle, stereo.bas left then right. Written up in docs/sound.md.]

summary: Tandy Speech/Sound Cartridge (26-3144A): its AY-3-8913 through the cartridge's microcontroller
description: Left over from PIZERO-149's survey. The SSC puts an AY-3-8913 and an SP0256-AL2 speech chip behind a PIC 7040 microcontroller; the CoCo writes commands to $FF7E (status read there, bit 7 PIC busy, bit 6 low while speaking, bit 5 low while the sound chip plays) and resets it at $FF7D. Emulating it means emulating the PIC's command protocol (a ROM disassembly and disk of SSC programs are at tlindner.macmess.org/?page_id=96; MAME emulates it), feeding chip 0 of the existing AY bank. Software: period SSC programs, and the Sierra games patched for SSC (Color Computer Archive, 2026-08-22). Speech would need an SP0256 model, a separate and larger job.

summary: Symphony-12 in stereo: chips 1-2 left, 3-4 right
description:
Left over from PIZERO-149. The real card has a mono/stereo jumper; in stereo MAME (coco_sym12.cpp) routes chips 1-2 left and 3-4 right. Built 2026-10-22, setting symphony12_stereo (on by default on every machine, as it is the cartridge's jumper, not the machine's).

What was done:
- lib/coco_machine/src/psg_ay8910.h: struct ay_bank gains stereo (the jumper) and sym12 (bit per chip, last written by the Symphony-12; a CoCo PSG or Deluxe write to chip 1 clears its bit, so a PSG game stays centred even with both carts on). ayb_render_lr mixes each side like the mono bank, by the chips on that side (n chips scale sum*2/(n+1)), so one Symphony-12 chip alone is as loud as a CoCo PSG. ayb_render is now the average of the two, the same as before when the jumper is off.
- lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp: the sample ring is int16 [8192][2] (+16 KB RAM: 81.8% -> 84.5% product, pizero_stream 84.1%, wavmeas 80.9%). audio_sample mixes DAC + SN76489 into both sides and the AY's left and right into each. The DC blocker and low-pass have a right-channel copy that runs only while the sides differ: taken from the left's state when they part, dropped once both filters hold the same state, so neither edge clicks and mono costs no more than before. coco_machine_audio_read_lr is new; coco_machine_audio_read returns the average (WAV dump). The tone counter uses the average.
- src/main.cpp: stream_next_sample fills a pair (pause fade and underrun hold per side); the non-streaming audio_encode_frame packs pairs too. dvi_di_set_audio_samples already took separate L and R, and its IEC channel status already numbers left 1 and right 2, so the data islands needed no change.
- src/settings.h: symphony12_stereo parsed, defaulted on, in the template after the machine block; the [settings] log prints symphony12=stereo|mono|off.
- Tests: test_symphony12_stereo_pans_its_chips (test_psg_ay8910), settings parse and default (test_settings). docs/ay-checks/stereo.bas: chip 1 left and chip 4 right take turns, then chips 2 and 3 hold a fifth.

Needs on hardware: stereo.bas heard left then right on the main monitor, and once with symphony12_stereo = off (all centred).

[2026-10-22 DONE: confirmed on hardware by the user ("it all sounds wonderful now"): sym12.bas clean through the fourth chip, allvoice.bas without crackle, stereo.bas left then right. Written up in docs/sound.md.]

summary: SN76489: run only the heard parts and cache the output, as the AY does; measure the AY on the CoCo 3
description: Left over from PIZERO-248. (1) The SN76489 (lib/coco_machine/src/csg_sn76489.h) skips ticks in which no counter runs out, but its noise counter (16-64 ticks) and every tone count even at attenuation 15, so once a program has written the chip it costs about 0.85 ms a frame on the board even when silent (product build: 6.9 ms idle before docs/ay-checks/allvoice.bas, 7.76 ms after it faded out). Give it the AY's treatment (psg_ay8910.h, PIZERO-248): heard parts only (a tone with attenuation below 15; tone 2 also when the noise follows it and is heard; the noise when its attenuation is below 15), the rest caught up on writes (sn_write), and a cached output while nothing heard changes. The exactness test test_render_skipping_matches_every_tick in test_csg_sn76489 already exists to guard it. (2) Measure symphony12 = on on the CoCo 3 at 1.79 MHz (sym12.bas, allvoice.bas under machine = coco3 with the cartridges turned on in the game's file) now that four chips cost about 1.6 ms; PIZERO-220 had the CoCo 3 peaking at 15.2 ms before.

summary: The CoCo sound path: multiplexer, sound enable and single-bit output; every source at once on the CoCo Zero; joystick reads kept out of the sound
description:
Found writing docs/sound.md (2026-10-22). The audio source (lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp, audio_update_level) hears only the 6-bit DAC (PIA1 port A bits 2-7). Not emulated: (1) the single-bit sound output, PIA1 port B bit 1 ($FF22), which some games use for clicks and beeps; (2) the sound enable, PIA1 CB2 ($FF23 bit 3); (3) the analog multiplexer, PIA0 CA2 ($FF01) and CB2 ($FF03), which picks the DAC, the cassette input or the cartridge's sound line. So the DAC is always heard, and the SN76489 and AY chips are mixed in directly, so a program that switches the multiplexer away from the cartridge, or turns sound off, does not silence them. Note: the comment in audio_update_level says the single-bit sound is PIA1 CB2, not PB1; that is backwards (PB1 is the single-bit output, CB2 the enable) and should be corrected with this work. XRoar's sound.c models all three and is the reference. Check against a game that uses single-bit sound, and that SOUND/PLAY are unchanged (BASIC sets the mux to the DAC and enables sound before playing).

[2026-10-22 BUILT, awaiting hardware.] User direction: get the real behaviour right, AND a setting that has every source connected at once on the CoCo Zero ('way cooler'), AND inherently avoid the sound games like Double Back make while reading the analog joystick.
- lib/coco_machine/src/coco_sound.h (new, host-tested by test/test_coco_sound): snd_line_mv works out the line in millivolts from XRoar's measured tables (sound.c, a real Dragon): source = PIA0 CB2<<1 | CA2 (DAC, cassette, cartridge line, nothing), enable = PIA1 CB2, single-bit = PIA1 PB1 when its DDR bit makes it an output (it shifts each source's gain and offset; with the mux off it drives the line alone; with neither the line holds). The cassette carries nothing (no tape playback), so only its offset. Volume unchanged: the DAC's 4,500 mV span maps to the old 360 a step (AUDIO_MV_GAIN_Q10).
- Setting sound_sources = all | switched (src/settings.h; profile: all on cocozero, switched on coco2/coco3). all: every source heard whatever the mux/enable say; the single-bit still shapes the DAC. switched: the real CoCo. Under switched the SN76489, the CoCo PSG and the Symphony-12 in mono come through the cartridge line (heard only when the mux selects it and the enable is on, at the measured cartridge gain); the Symphony-12 in stereo (its own jacks) and the Deluxe CoCo's chip (inside the machine, XRoar's non-muxed path) are always heard: ayb_render_routed in psg_ay8910.h, with a new deluxe flag.
- Setting joystick_quiet = on | off (on for cocozero, off for the stock machines). A DAC write followed within 256 ticks (16 CPU cycles at 0.89 MHz) by a read of PIA0 port A is a joystick trial: snd_probe_read takes its sound back from the write on, out of the sample in progress (g_aud.acc) and the one before it, which audio_sample now holds back one sample (about 21 us) for this. The heard DAC value (g_dac6) is kept apart from the register, so the comparator sees the trial and a later recompute does not bring it back. Telemetry: [snd] joystick_probes=N. ROM check: of every STA/STB $FF20 in bas12, extbas11, disk11 and coco3.rom, only JOYSTK ($A9F2) reads $FF00 right after; SOUND, PLAY and the cassette routines do not. JOYSTK itself turns the sound enable off first (BSR $A974 clears $FF23 bit 3), so on a real CoCo BASIC's joystick is silent and Double Back's buzz is authentic.
- The wrong comment in audio_update_level (single-bit 'is CB2, not PB1') is gone with the rewrite.
- Tests: test_coco_sound (5): the mux table, the single-bit, all mode, and a tone played while a successive-approximation read runs through the real audio integrator (with joystick_quiet the samples match the tone alone to within 1; without, they are off by thousands); mutation-checked 3 ways. test_settings covers the two settings. 284 host tests pass. RAM 85.0 percent product (stream 84.8, wavmeas 81.6, coco3 85.1).
- On the board: a BASIC JOYSTK loop counted about 3,500 trials a second taken out; SOUND 100,30 added none.
To confirm on hardware: Double Back quiet on the CoCo Zero while the joystick moves, and buzzing with joystick_quiet = off in its file; SOUND/PLAY and the AY demos unchanged; and under machine = coco2 with a GMC game, its music still plays (the game must select the cartridge line and enable sound, as on the real machine).

[2026-10-22 DONE: confirmed on hardware by the user ("everything sounds really good"). Documented in docs/sound.md (the multiplexer section and docs/images/sound-mux.svg).]

summary: Emulate the Yamaha YM2149 as well as the AY-3-8910: psg_chip = auto | ay8910 | ym2149
description:
User request 2026-10-22, after PIZERO-149/248/250/253. Every AY chip in the bank (lib/coco_machine/src/psg_ay8910.h) is modelled as a GI AY-3-8910 today, but the cartridges differ: the CoCo PSG carries a Yamaha YM2149, the Symphony-12 four AY-3-8910s, the Deluxe CoCo an AY-3-8913 (an 8910 in a smaller package). So the CoCo PSG is the one that is not quite right.

What differs, YM2149 against AY-3-8910 (MAME's ay8910.cpp models both and is the reference; XRoar's ay891x.c is 8910 only):
- Envelope: 32 steps a ramp, not 16, at the same overall period (so a step every EP ticks rather than 2*EP). Slow fades and fast-envelope 'buzz' basses sound smoother. The audible part.
- Output: a 32-level DAC with its own curve; a fixed 4-bit volume lands on every other level (2n+1). A small change in the channels' balance.
- Register read-back: the YM returns all 8 bits as written, where the AY masks the unused ones (AY_REG_MASK). Software can tell the chips apart this way, so this matters for correctness more than for sound.
- The YM's /2 clock select pin (SEL): the CoCo PSG's $FF5D clock bit already covers the pitch side.

Plan: a setting psg_chip = auto | ay8910 | ym2149, default auto (each cartridge gets its real chip: CoCo PSG a YM2149, Symphony-12 and Deluxe an AY). The two forced values put one chip everywhere, to hear a tune on the other. Per-chip type in struct ay8910 (set by the front-end that writes it, as the clock is), a YM level table and 32-step envelope, and ay_read honouring the type. The PIZERO-248 caching is unaffected (the envelope is just one more counted part), so no speed change is expected; check with the profiler anyway.

Tests: extend test_render_skipping_matches_every_tick to run both chip types; envelope step count and period for the YM; read-back masks per type; settings parse/default/template (test_settings). Document in docs/sound.md (the AY section and the At a glance table) and SETTINGS.md. Hardware check: psg.bas on the CoCo PSG with auto (YM) against psg_chip = ay8910, the envelope part should sound smoother on the YM.

summary: Sound out of a USB-C class-compliant headphone DAC, as an alternative to the video cable's audio
description:
User request 2026-10-23: support a USB-C class-compliant headphone DAC as an output stage alongside the video cable's audio.

What the code has today (checked 2026-10-23): TinyUSB (Adafruit TinyUSB Library in .pio/libdeps) has audio for the device side only (class/audio/audio_device.c), no host audio driver. Pico-PIO-USB 0.7.2 has no isochronous support in its host: usb_out_transaction (pio_usb_host.c) always waits for a handshake and counts a missing one as a failure, and only interrupt endpoints get the periodic scheduling (is_periodic). The USB host is full speed only, PIO-driven, its frame work in the 1 ms SOF timer on core 0.

Plan, in steps:
1. Spike (decides feasibility): with the DAC on the simple hub at boot, dump its configuration descriptor over serial: UAC1 or UAC2 at full speed, the AudioStreaming alt settings (format, channels, bit depth, rates), the endpoint's sync type (adaptive, async with a feedback endpoint, synchronous). A device that streams only at high speed cannot work.
2. Patch Pico-PIO-USB for isochronous OUT: token + DATA0 packet each frame, no handshake wait, no retry; schedule every frame.
3. A small UAC host class driver (TinyUSB custom host driver): find the playback interface, choose 48 kHz 16-bit stereo, SET_INTERFACE to that alt, set the sampling frequency (UAC1 endpoint SET_CUR, UAC2 clock source), then stream 192-byte packets a frame from the audio ring (coco_machine_audio_read_lr).
4. Rate: the producer's rate is servoed to the video clock (PIZERO-121); the USB frame clock comes from the board's timer. Adaptive devices follow us; for async ones read the feedback endpoint and send 47/48/49 samples a frame, and servo the ring to it.
5. Setting audio_output = video | usb | both (default video); usb falls back to video when no DAC enumerated at boot. Telemetry: packets sent, underruns, the feedback rate.

Constraints: one host port, so keyboard, pad and DAC through the simple hub (the larger hubs do not work); no hot-plug (PIZERO-51), so the DAC must be there at boot. CPU: PIO-USB encodes each packet in software on core 0, perhaps 5-10 percent of core 0 for 192 bytes a millisecond: measure.

Open: which dongle the user has (the spike answers what it offers).

[2026-10-23 Step 1 (spike) DONE: the first device is good.] The user's 4-port USB-C hub with a headphone jack: hub chip Genesys GL850G (05E3:0608). Its audio chip (VID 001F PID 0B21) appears on hub port 3 ONLY while a plug is in the jack (with nothing plugged in, ports 1 and 3 report no device at all). It is USB Audio Class 2.0 at full speed: playback interface 1, alt 2 = 16-bit stereo PCM on isochronous OUT endpoint 03, 192 bytes a frame = 48 kHz, sync type SYNCHRONOUS (locks to our SOF; no feedback endpoint); alt 1 is 24-bit, 288 bytes. Clock source 9, internal programmable (set 48,000 with a UAC2 CUR request). Feature unit 2: master mute and per-channel volume. Also a mono capture interface and two HID interfaces (volume keys). Full record: docs/measurements/usb-audio-hub-001F-0B21.txt.
Found on the way: TinyUSB's enumeration buffer is hard-coded at 256 bytes and a device whose configuration descriptor is longer is dropped silently (usbh.c TU_ASSERT); this one is 423. scripts/patch_tinyusb.py now guards CFG_TUH_ENUMERATION_BUFSIZE, and the pizero_usbdump env (USB_DESC_DUMP: [usbdesc] lines for every mounted device, in main.cpp) sets it to 512. The product build will need the same when the driver lands.
Next: step 2 (Pico-PIO-USB isochronous OUT), step 3 (UAC2 host driver: SET_INTERFACE 1 alt 2, clock 9 to 48 kHz, unmute, 48 sample pairs a frame). Rate: synchronous, so exactly 48 a frame from the board's timer; the ring's servo will have to follow the USB frame clock when USB is the output.

[2026-10-23 Second device, the user's USB-C headphone dongle (through the hub): also VID 001F PID 0B21, but USB Audio Class 1, 218-byte descriptor. Playback interface 1 alt 1: 16-bit stereo, 48,000 Hz only, isochronous OUT EP 03, ADAPTIVE, max 384. Record: docs/measurements/usb-audio-dongle-001F-0B21.txt. So one driver covers both: 48 sample pairs (192 bytes) a frame on OUT EP 03, no feedback endpoint either way (the hub's chip is synchronous, the dongle adaptive). Only the setup differs: UAC1 rate by endpoint SAMPLING_FREQ SET_CUR and mute/volume by its feature unit; UAC2 by clock source 9's CUR and its feature unit 2. The driver should handle both UAC1 and UAC2.]

[2026-10-23 Steps 2 and 3 (minimal) WORK: the user heard the 440 Hz test tone through the dongle.] Pico-PIO-USB is vendored in lib/pico_pio_usb (0.7.2, dc9193f; the unchanged copy is commit 29f10b0, so the changes read as a diff). Changes: the TX encoder's lengths and index are 16-bit (a 192-byte packet encodes to about 460 bytes; the old uint8_t wrapped), endpoint_t.encoded_data_len is uint16_t, and a new isochronous OUT stream (pio_usb.h: pio_usb_host_iso_out_stream, pio_usb_host_iso_frames): the 1 ms frame handler calls a fill function for the packet, builds DATA0 + CRC16, encodes it into its own buffer (PIO_USB_ISO_MAX 200 bytes, about 0.8 KB RAM, so the 32-entry endpoint pool did not grow), then sends the OUT token and the packet with no handshake. Fed from the frame handler because TinyUSB's completion events are serviced only about 60 times a second (USBHost.task once a main loop), far short of 1,000 packets a second.
src/usb_audio.cpp (USB_AUDIO): on mount, reads the configuration descriptor, finds a UAC1 or UAC2 playback alt with 16-bit stereo PCM at 48 kHz on an isochronous OUT endpoint, sends SET_INTERFACE, sets the rate (UAC1 endpoint SAMPLING_FREQ SET_CUR; UAC2 clock source CUR), opens the endpoint with tuh_edpt_open and starts the stream. Env pizero_usbtone (USB_AUDIO_TONE): a 440 Hz tone at about -12 dBFS.
Measured with the dongle (UAC1, adaptive): rate request taken; 1,000 packets a second; core 0 frame time about 9.2 ms against 6.9 ms without (about 2.3 ms a frame, mostly the busy-wait while the 192-byte packet goes out, about 150 us a millisecond, plus the encoding). A few frames at 13.5-13.8 ms in the first seconds (one late), to watch.
Next: feed the stream from the machine's audio ring instead of the tone; the ring has one consumer today (the video stream's DMA IRQ on core 1), so audio_output = usb gives the ring to USB and the video carries silence, and both needs a second read position; the producer's rate servo must follow the USB frame clock (48,000 a second exactly from the board's timer) when USB is the output; the audio_output setting; the hub's UAC2 chip (synchronous) to try too.

[2026-10-23 The machine's sound plays through the USB DAC; volume keys added.] The streaming builds (pizero_stream, so the product and the CoCo 3 build) now carry USB_AUDIO and a 512-byte enumeration buffer. usb_audio = on | off (default on): a DAC set up at boot takes the ring (main.cpp usb_audio_fill, in the frame interrupt: 48 pairs a frame, a fade on pause, the last pair held on underrun) and the video stream sends silence (g_audio_usb), so the ring keeps one reader; off or unplugged returns it. The rate servo needed no change: it follows whichever reader drains the ring. Heard by the user: ORCH90 and ALLVOICE through the dongle. ALLVOICE with the DAC: 13.4-14.0 ms a frame, 15.0-15.6 ms with 50-58 late frames a second at the DAC section, and the ring empty with up to 3,000 USB underruns a second for about 6 s (9.3-9.7 ms without USB): the stream costs more than the tone measured, to tighten (the encoder, the busy-wait).
User request: control the overall volume with the keyboard's volume keys and the dongle's buttons. src/hid_consumer.h (host-tested, test_hid_consumer: keyboard-style 16-bit arrays with report IDs, headset-style bitfields, listed-usage arrays, 32-bit extended usages, a plain keyboard left alone) parses each HID interface's report descriptor at mount for the Consumer page's Volume Increment, Decrement and Mute; main.cpp volume_keys steps volume 0-15, Mute toggles silence (Up or Down unmute), each press put into effect at once and saved to settings.txt two seconds after the last (volume_save_due). On the board: every press of up, down and mute registered, saves landed.
Left, to file at close: both outputs at once (a second reader; the two clocks drift); an on-screen volume display; the DAC's own hardware volume/mute set to full at setup; the USB stream's cost under heavy sound; the hub's UAC2 jack through the product build (only the dongle has played the machine's sound so far).

[2026-10-23 Volume keys: the user's keyboard (Keychron, report ID 4, 16-bit usage array) works. The dongle's headphone buttons do not, and it is not ours: with pizero_usbdump's new [usbhid] logging (each non-pad HID report on change, with the decoder's result, and every report descriptor at mount), the dongle's layout is ten 1-bit Consumer buttons (B5 B6 CD E2 B7 25B 25C 262 E9 EA, so Volume Up/Down are bits 8 and 9), a Telephony bit and padding; every button of the user's headphones came in as 04 00, Play/Pause. The dongle hears their remote as one hook button (CTIA/Android remotes signal Volume Up/Down by resistance on the mic contact; others, such as Apple's, read as one button). test_the_users_dongle pins the layout: its E9/EA bits decode, Play/Pause does not change the volume. Possible: Play/Pause as mute, the user's call.]

[2026-10-23 The hub's own jack (UAC2 chip, 423-byte descriptor): its consumer HID has the dongle's layout with report ID 1, parsed (volume keys found); a second, vendor-page HID interface (report ID 2, 63 bytes). With the user's headphones in its jack, 75 s of button presses produced NO report on either interface: this chip does not read that headset's remote at all (the dongle at least sent Play/Pause). With these headphones the keyboard's volume keys are the way; the firmware is ready for a CTIA remote's Volume Up/Down bits on either chip.]

[2026-10-23 The hub's jack plays the machine's sound (user), but 'a bit hot'. The driver now finds the feature unit feeding the analog output terminal (UAC1 1-bit or UAC2 2-bit controls per channel) and, after the rate, reads its volume range and level, sets each volume channel and unmutes (ua_vol_run, logged; refused steps logged and skipped). The hub's chip: range -60 to 0 dB, powers up at 0 dB (its top). New setting usb_audio_db (-60 to 0, default -10), applied at setup; test_settings covers it. Hub now set to -10 dB; awaiting the user's ear.]

[2026-10-23 DONE, closed at the user's word: the machine's sound plays through both USB DACs (the dongle and the hub's own jack), the keyboard's volume keys work, the DAC's own level is set at setup (usb_audio_db, default -10 dB). Documented in docs/sound.md ('Where the sound comes out', 'Turning it up and down'), docs/pipeline.md, SETTINGS.md and the README. Filed from what was left: PIZERO-257 (the video cable and a USB DAC at once), PIZERO-258 (an on-screen volume display), PIZERO-259 (the USB stream's cost under heavy sound). A DAC plugged in after power-on belongs to PIZERO-51 (hot-plug). Headset buttons: the board decodes any DAC's volume usages, but the user's headphones send only Play/Pause through the dongle and nothing through the hub's jack (their remote is not read as CTIA); nothing to do on the board.]

summary: The overlay draws in standard green whatever the program or a color setting did to the palette
description:
User report 2026-10-23: when the overlay comes up, green has sometimes been redefined (by a program writing the GIME-style palette at $FFB0, or by a color_green setting) to a color that is hard to see. Asked: show the overlay in green, and keep the custom color for when it closes.

Cause: coco_boot_card_present / coco_boot_card_present8 (src/coco_boot.cpp) took the card's ink and paper from the LIVE palette (entries 0 and 8), deliberately, so 'a recolored machine recolors the diagnostic too'. Every card (the F12 overlay, the settings editor, boot pages) followed the program's palette.

Fix: the cards use fixed factory colors, green 0x07E0 on black 0x0000 (CARD_INK / CARD_PAPER). In the product build the card already has its own two palette slots (PAL_CARD in g_pal565), so the machine's palette is never touched: nothing to save on open or restore on close, and the custom color is exactly as it was when the overlay closes.

[2026-10-23 DONE: confirmed on hardware by the user. With palette entry 0 recolored (POKE &HFFB0,9, dark blue), the F12 overlay showed green on black.]

summary: Sound from the video cable and a USB DAC at once
description: Left over from PIZERO-255. Today the sound goes to one output: while a USB DAC has it (usb_audio), the video stream sends silence (g_audio_usb in src/main.cpp), because the audio ring (coco_machine.cpp, g_audio_ring) has one reader. Both at once needs a second read index on the ring (a second coco_machine_audio_read_lr with its own g_audio_r2), one reader per output. The catch: the two outputs run on different clocks (the video's pixel clock and the board's timer for USB frames), about 0.02 percent apart, and the rate servo (PIZERO-121) can hold the ring against only one of them. Servo to one (USB, say) and let the other slip a sample now and then (repeat or drop one, ideally where the signal is quiet, or resample it by a hair). A setting: usb_audio = on | off | both, or audio_output. Measure the cost of the second reader (it is on core 1 for the video and in the USB frame interrupt on core 0, as now).

summary: Show the volume on screen when the volume keys change it
description: Left over from PIZERO-255. The keyboard's Volume Up, Volume Down and Mute keys change the volume setting (src/main.cpp volume_keys) and it is saved, but the only sign is the serial log ([settings] volume = N). Show it briefly on screen: a small bar or 'VOLUME 7' (or 'MUTE') for a second or two over the picture, then gone, without pausing the machine. There is no on-screen message mechanism for a running machine yet (the cards and the overlay replace the screen and pause it), so this needs a small overlay drawn into the scanout over the CoCo's picture, on both machines and both framebuffer layouts. Could serve other quick notices too (F8's artifact change, a screenshot saved).

summary: The USB DAC's stream costs too much under heavy sound: allvoice.bas runs over the frame
description:
Left over from PIZERO-255. Feeding a USB DAC costs about 2.3 ms of each 16.7 ms frame on core 0 with a test tone, and more under load: docs/ay-checks/allvoice.bas (every voice at once) took 13.4-14.0 ms a frame through the dongle against 9.3-9.7 ms on the video cable, with 15.0-15.6 ms and 50-58 late frames a second at its DAC section, the ring emptying and up to 3,000 USB underruns a second for about 6 s. Ordinary programs are fine.

Where the time goes, in the 1 ms USB frame interrupt (lib/pico_pio_usb/src/pio_usb_host.c usb_iso_out_frame): building and CRC-ing the 196-byte packet, NRZI and bit-stuff encoding it bit by bit in pio_usb_ll_encode_tx_data (about 1,600 iterations), and the busy-wait in pio_usb_bus_usb_transfer while the packet goes out (about 150 us). Ideas: a table-driven encoder (a byte at a time, carrying the NRZI state and the run of ones); encode the next packet outside the interrupt (in the main loop, double-buffered) so the interrupt only sends; return from the transfer once the DMA has the data instead of waiting for the end of the packet. Measure with the profiler and allvoice.bas; done when allvoice runs through a DAC without late frames.

summary: Play the Orchestra-90CC's own music program
description: Left over from PIZERO-148, which built the Orchestra-90CC's two DACs ($FF7A left, $FF7B right, src: coco_machine.cpp orch_write, a two-level audio integrator for exact timing) and proved them with docs/ay-checks/orch90.bas. The card's own music program is its cartridge ROM (XRoar loads it as 'orch90'); it is not on the card yet. Put the ROM on the card as a .ccc in /coco/cart, load it with F10 (orchestra90 = on, the CoCo Zero default; a stock machine needs it in the cartridge's own file), and play one of its songs on both outputs (the video cable and a USB DAC). Watch the [orch] writes counter and the frame time: the program mixes several voices in software and drives the DACs hard.

summary: A disk set to machine = coco3 runs on the CoCo 2: the switch says the card cannot start a CoCo 3, without saying why
description:
User report 2026-10-23: setting machine = coco3 in a disk's own file with TAB in the overlay is not recognized. Log of the user's try (3DGRAPH.DSK): the editor wrote 0:/coco/dsk/3DGRAPH.TXT, the launch read it ('[settings] machine=coco3 ...'), then '[machine] 0:/coco/dsk/3DGRAPH.DSK wants the CoCo 3, which the card cannot start: running it here'. So the file and the parse are right; machine_available(true) (src/main.cpp) said no: coco_boot_resolve found no coco3.rom in /coco/roms/ or /coco/, or f_stat gave a size other than 32,768. Earlier the same switch worked (SIERRA.TXT, RTSI.TXT, PIZERO-242), and that code is unchanged since. The message gives no reason, so the first step is to make it say which: not found, or found at PATH with N bytes.

[2026-10-23 Cause found with the new message: '[machine] coco3.rom not found in /coco/roms/ or /coco/'. The card had no coco3.rom anywhere (only bas12, extbas11, disk11, hdbdw3cc2 and coco.dsk in /coco/roms); it had one when SIERRA and RTSI switched (PIZERO-242), so it was lost when the card was rewritten. Copied ~/.xroar/roms/coco3.rom (32,768 bytes, sha1 e0d82953...) to /coco/roms/ at the user's request, the ._ file removed. machine_available now logs why it says no: not found, unreadable (FRESULT), or the wrong size. Open: whether the overlay should say so on screen and refuse the launch, rather than run the game on the CoCo 2 silently (asked the user).]

[2026-10-23 The user chose: show the message and do not launch. overlay_launch_request (src/main.cpp) now checks, before the overlay closes, whether a game set to the other machine can have it (machine_wanted, machine_available); if not, the launch is refused and the status line says 'NEEDS COCO3.ROM IN /COCO/ROMS' (or BAS12.ROM). With the ROM back, 3DGRAPH's switch then hit PIZERO-262 (the CoCo 3 did not start for lack of heap), now fixed.]

summary: The CoCo 3 no longer starts: today's RAM growth left the heap too small for its second 64 KB
description:
Found 2026-10-23 through PIZERO-261: with coco3.rom restored, 3DGRAPH's switch restarted the board as a CoCo 3 and it stopped on 'EMULATOR DID NOT START' (coco_machine_init failed). coco3_init (lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp) takes 64 KB from the rp_mem pool and 64 KB more from the heap, plus a few KB for its parts; the heap had 62,800 bytes free before the machine. Static RAM grew 81.8 to 85.7 percent on 2026-10-22/23 (PIZERO-250's stereo ring doubled it to 32 KB; PIZERO-148, PIZERO-255's USB audio, enumeration buffer and HID maps), which came out of the heap. The CoCo 3 was last confirmed on hardware at 81.8 percent (PIZERO-242); no build since was tried as a CoCo 3. My miss: the build rule (CLAUDE.md) says to test both machines when a change touches the machine core.

Fix: the audio ring back to 16 KB (AUDIO_RING_SAMPLES 4096 pairs; half full is about 43 ms, over five frames' bursts; the servo follows the size). The fault page's detail said 'ROM READ OK, 8192 BYTES' even for the CoCo 3's 32 KB ROM: it gives the real size now. The failure logs the free heap against what the machine needs.

[2026-10-23 Fixed on the board: product static RAM 82.6 percent (stream 82.3, wavmeas 78.9). Free heap 79,184 bytes before the machine (62,800 at 85.7); the CoCo 3 starts, 9,696 bytes left with its 128 KB, so it needs about 69.5 KB. CLAUDE.md's build rule now says to boot as a CoCo 3 and read '[mem] free heap N bytes with the CoCo 3's 128 KB' after any change that adds RAM. docs/pipeline.md says 4096-deep. Awaiting the user: 3DGRAPH on the CoCo 3, and sound on the smaller ring.] [2026-10-26 CLOSED in full on the user's word: the CoCo 3 starts on the product build (1f07938). No remainder filed, at the user's direction; the 3DGRAPH and smaller-ring sound checks were not done separately.]

summary: The CoCo 3 draws nothing: a black screen even at the BASIC prompt
description:
User report 2026-10-23, after PIZERO-262 got the CoCo 3 starting again (82.6 percent RAM, 79 KB heap, 9.7 KB left once it has its 128 KB). A disk set to machine = coco3 (a blank one made with N, TTTEST.DSK, autorun off) comes up black. Established:
- The launch path is right: the disk is made, its .TXT says machine = coco3, the launch reads it and goes to the BASIC prompt ('[launch] autorun = off: BASIC prompt'); the board is a CoCo 3 ('[boot] machine: CoCo 3', coco3.rom 32,768 bytes).
- The machine runs: [run] 60 fps, about 7.9 ms a frame of emulation, no freezes.
- The framebuffer itself is black: a screenshot (Ctrl-P over serial, /coco/screendumps/SCR0002.PNG, copied to .pio/shots) has every one of its 307,200 pixels at index 0. So the CoCo 3 writes nothing into g_fb; not the palette, not the TV.
- Ruled out by reading: the overlay invalidates the CoCo 3's line skipping every frame it is open (main.cpp, coco_machine_video_invalidate); coco_machine_set_framebuffer(g_fb) is called once at boot and nothing re-inits g_c3bus.fb; the GIME and coco3_bus code allocate nothing after start-up; the coco3_cpu_cycle changes since PIZERO-242 (the AY and Orchestra-90 hooks, which do nothing with those cartridges off as the coco3 profile has them, and the PIA audio hooks) do not touch the display.
- The CoCo 3 was last seen working on hardware at PIZERO-242 (commit 0ed0a64, 2026-10-21); about 40 commits since, all sound, USB and overlay work, none tried as a CoCo 3 (see PIZERO-262 and the build rule now in CLAUDE.md).
Next: bisect on the board between 0ed0a64 and HEAD (about 6 builds), building old commits in a scratch copy under .pio/ (git-ignored); the user was asked, the session ended before an answer. Also worth a look first: whether the CoCo 3's BASIC ever got going (a GIME register dump or the 6809 PC in the log), since nothing at all is drawn, not even the border.

[2026-10-23 Cause found: the card's coco3.rom was damaged, not the firmware. With the card in the Mac, /coco/roms/coco3.rom hashed e159b5d2... against e0d82953... for every good copy (~/.xroar/roms, ~/Downloads, the copy PIZERO-261 put there at 02:38). 801 bytes differ, all from offset $6C08 to the end ($EC08-$FFFF as the 6809 sees it), about 40 a page, the rest identical; the reset vector reads $CE19 instead of $8C1B. So the 6809 starts in the wrong place, BASIC never loads the GIME palette, and every pixel is colour 0, as the screenshot showed. The other ROMs match their references; every .TXT parses; the disk images are standard sizes (TextDemo.dsk's 159,488 is from 2001). fsck_msdos -n: no cross-links, 768 orphaned clusters (about 3 MB, the mark of an interrupted write). The good ROM is back on the card (verified), the damaged one kept at .pio/evidence/coco3.rom.card-damaged. Open: how a file the firmware only reads got rewritten in place (its date is still the Mac's 02:38 copy, so not through FatFs's f_write with its fixed date); a write into the wrong clusters while the card was swapped under a running board is the first suspect. Next: the user boots a coco3 game with the restored ROM.] [2026-10-26 CLOSED on the user's word: the CoCo 3 booted on the product build (1f07938) from a card with a good coco3.rom. The cause was the damaged ROM, not the firmware. The open question (how a file the firmware only reads came to be rewritten in place) moves to PIZERO-274.]

summary: Benchmark the 6809 emulation on the RP2350's RISC-V cores (Hazard3) against the Cortex-M33, using pizero_cpu179
description:
User request 2026-10-26, after a discussion of whether to use the RP2350's two RISC-V cores (Hazard3) instead of the two Cortex-M33s. Conclusion of that discussion: not worth switching the product on spec, but worth ONE measurement, because the 6809 interpreter is the only part of the firmware whose speed depends on the CPU core (video, USB and audio run mostly on PIO, DMA and the SIO TMDS encoder).

QUESTION: does the 6809 emulation run faster or slower per emulated cycle on Hazard3 than on the M33, with the same source and the same clock (252 MHz)?

EXPECTATION (unmeasured): about the same or slightly slower. Hazard3 is close to the M33 on CoreMark, GCC's Arm code generation is more mature, and branchy interpreter code tends to favour the Arm. Hazard3 has no FPU, no DSP/SIMD and no double coprocessor; that costs little today (lib/coco_machine/src/audio_lowpass.h uses double only to work out coefficients, then runs fixed-point).

BASELINE TO COMPARE AGAINST: PIZERO-130 and PIZERO-131. On the M33 the 6809 costs about 101-102 host clocks per emulated cycle (was 185.4 before PIZERO-131); env pizero_cpu179 (platformio.ini, CPU_SPEED_MUL=2, 29,830 cycles a frame) is the 1.79 MHz load. Method in PIZERO-130: BASIC prompt after autorun typed DIR, OPIL-EN.dsk in drive 0, keyboard attached, 3 minutes, scripts/soak.py record then analyse --kind bench, logs into docs/measurements/logs/. Re-run the Arm side on the same day and board rather than trusting the October numbers, since the firmware has grown since.

ARM-SPECIFIC CODE a RISC-V build must stub or replace (surveyed 2026-10-26):
- lib/xroar_core/include/cpu_prof.h: DWT CYCCNT at 0xE0001004 (PIZERO-209's profiler). RISC-V has the mcycle CSR. Only needed if the [prof] split is wanted; the bench needs only frame timing.
- src/wd_post.cpp lines ~96-129: Arm exception-frame reading and inline asm for the fault post-mortem. Stub out for the benchmark.
- src/main.cpp ~2443/2446: 'cpsid i' and 'udf #0' in the deliberate-fault test path. Guard with #ifdef __arm__.
- lib/libdvi/tmds_encode.S: Arm Thumb asm, used only by video_encoder = software. The default (hardware, the SIO TMDS encoder, PIZERO-175) does not need it; check whether the SIO encoder is reachable from Hazard3 as it is from the M33.
- lib/pico_pio_usb/src/pio_usb_ll.h:155: a run of nops in a timing path; harmless as asm but its timing assumes the M33. USB could simply be left out of the benchmark build if it misbehaves.
- __dmb() in src/main.cpp and lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp comes from the Pico SDK and exists on both architectures.

UNKNOWNS, to settle first (cheapest step): whether the earlephilhower arduino-pico core under PlatformIO (platform = maxgerhardt/platform-raspberrypi, board waveshare_rp2350_pizero) builds for RP2350 RISC-V, which option selects it, and whether the RISC-V toolchain is installed (~/.platformio/packages has toolchain-rp2040-earlephilhower from 2026-03-04; check whether it carries a riscv32 gcc). Also whether TinyUSB host and Pico-PIO-USB build for RISC-V; if not, a benchmark env without USB is enough, driving BASIC from the serial console (serial_keyboard = on).

DO: a new env pizero_cpu179_riscv extending pizero_cpu179 that builds for Hazard3 (a real env, never PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS, docs/BUILD.md §4b), with the Arm-only lines above guarded. Measure both envs on one board, same card and same scenario. Record emulation us per frame, host clocks per emulated cycle and fps for each; archive the logs with the git hash in docs/measurements/ and add a short result section to docs/coco3-feasibility.md. Note the env in docs/BUILD.md.

NOT IN SCOPE: switching the product to RISC-V, porting the fault post-mortem or the profiler properly, or mixed-architecture (one Arm core, one RISC-V core), which the hardware allows but neither the SDK nor arduino-pico supports.

DONE WHEN: the two numbers sit side by side in docs/coco3-feasibility.md with the logs archived, and the issue says in one line whether RISC-V is worth pursuing. If the RISC-V build cannot be made to run without large changes, closing with that finding and what blocked it counts as done.

summary: YMF262 (OPL3) FM sound, as on the MEGA mini MPI: emulate the chip at $FF50-$FF54
description:
User request 2026-10-26: emulate the Yamaha YMF262 (OPL3) FM synthesiser, as found in Ed Snider's (Zippster's) MEGA mini MPI (MMMPI), so CoCo software written for it plays on the CoCo Zero. No OPL3 issue existed here (searched issues.jsonl and docs/ 2026-10-26). Stock XRoar has no OPL3 or MMMPI emulation either (checked in ~/github/coco #580, 2026-10-14).

THE HARDWARE (from coco issue #580, which drives the chip from Forth on a real MMMPI; sources: MEGAmini manual thezippsterzone.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/MEGAmini-manual.pdf, Zippster's OPL3 article 2018-12-01, Yamaha YMF262 datasheet archive.org/details/yamaha-ymf-262-opl-3, Programmer's Guide fit.vutbr.cz/~arnost/opl/opl3.html):
- The OPL3 is a virtual Multi-Pak slot: software sets /SCS to virtual slot 5 in $FF7F (low nibble 0100), keeping the /CTS high nibble, and restores $FF7F afterwards.
- Ports in that slot: $FF50 port 0 register select (read = status), $FF51 port 0 data, $FF52 port 1 register select, $FF53 port 1 data, $FF54 read or write = chip reset.
- Chip clock 14.318 MHz, so the native sample rate is 14,318,180 / 288 = 49,716 Hz. Writes need 32 chip clocks (~2.2 us) after a register select.
- Audio reaches the CoCo through the cartridge SND line (an analog switch on the MMMPI, extended register $FF42 at virtual slot 16, bits 2-0 = 100 for the YMF262), and separately from the MMMPI's own stereo line-out.

HOW IT FITS THIS FIRMWARE (read 2026-10-26):
- There is no Multi-Pak emulation: every sound device sits at fixed addresses whatever $FF7F holds (docs/sound.md, 'At a glance'). The simplest decode is $FF50-$FF54 always, when the setting is on, as the CoCo PSG ($FF5D-$FF5F) and Symphony-12 ($FF60-$FF63) do. Decide whether to honour $FF7F's slot 5 too.
- COLLISION TO RESOLVE: $FF40-$FF5F is the cartridge I/O window in lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp (~line 1165, cart_io_write; ~788 and ~899 note that a bank-switched Games Master cartridge takes every odd address there). $FF51 and $FF53 are odd, so with a GMC image loaded the two would fight. On real hardware the MMMPI's slot select keeps them apart, which is the argument for honouring $FF7F.
- The RSDOS latch is $FF40-$FF47 and the FDC $FF48-$FF4B, so the disk controller does not overlap $FF50-$FF54. Check the decoding's mirrors anyway.
- Rendering: each chip renders once per 48 kHz output sample on core 0 (docs/sound.md, 'Rendering only what can change', PIZERO-248). The OPL3 runs at 49,716 Hz, so it needs resampling to 48 kHz, or a core that steps at an arbitrary rate. It is stereo, which the Symphony-12's stereo path already carries (symphony12_stereo, PIZERO-250).

THE RISK IS CPU TIME. Measured on the board (docs/sound.md): idle at the BASIC prompt about 6.9 ms of the 16.7 ms frame; every current sound source at once (docs/ay-checks/allvoice.bas) 9.3-9.7 ms; the four Symphony-12 AYs about 1.6 ms after PIZERO-248's skipping work. An OPL3 has 36 operators with phase generators, envelopes and a log-sin/exp path per sample, which is far heavier than an AY. A CoCo 3 at 1.79 MHz leaves less room still (PIZERO-131). RAM is tight too: the CoCo 3 takes 64 KB of its RAM from the heap, and static growth stops it starting (CLAUDE.md, PIZERO-262), so boot as a CoCo 3 and read '[mem] free heap' after adding the core.

CANDIDATE CORES (verify each licence against XRoar's GPL before use; none measured on this board yet):
- Nuked-OPL3: cycle-accurate, the reference for correctness, generally reported as the most expensive.
- ymfm (Aaron Giles, BSD-3, C++): covers OPL, OPL2 and OPL3, between the two in cost.
- DOSBox's DBOPL: built for speed.
- emu8950 (Mitsutaka Okazaki): OPL2/Y8950 only, but Graham Sanderson's optimised build ran OPL2 music on an RP2040 in rp2040-doom. Possibly a template for an OPL3-lite, or a fallback that covers OPL2-compatible register use.

PLAN:
1. SPIKE: build two candidate cores as a host test and on the board, render a busy patch set (all 18 two-operator channels keyed) and an idle chip, and measure ms per frame on core 0. Also measure the cost when nothing has been written, which must be about zero (render only once the chip has been written, as the SN76489 does). Record the numbers in docs/sound.md or docs/measurements/. If no core fits beside the CoCo 2 at 60 fps, stop and record why.
2. Integrate the chosen core: lib/coco_machine/src/ beside psg_ay8910.h, with SOUND_HOT / SOUND_TABLE placement as the AY has, the address decode above, stereo into the existing L/R mix, and a host test in the style of test_psg_ay8910.
3. A setting, opl3 = on | off, following the device pattern in docs/sound.md (on in the cocozero profile, off on the stock coco2 and coco3, a game's own file can change it). Document it in SETTINGS.md and docs/sound.md (the 'At a glance' table, its cost, telemetry like '[ay] writes=N').
4. Test with real MMMPI OPL3 software, or with coco #580's Forth demo once that exists (it is still open there). XRoar cannot cross-check, so a host render of a register log against a reference core is the check.

NOT IN SCOPE: the rest of the MMMPI (its UART B at $FF50-$FF5B in virtual slot 6, the extended MPI registers, slot switching for real cartridges), the cartridge-SND analog switch beyond what is needed to hear the chip, and OPL2-only cards.

DONE WHEN: an OPL3 program plays on the board as a CoCo 2 at 60 fps with no audio underruns, its cost is measured and written into docs/sound.md, and the setting is documented. The CoCo 3, a GMC loaded at the same time, and further software can be follow-up issues.

summary: 4-bit framebuffer: halve g_fb from 150 KB to 75 KB
description:
User request 2026-10-26: recover RAM. This is the largest single win.

TODAY: g_fb is 640 x 240 at 8 bits per pixel, indexed through g_pal565[256] (src/main.cpp ~236-249, the VIDEO_640 path, FB640_W 640, FRAME_HEIGHT 240): 153,600 bytes, the biggest object in RAM.

WHY 4 BITS IS ENOUGH: the GIME has 16 palette registers, so every CoCo 3 mode shows at most 16 colours at once; the CoCo 2's palette is already 16 entries (PAL_VDG, g_pal565[80..95]). A nibble per pixel holds either. 640 x 240 / 2 = 76,800 bytes, saving 76,800.

WHAT GETS IN THE WAY:
- The overlay, boot pages and cards draw in their own entries (PAL_CARD at g_pal565[64..], 'factory green on black, whatever the palette holds', PIZERO-256), outside the 16. Options: reserve two of the 16 while a card is up and restore them after, swap the 16-entry palette while the overlay shows, or give the overlay a small buffer of its own. A CoCo 3 program can use all 16 colours, so reserving slots permanently is out.
- CoCo 2 artifact colours: check whether the VDG renderer produces any colour outside its 16 entries.
- Core 1's scanline encoder reads g_fb per line; it must unpack nibbles through the palette. Re-measure its per-line budget (PIZERO-36, PIZERO-175 have the method) and the video modes' render cost on core 0 (PIZERO-218), since every renderer writes nibbles instead of bytes.
- Every renderer that writes g_fb (VDG, GIME modes, 80-column text, the overlay's text, screenshots, PIZERO-165) changes.

BONUS: two 75 KB buffers are the size of today's one, so this is also the route to double buffering on the CoCo 3 without tearing (PIZERO-217).

Numbers from the product build at 1f07938 (arm-none-eabi-nm -S --size-sort on .pio/build/pizero_stream_60/firmware.elf, 2026-10-26): .bss 355,192 bytes, .data 77,736, heap at link 90,968; the CoCo 3 takes 64 KB of its 128 KB from the heap (g_pool, 64 KB in lib/psram_stub/rp_pico_alloc.c, is the first 64 KB), and PIZERO-262 showed static growth stops it starting (at 85.7% RAM it failed; 82.6% leaves about 9.7 KB). CHECK FOR ANY CHANGE HERE: boot as a CoCo 3 and read the serial line '[mem] free heap N bytes with the CoCo 3's 128 KB' before and after (CLAUDE.md). Long-term fix for all of this is PSRAM (PIZERO-244, the Waveshare PSRAM board; PIZERO-01: the PiZero's PSRAM pad is unpopulated).

DONE WHEN: the product build runs both machines with a 4-bit framebuffer, at 60 fps with no audio shortfall in the PIZERO-218 scenarios, the overlay and boot pages look as before, and the CoCo 3's free heap has grown by about 75 KB. Double buffering is a follow-up under PIZERO-217.

summary: Audit the 78 KB of code in RAM: move what does not need RAM speed back to flash
description:
User request 2026-10-26: recover RAM.

TODAY: about 78 KB of functions and tables are placed in SRAM (.data holds 77,736 bytes; functions in the 0x2000_0000 range by nm total 78,099). The largest: mc6809_run 18,286, ea_indexed 5,272, coco_mem_cycle 3,488, coco3_cpu_cycle 2,576, coco_mem_nvma 2,376, coco_mem_tick 2,324, g_gm_lut 2,052, coco_machine_render_frame 1,980, audio_catch_up_run 1,674, font_6847t1 1,536, ay_render 1,484, initialize_host_programs 1,456, three copies of pio_usb_ll_encode_tx_data (1,260 + 1,210 + 1,184), dvi_dma_irq_handler 1,236, pio_usb_host_frame 1,032, __malloc_av_ 1,032, mc6883_mem_cycle 972, audio_emit 958, sd_card 728, dcd_event_handler 676.

KEEP IN RAM: the 6809 core and the bus path (PIZERO-131, PIZERO-213 put them there for speed: about 40 KB), the DVI IRQ and data-island encoder (PIZERO-37), the sound render path (SOUND_HOT / SOUND_TABLE, PIZERO-248), and anything that runs while flash is unavailable.

CANDIDATES TO MOVE: code that runs once or rarely (initialize_host_programs runs at USB start), SD and FatFs paths outside the disk-transfer loop, TinyUSB device-side code (dcd_event_handler: the board is a USB device only for the serial console), and duplicated constprop copies. Find where each comes from (__not_in_flash_func, __time_critical_func, a linker section, or the SDK or library defaults) before moving it.

METHOD: one move at a time, then measure on the board: [run] frame timing at the BASIC prompt and in a game (PIZERO-130's scenario), and USB keyboard, gamepad and DAC still working. The 64 KB of USB, SD and libdvi defaults are not ours to change lightly; prefer our own attributes first.

Numbers from the product build at 1f07938 (arm-none-eabi-nm -S --size-sort on .pio/build/pizero_stream_60/firmware.elf, 2026-10-26): .bss 355,192 bytes, .data 77,736, heap at link 90,968; the CoCo 3 takes 64 KB of its 128 KB from the heap (g_pool, 64 KB in lib/psram_stub/rp_pico_alloc.c, is the first 64 KB), and PIZERO-262 showed static growth stops it starting (at 85.7% RAM it failed; 82.6% leaves about 9.7 KB). CHECK FOR ANY CHANGE HERE: boot as a CoCo 3 and read the serial line '[mem] free heap N bytes with the CoCo 3's 128 KB' before and after (CLAUDE.md). Long-term fix for all of this is PSRAM (PIZERO-244, the Waveshare PSRAM board; PIZERO-01: the PiZero's PSRAM pad is unpopulated).

DONE WHEN: at least 10 KB is back in the heap with no measurable slowdown, the moves and their measurements are listed in this issue, and docs/BUILD.md notes the rule for what may live in RAM.

summary: Run the CoCo ROMs from flash instead of a 32 KB RAM copy
description:
User request 2026-10-26: recover RAM.

TODAY: g_coco_rom is a 32 KB static buffer (src/main.cpp:689, PIZERO-133; a CoCo 2 uses only its first 16 KB), filled from /coco/roms on the card at every boot (coco_boot_load_rom_from_sd / coco_boot_load_coco3_rom, src/coco_boot.cpp ~558-600).

IDEA: keep a copy of the machine ROM in a reserved flash area and let the 6809 read it through XIP. At boot, compare the card's file with the flash copy (a hash, which PIZERO-264 is adding anyway) and reprogram the area only when they differ. Saves 32 KB of static RAM.

RISKS TO MEASURE FIRST:
- Speed: BASIC runs from ROM, so instruction fetches would go through the XIP cache (16 KB). Measure host clocks per emulated cycle at the BASIC prompt and in a ROM-heavy loop against today (PIZERO-130's method). If it is slower, stop here and record it.
- Flash writes stall XIP for both cores: core 1 is scanning out video, and the DVI IRQ and its data must be in RAM. Program the area before the DVI starts, or with core 1 parked (arduino-pico has rp2040.idleOtherCore for flash writes). Today setup() brings the DVI up before mount_sd (src/main.cpp ~2168-2178), so the order matters.
- Check how the machine reads ROM: if lib/coco_machine takes a pointer, the change is mostly where the bytes live; if it copies, that copy has to go too.
- Wear: one write each time the ROM file changes, which is negligible.

Numbers from the product build at 1f07938 (arm-none-eabi-nm -S --size-sort on .pio/build/pizero_stream_60/firmware.elf, 2026-10-26): .bss 355,192 bytes, .data 77,736, heap at link 90,968; the CoCo 3 takes 64 KB of its 128 KB from the heap (g_pool, 64 KB in lib/psram_stub/rp_pico_alloc.c, is the first 64 KB), and PIZERO-262 showed static growth stops it starting (at 85.7% RAM it failed; 82.6% leaves about 9.7 KB). CHECK FOR ANY CHANGE HERE: boot as a CoCo 3 and read the serial line '[mem] free heap N bytes with the CoCo 3's 128 KB' before and after (CLAUDE.md). Long-term fix for all of this is PSRAM (PIZERO-244, the Waveshare PSRAM board; PIZERO-01: the PiZero's PSRAM pad is unpopulated).

DONE WHEN: both machines boot from a flash-resident ROM, the speed difference is measured and written here, and the CoCo 3's free heap has grown by about 32 KB. If XIP is too slow, closing with the measurement counts as done.

summary: Allocate the 16 KB cartridge buffer only when a cartridge is loaded
description:
User request 2026-10-26: recover RAM.

TODAY: g_cart_rom[COCO_CART_MAX] is a 16 KB static buffer (src/main.cpp ~696-700; 8 KB in builds that define the smaller size), held whether or not a cartridge is in. Bank-switched Games Master images (32-256 KB, PIZERO-142) are read differently and should be checked so this does not break them.

IDEA: allocate it when a cartridge is loaded and free it when it is removed. A session without a cartridge gets 16 KB more heap.

CAVEAT: a CoCo 3 with a cartridge still needs the 16 KB, so this helps the CoCo 3 only when no cartridge is in. Allocate the cartridge before the CoCo 3's 64 KB so a failure is reported clearly (the 'EMULATOR DID NOT START' page) rather than as a crash; check that the order of allocations does not fragment the heap.

Numbers from the product build at 1f07938 (arm-none-eabi-nm -S --size-sort on .pio/build/pizero_stream_60/firmware.elf, 2026-10-26): .bss 355,192 bytes, .data 77,736, heap at link 90,968; the CoCo 3 takes 64 KB of its 128 KB from the heap (g_pool, 64 KB in lib/psram_stub/rp_pico_alloc.c, is the first 64 KB), and PIZERO-262 showed static growth stops it starting (at 85.7% RAM it failed; 82.6% leaves about 9.7 KB). CHECK FOR ANY CHANGE HERE: boot as a CoCo 3 and read the serial line '[mem] free heap N bytes with the CoCo 3's 128 KB' before and after (CLAUDE.md). Long-term fix for all of this is PSRAM (PIZERO-244, the Waveshare PSRAM board; PIZERO-01: the PiZero's PSRAM pad is unpopulated).

DONE WHEN: no static cartridge buffer remains, cartridges (a 16 KB ROM pack, a Games Master image, a disk controller) still work on both machines, and the free-heap gain is measured with and without a cartridge.

summary: Trim the framebuffer to the 225 lines the CoCo 3 can show, with solid borders
description:
User request 2026-10-26: recover RAM.

TODAY: g_fb has FRAME_HEIGHT = 240 rows of 640 bytes (src/main.cpp:159, 242), line-doubled to 480 on screen. The CoCo 3's tallest mode is 225 lines and the CoCo 2's 192, so the top and bottom rows only ever hold border colour.

IDEA: store 225 rows and have core 1's scanline encoder send the border colour for the rest. Saves 15 x 640 = 9,600 bytes at 8 bits per pixel (4,800 if PIZERO-268 lands first).

CHECK FIRST: whether anything draws into those border rows: the overlay, the boot pages and cards (PIZERO-92, PIZERO-256), the info page (PIZERO-156), and screenshots (PIZERO-165), which save the whole 640 x 240 frame.

Numbers from the product build at 1f07938 (arm-none-eabi-nm -S --size-sort on .pio/build/pizero_stream_60/firmware.elf, 2026-10-26): .bss 355,192 bytes, .data 77,736, heap at link 90,968; the CoCo 3 takes 64 KB of its 128 KB from the heap (g_pool, 64 KB in lib/psram_stub/rp_pico_alloc.c, is the first 64 KB), and PIZERO-262 showed static growth stops it starting (at 85.7% RAM it failed; 82.6% leaves about 9.7 KB). CHECK FOR ANY CHANGE HERE: boot as a CoCo 3 and read the serial line '[mem] free heap N bytes with the CoCo 3's 128 KB' before and after (CLAUDE.md). Long-term fix for all of this is PSRAM (PIZERO-244, the Waveshare PSRAM board; PIZERO-01: the PiZero's PSRAM pad is unpopulated).

DONE WHEN: g_fb holds 225 rows, both machines' modes and every overlay page look as before, screenshots still save the full frame, and the heap gain is measured.
