summary: Find how coco3.rom on the card was rewritten in place (801 bytes changed from $6C08, PIZERO-263)
description: Remainder of PIZERO-263, filed 2026-10-26 when it closed. On 2026-10-23 the card's /coco/roms/coco3.rom was the right size (32,768) but 801 bytes differed from every good copy, all from offset $6C08 to the end, about 40 a page; the reset vector read $CE19 instead of $8C1B, so the CoCo 3 drew nothing. The firmware only reads ROMs (read_rom_file, src/coco_boot.cpp ~104), and the file kept the Mac's 02:38 copy date, so it was not rewritten through FatFs's f_write with its fixed date. fsck_msdos -n on that card found no cross-links but 768 orphaned clusters (about 3 MB), the mark of an interrupted write. First suspect: a write landing in the wrong clusters while the card was swapped under a running board (the firmware writes settings.txt, drives.txt, laststate.txt, log/boards.txt and screenshots). The damaged copy is kept at .pio/evidence/coco3.rom.card-damaged. DO: compare the damaged bytes with what the firmware writes (settings text, screenshot PNG data, the boards.txt line) to identify the source; check whether the firmware can write after the card is pulled (no card-detect use: GPIO 22 is unused, src/hw_config.c); consider unmounting or refusing writes when a write fails. PIZERO-264 (hash each ROM before it loads) would catch the symptom. DONE WHEN: the source of the bad bytes is named, or ruled down to 'not from the firmware' with the evidence, and any firmware fix is filed or made.

summary: Clock for CoCo software: emulate a real CoCo clock cartridge so NitrOS-9 and BASIC programs read the date and time
description: User request 2026-10-26: expose the board's clock to the emulated machine. WHAT THE BOARD HAS (PIZERO-201, done): the RP2350 has no RTC block and this board no RTC chip or backup cell. The power manager's always-on timer (pico/aon_timer.h) runs while powered and survives a watchdog reboot but is zero at power-on; src/coco_boot.cpp:318-379 starts it at boot from the newest modification time of the card's own files plus one minute, so it is approximate after a power cut and drifts with the crystal. It is a register read, so serving it on the bus is free. THE OBVIOUS WAY: emulate a clock chip that real CoCo software already drives, rather than invent a register, so NitrOS-9 Level 1 and 2 (PIZERO-199, PIZERO-236) keep time with their stock clock2 module and the date stamps on files it writes become real. Candidates to check in the NitrOS-9 source (level1/modules/clock2_*.asm, not in ~/github on 2026-10-26, fetch it): the Disto and Burke and Burke cartridges (OKI MSM5832 style, believed to sit in the $FF50 area, which collides with the Games Master Cartridge's odd mirrors of $FF41 in $FF40-$FF5F and with PIZERO-267's OPL3 at $FF50-$FF54) and the SmartWatch (DS1216 under the ROM, which needs a read-sequence unlock on ROM accesses, invasive on the hot path). Pick the one that is supported by the most software and collides with nothing, and say why in the issue. DO: (1) the chosen chip's registers on the bus, reading the aon timer and converting to its BCD fields; (2) writes from the guest set the aon timer (aon_timer_set_time_calendar), so OS-9's setime corrects the approximate seed for the rest of the session; (3) setting clock = on|off, default on (an improvement, CLAUDE.md), off for a program that probes the area for something else; (4) a NitrOS-9 boot disk built with that clock2 module, and a short BASIC program in docs/ that prints the time. NOT IN SCOPE: keeping time across a power cut (no cell; a battery-backed RTC on I2C0 GPIO 6/7 would be its own hardware issue) and getting the time from the network or USB.

summary: Chip temperature readable by CoCo programs from a CoCo Zero board register
description: User request 2026-10-26: expose the RP2350's temperature sensor to the emulated machine. WHAT THE BOARD HAS: the on-chip sensor on ADC channel 8 of the RP2350B (no GPIO), already read by analogReadTemp() for the F1 INFO page (PIZERO-156, PIZERO-206). It is rough, a few degrees, and reads the die, not the room. No CoCo device ever had a temperature sensor, so there is no software to stay compatible with: this is a new register. THE BOARD REGISTER BLOCK (shared by PIZERO-276 and PIZERO-277, decide it once in whichever lands first): a small read-mostly block in a free part of the I/O page, proposed $FF6C-$FF6F, with a fixed signature byte so a program can tell it is on a CoCo Zero before trusting the others. $FF60-$FF63 is the Symphony-12, $FF7A-$FF7B Orchestra-90, $FF7D-$FF7E the speech device, $FF7F the Multi-Pak select (docs/sound.md lines 12-18 and 232-297); the CoCo 2 decodes nothing at $FF60-$FFBF and the CoCo 3 GIME starts at $FF90, so $FF64-$FF79 looks free on both, but check it against the bus slow path in lib/coco_machine and against PIZERO-267's OPL3 plan before fixing the address. Document it in docs/ beside the sound chip map, with a BASIC example (PEEK). DO: (1) one register returning whole degrees C as a signed byte (and perhaps a second with tenths), from a value cached once a second in the frame's slack after emulation, never by an ADC conversion on the bus access itself (a conversion is microseconds and the ADC is shared); (2) a setting to hide the block, default on per the improvements rule; (3) a BASIC example that prints it. NOT IN SCOPE: calibrating the sensor, and acting on the temperature (throttling).

summary: Hardware random numbers for CoCo programs: a TRNG register, and BASIC's RND seeded from it at power-on
description: User request 2026-10-26: expose the RP2350's random number generator to the emulated machine. WHAT THE BOARD HAS: the RP2350 has a true random number generator peripheral (TRNG), reached through the SDK's pico_rand (get_rand_32), which mixes it with other entropy. A real CoCo has none: BASIC's RND is a pseudo-random sequence from a fixed seed, so every power-on gives the same numbers until a program reseeds it (RND with a negative argument, or a seed from TIMER). THE BOARD REGISTER BLOCK (shared by PIZERO-276 and PIZERO-277, decide it once in whichever lands first): a small read-mostly block in a free part of the I/O page, proposed $FF6C-$FF6F, with a fixed signature byte so a program can tell it is on a CoCo Zero before trusting the others. $FF60-$FF63 is the Symphony-12, $FF7A-$FF7B Orchestra-90, $FF7D-$FF7E the speech device, $FF7F the Multi-Pak select (docs/sound.md lines 12-18 and 232-297); the CoCo 2 decodes nothing at $FF60-$FFBF and the CoCo 3 GIME starts at $FF90, so $FF64-$FF79 looks free on both, but check it against the bus slow path in lib/coco_machine and against PIZERO-267's OPL3 plan before fixing the address. Document it in docs/ beside the sound chip map, with a BASIC example (PEEK). DO: (1) a read-only register returning a fresh random byte on every read, served from a small buffer refilled in the frame's slack so a read on the bus costs nothing (check the TRNG's rate and whether get_rand_32 blocks before deciding the buffer size); (2) settings key rnd_seed = on|off, default on (an improvement): at each reset, write a random seed into Color BASIC's RND seed bytes (find their address in the Color BASIC and CoCo 3 ROMs, it differs if the ROM moved it), so RND differs from one power-on to the next; off gives the authentic fixed sequence back, for a game or test that relies on it, in its own NAME.TXT; (3) a BASIC example. CHECK: that seeding at reset does not upset the cold-start check or a program that saves and compares the seed, and that the NitrOS-9 boot is unaffected.

summary: SID sound chip as on the CoCoXSID cartridge ($FF40-$FF58), with the slot select it needs beside the disk controller
description:
User request 2026-10-26: emulate the SID chip as found on the CoCoXSID cartridge, so CoCo software written for it plays on the CoCo Zero. Reference: ~/github/soundchips/sid.md (the CoCoXSID section and register map, read 2026-10-26; commit 5fce9ac there) and its datasheet datasheets/mos-6581.pdf. Stock XRoar has no SID emulation, so CoCoXSID software runs only on real hardware today.

THE HARDWARE (from sid.md): CoCoXSID, prototyped by Sheldon MacDonald and built by Brendan Donahe, is a cartridge for the CoCo 1, 2 and 3 holding an xSID or SwinSID (both software SIDs on a microcontroller), not an original 6581/8580. Its 25 write registers keep the C64 layout moved from $D400 to $FF40: voice 1 $FF40-$FF46, voice 2 $FF47-$FF4D, voice 3 $FF4E-$FF54, filter cutoff $FF55-$FF56, resonance and routing $FF57, mode and volume $FF58. The four C64 read registers would be $FF59-$FF5C; whether the cartridge answers reads is not known. Mono per cartridge, to the CoCo SND pin or an external jack; two cartridges in a Multi-Pak (slots 1 and 2, a Y cable) give 6-voice stereo. The forum MML player's note table assumes a 1.000 MHz SID clock, not the CoCo's 0.894886 MHz E clock; no source says what the board supplies, so start with 1 MHz and check by ear against a known tune.

SOFTWARE TO TEST WITH (sid.md, disks at polylith.com/CoCoXSID and the smdreloaded.com programming thread): Quarx (CoCo 3, cartridge in MPI slot 1), Bike Racer (bike.bin is the SID build), Sheldon's stereo SID Player for .MDM files (slots 1 and 2), and the MML player example with mml.dsk.

HOW IT FITS THIS FIRMWARE (read 2026-10-26):
- COLLISION, the main design question: $FF40-$FF5F is the cartridge I/O window. The Disk BASIC controller uses $FF40 (drive latch) and $FF48-$FF4B (WD179x), the Games Master Cartridge's SN76489 answers the odd mirrors of $FF41 there (lib/coco_machine/src/cart_gmc.h, csg_on_latch_mirror), and PIZERO-267's OPL3 wants $FF50-$FF54. The SID overlaps all three. On real hardware the Multi-Pak's $FF7F slot select keeps them apart, and the CoCoXSID software expects to select its slot; there is no Multi-Pak emulation here (every sound device answers at fixed addresses whatever $FF7F holds, docs/sound.md). So this needs at least a minimal $FF7F model: the SCS nibble picks which device answers $FF40-$FF5F, with the disk controller in its slot and the SID in slot 1 (and a second SID in slot 2). That model is shared with PIZERO-267; whichever lands first builds it. A program that never touches $FF7F with a disk mounted must keep working exactly as today.
- The CoCo PSG at $FF5D-$FF5F does not overlap the write registers; check it against the read registers $FF59-$FF5C.
- Rendering: each chip renders once per 48 kHz output sample on core 0 (docs/sound.md, 'Rendering only what can change', PIZERO-248). Stereo for two cartridges goes into the existing L/R mix (symphony12_stereo, PIZERO-250).

THE RISK IS CPU TIME, BUT THE BAR IS LOW: the real cartridge carries a SwinSID or xSID, a software SID on a small microcontroller, so matching it does not need a cycle-exact 6581. Measured on the board (docs/sound.md): idle at the BASIC prompt about 6.9 ms of the 16.7 ms frame as a CoCo 2; the four Symphony-12 AYs about 1.6 ms; a full-screen loop on the 1.79 MHz CoCo 3 about 13.7 ms (docs/coco3-retrospective.md), and Quarx is a CoCo 3 title, so the CoCo 3 budget matters here. reSID (the accurate one) is far too heavy: Pico-based SID replacements give it a whole core. RAM is tight: boot as a CoCo 3 and read '[mem] free heap' after adding the core (CLAUDE.md, PIZERO-262).

CANDIDATE CORES (verify each licence against XRoar's GPL before use; none measured on this board yet): a light SID core with a simple state-variable filter (Hermit's cSID-light is one example), and reSID or reSIDfp only as the host-side reference for checking output, not for the board.

PLAN:
1. SPIKE: build a candidate core as a host test and on the board, render three gated voices with the filter on, and measure ms per frame on core 0 as a CoCo 2 and a CoCo 3; also the cost before the chip is ever written, which must be about zero. Record the numbers in docs/sound.md. If it does not fit beside the CoCo 3 at 60 fps, record why and say what does fit (the CoCo 2 only, or no filter).
2. The minimal $FF7F slot model above, with the disk controller, GMC and SID each in a slot.
3. Integrate the core in lib/coco_machine/src/ beside psg_ay8910.h, with SOUND_HOT / SOUND_TABLE placement as the AY has, a host test in the style of test_psg_ay8910, and telemetry like '[ay] writes=N'.
4. A setting, sid = on | off (and perhaps sid_stereo for the second cartridge), following the device pattern in docs/sound.md: on in the cocozero profile, off on stock coco2 and coco3, changeable in a game's own file. Document it in SETTINGS.md and the docs/sound.md 'At a glance' table.
5. Test with Bike Racer and the MML player, then Quarx on the CoCo 3.

NOT IN SCOPE: the paddle inputs, 6581-versus-8580 filter and combined-waveform differences, volume-register sample playback beyond what falls out of the core, and the rest of the Multi-Pak (switching real cartridge ROMs).

DONE WHEN: a CoCoXSID program plays on the board with no audio underruns and the disk controller still works beside it, its cost is measured and written into docs/sound.md, and the setting is documented. Stereo, the CoCo 3 if it does not fit at first, and more software can be follow-up issues.

summary: Interactive I/O page map: where each sound chip sits, and which live beside Disk BASIC without a slot switch
description: User request 2026-10-26: an interactive SVG of the $FF00-$FFFF I/O page showing where every sound device, shipped and planned, sits, and which of them work beside Disk BASIC without a Multi-Pak slot switch. Lives at docs/io-map.svg, opened directly in a browser (it carries its own script). Facts it is drawn from (read 2026-10-26): the disk controller decode in lib/coco_machine/src/coco_machine.cpp fdc_io_write (A & 0xF: drive latch at offsets 0-7, WD279x at 8-B, C-F ignored) repeats over $FF40-$FF5F, so the latch also answers $FF41-$FF47 and $FF50-$FF57 and the WD $FF58-$FF5B, but Disk BASIC and OS-9 use only $FF40 and $FF48-$FF4B; the SN76489 takes the odd latch mirrors (cart_gmc.h csg_on_latch_mirror, (a & 9) == 1); the AY front-ends, Orchestra-90, GIME timer ($FF90-$FF95) and palette ($FFB0-$FFBF) are decoded ahead of the PIAs and cart window (coco_machine.cpp ~1144-1165); docs/sound.md 'At a glance'; the planned OPL3 (PIZERO-267, $FF50-$FF54), SID (PIZERO-278, $FF40-$FF58 write, $FF59-$FF5C read) and Speech/Sound cartridge (PIZERO-249, $FF7D-$FF7E). Verdict it shows: everything shipped coexists with Disk BASIC; the OPL3 would too, on latch mirrors Disk BASIC never uses, but it clashes with the always-on SN76489 at $FF51 and $FF53; the SID cannot, since its voice registers sit on $FF40 and $FF48-$FF4B themselves. DO: the SVG, a link to it from docs/sound.md. Keep it in step when a device is added or moved. NOT IN SCOPE: deciding the Multi-Pak model (PIZERO-267, PIZERO-278) or the board register address (PIZERO-276, PIZERO-277). DONE 2026-10-28: the user opened the map and confirmed it works and is useful.

summary: PSRAM sample bring-up firmware: detect the chip's size, test all of it, and measure CoCo RAM speed from PSRAM
description: Filed 2026-10-29 when the user sent Waveshare an RFQ to fit 8 MB or 16 MB PSRAM (PIZERO-244). Have the test firmware ready before the samples arrive, so they can be judged in a day. WHAT IS THERE: the U1 footprint shares the QSPI bus with the flash, chip select GPIO 47 with a 10K pull-up R39 (docs/supplier-primer.md section 6). The earlephilhower core already supports PSRAM: build with -DRP2350_PSRAM_CS=47 and cores/rp2040/psram.cpp runs psram_init at startup, sizes the chip (__psram_size) and provides pmalloc() and the PSRAM attribute; checked in ~/.platformio/packages/framework-arduinopico 2026-10-29, not yet tried on this board. Today the firmware links lib/psram_stub (rp_mem_malloc on a 64 KB SRAM pool), the no-PSRAM stand-in for the upstream psramlib the AMOLED port used. DO: (1) a diagnostic env (pizero_psram) with the flag set, documented in docs/BUILD.md; (2) at boot log '[psram] N bytes' and show it on the F1 INFO page; a board with no chip must boot exactly as today, so check what psram_init does with nothing fitted; (3) a memory test over the whole chip (walking bits and address-in-address), logged pass or fail; (4) the speed question the order hangs on: put the CoCo's RAM in PSRAM and run the 1.79 MHz CoCo 3 frame-time benchmarks (docs/coco3-feasibility.md, the full-screen HCLS loop at about 13.7 ms of 16.7 ms from SRAM) and a random-access worst case, and record ms per frame and late frames in docs/measurements/. If a 128 KB CoCo 3 from PSRAM holds 60 fps, the 512 KB CoCo 3 is the next issue. Before samples arrive, (1) and (2) can be built and run on the stock board to prove the no-chip path. NOT IN SCOPE: the 512 KB CoCo 3 itself, and moving other buffers into PSRAM (PIZERO-268 to PIZERO-273 recover SRAM by other means).

summary: Second USB host on the native USB-C port (the RP2350's own controller), once a debug probe replaces USB flashing and serial
description: Filed 2026-10-29 as future work, at the user's request, after discussing the board's SWD debug header (H1, RUN & DEBUG: SWCLK, GND, SWDIO). IDEA: once a debug probe takes over flashing (SWD) and the log (the probe's UART on GPIO 0/1, as pizero_fdctrace_uart already does with Serial1), the native USB-C port is no longer needed as a USB device, and the RP2350's built-in USB controller can run as a host. That gives a second USB host beside the PIO-USB one (D+ GPIO 28, D- 29, Pico-PIO-USB under Adafruit TinyUSB 3.7.7, docs/usb-retrospective.md), done in hardware rather than on PIO, still full speed (12 Mbit/s). WHY IT MATTERS: (a) hot-plug: PIZERO-51 found the PIO-USB host never notices a device plugged in after boot and every software path failed; the native controller has its own connect and disconnect detection, so test hot-plug there FIRST, since a yes settles what PIZERO-51 should recommend (for example, the keyboard on the native port); (b) CPU: the native controller does in hardware what PIO-USB does in software; (c) a second root port, independent of the PIO-USB library's hub handling (PIZERO-54, PIZERO-159). PROBLEMS TO SOLVE: (1) POWER, the main one. Read from the schematic (docs/RP2350-PiZero-schematic.pdf), not yet measured: the native port's VBUS is the board's 5 V input (through D1 to VSYS) and the same VBUS net feeds the PIO-USB port's devices; the 40-pin header's pins 2 and 4 are also labelled VBUS. As a host the native port must supply 5 V, so power would come in on those header pins or through a powered hub. Check with a meter before connecting anything, since a wrong guess back-feeds a supply. A POWERED HUB on the native port powers its devices but not the board (a hub must not drive VBUS upstream), and a self-powered hub often waits for upstream VBUS before connecting at all, so the board's VBUS must still be live: feeding 5 V into header pins 2 and 4 covers both the board and the hub's upstream sense. Measure a hub's upstream lead with only the hub powered first: some cheap hubs back-feed 5 V against the spec, which would fight the header supply. (2) The cable: the native port presents Rd (5.1K on CC) as a sink; the firmware ignores CC, so a USB-C OTG adapter (C plug to A socket) or a USB-C hub should work, but try it. (3) Software: the earlephilhower core runs the native port as a device for USB serial; host mode there means changing the core's USB setup. Whether TinyUSB can run two host ports at once (native rhport plus PIO-USB) is not known; if not, one port runs without TinyUSB, which is more work. (4) Losing USB flashing and serial: with this on, the probe is the only easy way back, the BOOTSEL button the last resort. FIRST STEP: a standalone test build with a USB keyboard on the native port: does it enumerate, and does it come back after unplug and replug. NOT IN SCOPE: making this the product configuration (the kit's users have no probe, so the product keeps USB serial and flashing on the native port unless a later decision changes that). DEPENDS ON: a debug probe (Raspberry Pi Debug Probe, or a Pico running debugprobe) and a PlatformIO debug setup (debug_tool = cmsis-dap).
